articles.title_original: MXene-based sensors for PFAS and micro/nanoplastics detection: Fabrication strategies, sensing mechanisms, and analytical performance
articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene Sensors for PFAS and Microplastic Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Emerging contaminants, including microplastics (MPs), nanoplastics (NPs), and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), have come to the forefront of environmental research due to their bioaccumulation potential, persistence, and related environmental and health impacts. One of the major challenges in managing these contaminants is their accurate detection and quantification in complex environmental samples. Although a wide range of detection platforms have been reported, achieving high sensitivity, selectivity, stability, and real-time monitoring remains an ongoing scientific hurdle. This review critically examines the recent progress and emerging opportunities of MXene-based sensors for the detection of MPs/NPs and PFAS in aqueous environments. Particular focus is given to MXene synthesis and functionalization strategies, sensor fabrication approaches, detection mechanisms, and analytical performance. The relationships between material synthesis, physicochemical properties, and sensing performance are also explored, providing insights into the rational design of MXene-enabled sensing platforms. Furthermore, key technological barriers, such as oxidation-induced instability, matrix interference from coexisting species, reproducibility concerns, and challenges in translating laboratory-scale devices into practical field applications, are critically discussed. Finally, we outline future research directions aimed at overcoming these limitations and accelerating the development and commercialization of MXene-based sensing technologies for environmental monitoring. Overall, this article provides a comprehensive and insightful resource for researchers and practitioners working at the interface of emerging contaminants, nanomaterials engineering, and sensor development.
articles.summary_en: An academic review assesses MXene-based sensor fabrication, functionalization, detection mechanisms, and analytical performance for PFAS, microplastics, and nanoplastics in water. It identifies oxidation, matrix interference, reproducibility, and field-scale deployment as key barriers to practical environmental monitoring.

articles.title_original: Using Graphene Oxide Coatings to Filter Microplastics Out of Water
articles.title_en: Graphene Oxide Coating Improves Microplastic Filtration
articles.excerpt_original: Microplastics are plastic particles smaller than 5 millimeters. They include long fibers from textiles, irregular fragments, and thin films. They are now found in rivers, lakes, and drinking water, and this is becoming a serious problem. Ordinary filter paper has pores that are too large to stop most of these particles, so they pass through. This project tested whether a thin coating of graphene oxide (GO) could turn ordinary paper into a better barrier. We made GO from graphite powder by chemical oxidation and placed it on standard cellulose filter paper to make an affordable filter. In a first trial, the plain paper filter caught only about 11.2% of the microplastic in the water, while the GO-coated filter caught about 94.0%. The GO filter was also much slower: 1.08 mL/min compared with 5.88 to 8.50 mL/min for plain paper. This pattern is consistent with a physical barrier effect, in which the GO layer holds particles back at the paper surface and also slows the water. The first trial used one run per condition and different sample volumes (50 mL and 20 mL), so it is only preliminary. The study was therefore repeated with equal inputs, triplicate runs, and two extra controls, yielding a salt-corrected retention efficiency of 91.4 ± 1.8% for the GO-coated membrane compared with 10.5 ± 1.2% for plain filter paper (mean ± SD, n = 3). Overall, the results suggest that a simple, low-cost GO coating may improve microplastic removal, and that the idea is worth testing further to protect local waterways.
articles.summary_en: An ACS study found that graphene oxide-coated cellulose paper retained 91.4 ± 1.8% of microplastics, versus 10.5 ± 1.2% for plain filter paper. However, the coating substantially reduced flow rate, and the results remain preliminary despite triplicate testing.

articles.title_original: First-principles insights into the adsorption of graphene and graphene oxides on anhydrous and hydrated iron oxide
articles.title_en: DFT Reveals How Graphene Oxides Bind to Hydrated Hematite
articles.excerpt_original: Density functional theory calculations at the optB88-vdW+U level have been utilised to investigate the adsorption of graphene and graphene oxides with varying degrees of oxidation on anhydrous and hydrated Fe-terminated α−Fe2O3. Our calculations show that graphene and graphene oxide adsorb via physisorption and chemisorption, respectively. Graphene oxides were found to adsorb more strongly than pristine graphene on hematite in both anhydrous and hydrated conditions. Moreover, we deployed a combination of charge density difference, Bader charge, and crystal orbital Hamilton population analyses to provide both qualitative and quantitative insights into the adsorption mechanisms of graphene and graphene oxides on hematite. Specifically, we reveal that graphene oxides form Fe−O−C interfacial bridges on anhydrous hematite but increasingly complex Fe−O−H· · ·O−C bonds on hydrated surfaces. We further show that the strength and character of interfacial bonding are governed by the accessibility and topology of interfacial bridges, rather than by oxygen content alone. Adsorption therefore reflects a balance between bridge formation, charge redistribution, and the structural deformation of the carbon sheet. Explicit hydration weakens adsorption and changes the relative stability of the interfaces, while different oxidation levels favour distinct bonding configurations and electronic responses. articles.summary_en: ACS researchers used first-principles calculations to show that graphene physisorbs while graphene oxide chemisorbs more strongly on anhydrous and hydrated hematite. articles.title_original: Strain-driven and electric-field-tunable self-morphotropic phase boundary in nitride perovskite
articles.title_en: Strain and Electric Fields Tune Piezoelectricity in LaWN₃
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Ultrahigh piezoelectricity has long been associated with chemically complex morphotropic phase boundaries (MPBs). However, integrating conventional lead-based oxide perovskites onto Si platforms remains challenging, owing to compositional complexity, chemical incompatibility, and thermal-budget constraints. Here, using first-principles calculations, we identify a strain-driven self-morphotropic phase boundary (SMPB) in lanthanum tungsten nitride (LaWN 3 , LWN). Biaxial strain ( η ) induces a sequential symmetry progression and enables polarization rotation and ultrahigh piezoelectric responses. We further demonstrate that this SMPB is dynamically tunable by an electric field, yielding ultrahigh piezoelectric stress ( e ij ) and strain ( d ij ) coefficients that exceed those of conventional nitride piezoelectrics (e.g., AlN, AlScN, GaScN) by orders of magnitude. Our results establish a deterministic pathway to ultrahigh piezoelectricity in nitride perovskites, offering a compelling materials platform for adaptive electromechanical devices in next-generation telecommunications and integrated microelectronics.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations identify a strain-driven self-morphotropic phase boundary in lanthanum tungsten nitride, enabling polarization rotation and predicted piezoelectric responses exceeding those of conventional nitride materials. The findings suggest potential for adaptive electromechanical devices in telecommunications and integrated microelectronics, subject to experimental validation.

articles.title_original: Correlating Spin and Optical Properties of Quantum Emitters in hBN
articles.title_en: Study Correlates Spin and Optical Properties of hBN Quantum Emitters
articles.excerpt_original: Optically addressable spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are well suited for near-surface quantum sensing. They offer bright, wavelength-tunable single-photon emission with high optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast at room temperature. Here, we synthesize a high density of visible defects in carbon-doped hBN flakes with a high yield (14%) of ODMR-active emitters. We find that the zero-field splitting parameter D is directly correlated with the zero-phonon line of an emitter, while the ODMR contrast shows no such correlation. We further analyze an individual narrowband defect showing 68% ODMR contrast and enhance its photon collection by ∼40% using a solid immersion lens. By advancing both the practical synthesis of the spin complexes and the understanding of their microscopic origin, our results move us toward the deterministic creation of ODMR-active quantum emitters.

articles.title_original: Localized strain-engineered 1D electron guides in 2D MoS2 devices with synaptic memory and high-mobility transistor functionalities
articles.title_en: Wafer-Scale Strain Engineering Enables MoS2 Synaptic Memory and High-Mobility Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Local strain engineering has been studied as an effective strategy to modify the electronic band structure of two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors. However, using precisely controlled localized strain as a scalable tool for directing and controlling charge dynamics in 2D electronics remains largely underexplored. Here, we introduce wafer-scale localized strain engineering that applies periodically localized one-dimensional (1D) uniaxial strain to monolayer MoS 2 -based dual-functional electronics. By transferring MoS 2 onto a line-patterned HfO 2 substrate, we can deterministically generate a periodic localized 1D potential well. This approach creates a well-defined 1D potential landscape that facilitates dual functionality within a single material platform, depending on the alignment between the potential well orientation and the direction of carrier transport. Charge transport perpendicular to the 1D potential wells results in controlled charge trapping, thereby yielding a multibit synaptic memory device, whereas transport parallel to the potential wells experiences reduced lattice scattering and an effective mass with trap-free carrier conduction, leading to a high-mobility field-effect transistor. Systematic transport analyses elucidate how localized uniaxial strain modulates charge-trap density, lattice scattering, and effective mass, giving rise to direction-dependent charge transport. These findings highlight localized 1D strain as an effective design parameter for high-performance, scalable multifunctional 2D electronics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated periodic localized strain in monolayer MoS2 devices using line-patterned HfO2 substrates. The resulting direction-dependent transport enables multibit synaptic memory or high-mobility transistor operation on a single 2D semiconductor platform.

articles.title_original: Preparation, structural characterization, and mechanical properties of chitosan foams reinforced with graphene and graphene oxide
articles.title_en: Graphene oxide strengthens lightweight chitosan foams
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Chitosan (CS) is a promising biopolymer for the development of porous materials, although the limited mechanical resistance of CS-based foams can restrict their practical applications. This study investigated the preparation, structural characteristics, and mechanical properties of CS foams reinforced with graphene (G) or graphene oxide (GO), with and without glutaraldehyde crosslinking and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB) addition. Eight formulations were produced by mechanical air incorporation/foaming method followed by conventional oven drying. The materials were characterized by dynamic light scattering (DLS), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), apparent density, compression testing, and water uptake measurements. DLS analysis indicated smaller apparent hydrodynamic sizes for GO than for G dispersions, while SEM revealed a porous morphology with more defined pores and thicker walls compared in crosslinked foams. XRD analysis indicated reduced crystalline organization in the foams compared with pure CS. Apparent densities ranged from 38.6 to 50.6 kg·m -3 . The crosslinked GO-containing formulation (CS-R-GO) exhibited the highest mean compressive stress (57.7 kPa), approximately 3.1 times that of unmodified CS foam, and the highest water uptake after 1 h of immersion (3929%). These findings demonstrate the feasibility of producing lightweight CS-based foams without freeze-drying, also highlighting the combined use of GO reinforcement and glutaraldehyde crosslinking as a promising formulation strategy for improving the dry compressive mechanical resistance.
articles.summary_en: Researchers produced porous chitosan foams reinforced with graphene or graphene oxide using mechanical foaming and oven drying. articles.title_original: Transient LiCl Transport through Angstrom-Scale Graphene Slits: A Molecular Dynamics Study
articles.title_en: Molecular dynamics reveals width-dependent LiCl transport through graphene slits
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Concentration-gradient-driven transport of aqueous LiCl through idealized neutral graphene slits with geometric widths of 6.15–11.07 Å was investigated using classical molecular dynamics simulations. Four independent 20 ns trajectories were analyzed for each slit width. In the 6.15 and 7.38 Å slits, Li+ and Cl– occupancy and signed net reservoir transfer were strongly suppressed, whereas water crossed all five slits. Atom-identity-resolved directional event counting revealed substantial bidirectional recrossing around the central graphene plane. Nevertheless, a conservative complete-translocation analysis identified the largest observed adjacent increase in finite-time, gradient-directed net reservoir transfer between 7.38 and 8.61 Å for both Li+ and Cl–, while the subsequent adjacent increases over 8.61–11.07 Å were smaller. These observations indicate a finite-width crossover from strong ion exclusion to measurable transfer rather than a unique critical threshold or a strict transport plateau. Density distributions showed progressive ion access to the wider slits and ion-specific interfacial organization near graphene. The pore hydrogen-bond number density was lowest in the narrowest confined regions and generally increased as confinement was relaxed. Representative slit-entry free-energy profiles further identified distinct metastable positions for Li+ and Cl– near the pore plane. These results provide a molecular-level picture of confinement-controlled LiCl transport and the associated changes in interfacial organization and confined water structure.
articles.summary_en: ACS simulations show strong Li+ and Cl− exclusion in graphene slits narrower than 7.38 Å, followed by measurable transport as widths increase. The findings indicate a gradual confinement crossover rather than a single critical pore size, informing graphene-based ion-separation membrane design.

articles.title_original: Atomic‐Scale Origin of Charge Density Wave–Driven Metal–Semiconductor Transition in an Incommensurately Modulated Metal–Organic Framework
articles.title_en: Atomic-scale study links structural modulation to metal–semiconductor switching in MOF crystals
articles.excerpt_original: Although metal–organic frameworks are widely recognized for their long‐range crystalline periodicity, they can also exhibit intrinsic aperiodic structures associated with incommensurate modulation, whose observation has been exceptionally rare. In low‐dimensional condensed matter physics, these unique structures often give rise to novel physical phenomena such as charge density wave. However, owing to limited direct experimental evidence, the relationship between incommensurate structural modulation and temperature‐dependent electronic transport in conductive metal–organic frameworks remains incompletely understood. Here, using high‐quality Pr 3 HHTP 2 (HHTP = 2,3,6,7,10,11‐hexahydroxytriphenylene) single crystals as a model system, we resolve the incommensurately modulated structure at 100 K (modulation vector q = 0.39143(12) c * ) via temperature‐dependent single‐crystal x‐ray diffraction. The observed reversible metal–semiconductor transition near 350 K occurs in a similar temperature range to the disappearance of the structural modulation, supporting a connection between lattice distortion and electronic behavior. The modulation reappears upon cooling, with guest water molecules influencing both the extent of its recovery and the electrical conductivity of the material. This work establishes a concrete experimental criterion for one‐dimensional charge density wave in metal‐organic frameworks and provides an ideal platform for probing coupled electronic–lattice modulations.
articles.summary_en: Researchers resolved incommensurate structural modulation in Pr₃(HHTP)₂ single crystals and found its reversible disappearance near 350 K coincides with a metal–semiconductor transition. The findings clarify how lattice distortions and guest water molecules influence conductivity in conductive metal–organic frameworks.

articles.excerpt_original: The interaction between charge carriers with opposite charge, i.e. excitonic correlation between electron and hole, and the charge carriers’ interactions with underlying crystal lattice govern the opto-electronic response of semiconductors. The latter is dominated in ionic crystals by the Fröhlich interaction corresponding to the long-range electric field generated by polar phonons at the zone-center. Theoretical description of complex interplay arising from competition and interference between these two interactions, excitonic and polaronic, has been a formidable challenge. At the same time, the emergence of optoelectronics based on ionic semiconductors such as metal-halide perovskites has made it highly relevant to revisit theoretical models developed in the past, and push them further for application to real ionic semiconductors of interest. To this end, the present paper reviews the physics of Fröhlich excitonic polarons from the point of view of empirical approaches and supplements it with a few original developments to the state-of-the-art. At first, we review the models for excitonic polarons in ionic semiconductors, initially built by Toyozawa and Hermanson in analogy with Lee-Low-Pines (LLP) model for free polarons, and later extended by Pollman and Büttner (PB). These models have been applied in past to the simpler cases of weakly interacting polarons (e.g. GaAs). We further consider their applicability to ionic solids such as TlCl or 3D lead halide perovskites, where the electron–hole correlations are relatively stronger. In these compounds, electrons and holes have almost equal effective masses, which allows us to derive a new analytical expression of the approximated version of the PB effective interaction potential. articles.summary_en: This academic review examines empirical models describing the interplay between excitonic and polaronic interactions in ionic semiconductors, including lead-halide perovskites. It also presents an analytical refinement for systems with stronger electron–hole correlations and similar effective masses.

articles.title_original: A van der Waals Double‐Floating‐Gate Memory for Optoelectronic Three‐Factor Learning
articles.title_en: Van der Waals Graphene Memory Enables Three-Factor Learning
articles.excerpt_original: Three‐factor learning, in which synaptic weight updates are regulated by local activity and an additional modulatory signal, provides a powerful framework for adaptive neuromorphic computing but remains difficult to implement in compact hardware. Here, a fully van der Waals (vdW) double‐floating‐gate (DFG) memory based on an α‐In 2 Se 3 /hexagonal boron nitride (h‐BN)/multilayer graphene (MLG)/h‐BN/MLG heterostructure is demonstrated. The coupled floating gates provide an additional electrostatic degree of freedom for state‐dependent conductance modulation. The device exhibits a threshold‐voltage shift exceeding 65 V, an on/off current ratio approaching 10 6 , and 48.7% and 55.1% reductions in LTP and LTD nonlinearity, respectively. Over the single‐floating‐gate counterpart, enabling ∼92.5% recognition accuracy on the Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST) handwritten‐digit dataset. Gate‐programmable broadband optoelectronic responses extend to the 1310 nm optical communication band. Under 1310 nm illumination, persistent conductance changes are jointly governed by the initial conductance state, optical input, and gate‐programmed modulation of the learning rate, thereby realizing a hardware‐level analog of three‐factor learning. These results highlight the potential of this multifunctional vdW memory for adaptive optoelectronic in‐memory computing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a double-floating-gate memory using multilayer graphene and other van der Waals materials, achieving nearly 92.5% MNIST recognition accuracy and programmable optoelectronic responses at 1310 nm. The device supports hardware-level three-factor learning for adaptive neuromorphic and in-memory computing.

articles.title_original: High Proton Conductivity and Enhanced Fuel Cell Performance from Zirconium/Phytic Acid-Modified Boron Nitride Nanosheets
articles.title_en: Zirconium–Phytic Acid Boron Nitride Membrane Improves Fuel Cell Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract The widespread adoption of polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) is currently hindered by the high cost and poor performance of conventional Nafion electrolytes at elevated temperatures. To address these limitations, this study presents a novel boron nitride (BN)-based hybrid membrane as a high-performance alternative. We report the synthesis of a zirconium/phytic acid-modified hydroxylated boron nitride (Zr/Ph–BN–OH) nanosheet membrane designed for enhanced proton transport. The hybrid membrane demonstrates exceptional proton conductivity, reaching 1.07 × 10–2 S cm–1 at 85 °C and 90% relative humidity (RH). In fuel cell performance tests at 70 °C and 90% RH, the optimized Zr/Ph–BN–OH membrane achieved a peak current density of 1321 mA cm–2 and a maximum power density of 312 mW cm–2. This power density represents a more than 10-fold increase over pristine BN (10 mW cm–2) and a 2-fold improvement over Nafion (122 mW cm–2) under identical operating conditions. The superior performance is attributed to the synergistic effects of hydroxylation, phytic acid intercalation, and Zr4+-mediated cross-linking, which collectively enhance water uptake and promote the reformation of robust hydrogen-bonded networks within the conduction channels. These findings demonstrate a proof-of-concept strategy for transforming chemically stable BN nanosheets into efficient proton-conducting membranes and provide useful design guidance for next-generation noncarbon proton exchange membranes.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a zirconium/phytic acid-modified boron nitride nanosheet membrane for proton exchange membrane fuel cells. The membrane achieved 312 mW cm−2 maximum power density at 70 °C, exceeding pristine boron nitride and Nafion under the reported test conditions, but remains a proof-of-concept noncarbon electrolyte.

articles.title_original: Monolayer h‐BN RF Switch Toward Monolithic Inductor Switching in Wide‐Tuning‐Range LC ‐VCOs
articles.title_en: Monolayer h-BN Memristor Enables Reconfigurable RF Switching
articles.excerpt_original: Next‐generation wireless systems demand monolithic three‐dimensional (3D) system‐on‐chip architectures to overcome planar scaling limits and reduce interconnect delays. Realizing this back‐end‐of‐line (BEOL) integration on complementary metal‐oxide‐semiconductor (CMOS) platforms requires ultracompact, high‐performance radio‐frequency (RF) switches. Here, we present a non‐volatile RF switch based on a monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (h‐BN) memristor employing an Ag/h‐BN/Ag structure. The device exhibits a low SET voltage of 1.11 V and stable endurance exceeding 500 cycles. At 20 GHz, it achieves an insertion loss of 0.81 dB and an isolation of 32.91 dB, enabled by a low on‐resistance ( R ON ) of 4.3 Ω and an ultralow off‐capacitance ( C OFF ) of 1.8 fF, corresponding to a cut‐off frequency ( F CO ) of 20.5 THz. To verify its feasibility at the circuit level, the h‐BN RF switch was applied to an LC ‐type voltage‐controlled oscillator ( LC ‐VCO), whose inductance can be reconfigured. The simulation results indicate that modulating the switch state and thereby changing the effective inductance enables wideband frequency tuning from 1.44 to 7.45 GHz, corresponding to a frequency tuning range (FTR) of 135%. These results verify the feasibility of the atomically thin h‐BN RF switch for inductor switching in reconfigurable LC ‐VCOs, presenting a promising route toward miniaturized high‐frequency circuit designs.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate a non-volatile monolayer hexagonal boron nitride RF switch with low insertion loss, high isolation, and endurance exceeding 500 cycles. Integrated into an LC-VCO simulation, the switch enables a reported 135% frequency tuning range, highlighting potential for compact high-frequency semiconductor circuits.

articles.title_original: An Aerogel Composite Cooler with Radiative-Phase-Change Hybrid Cooling for Highly Effective Outdoor Electronics Thermal Management
articles.title_en: Aerogel Composite Enables Hybrid Cooling for Outdoor Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: Conventional radiative cooling suffers from limited cooling capacity, while phase change based temperature control techniques are plagued by material leakage, making them insufficient to satisfy the growing requirements of outdoor electronics. Herein, we propose a leakproof radiative-phase-change hybrid cooling aerogel composite (RPHCAC) cooler that integrates directionally structured chitosan (CS)/carbon nanotubes (CNTs) aerogel encapsulating beeswax (BW) as the phase change material (PCM) inside a coating of polydimethylsiloxane/hexagonal boron nitride (PDMS/h BN), which achieves a high solar reflectivity of 95.6% with a high latent heat of 163.4 J g-1. Importantly, aerogel composite cooler exhibits a water contact angle of approximately 123.9°, maintaining its water‑repellent character with self‑cleaning functionality. Under direct sunlight, this RPHCAC cooler attains an average temperature reduction of 11.7 °C below ambient and displays a maximum temperature drop of 47.5 °C when further subjected to an intense thermal shock of 2000 W ⋅m−2, which is primarily attributed to the temperature pinning effect of the PCM and the good optical property of the PDMS/h BN coating. By integrating radiative cooling with latent heat storage, this work offers an effective strategy to safeguard outdoor electronics against solar radiation, thus pushing passive thermal management technologies closer to real world deployment.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a leakproof aerogel cooler combining radiative cooling with beeswax phase-change heat storage. The device reduced temperature by 11.7 °C below ambient in sunlight and reached a 47.5 °C drop under intense thermal shock, indicating potential for passive thermal management of outdoor electronics.

articles.title_original: High-κ bismuth molybdate single-crystalline dielectric for high-temperature two-dimensional transistors
articles.title_en: Bismuth Molybdate Dielectric Enables High-Temperature 2D Transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors represent promising alternatives to traditional silicon for next-generation electronic devices. However, there are still significant challenges in high-temperature 2D electronic devices integrated by existing high-κ dielectrics. Here, we report a BiOCl-assisted chemical vapor deposition method to synthesize high-quality bismuth molybdate (Bi 2 MoO 6 ) single-crystalline nanosheets with controllable thickness and good thermal stability. High-κ (54.2) nature is identified within as-grown Bi 2 MoO 6 nanosheets, with wide bandgap (∼3.85 eV) and large breakdown field strength (∼3.9 MV/cm) at room temperature. As results, Bi 2 MoO 6 top-gate MoS 2 transistor exhibits a negligible hysteresis and an average subthreshold swing less than 100 mV dec −1 within 3 orders of magnitude of current range, as well as excellent operational stability. Moreover, the transistor maintains a high on/off current ratio of > 10 4 and a hysteresis of less than 10 mV/(MV cm −1 ) at the high temperature up to 500 K, meeting the requirements of high-temperature electronic devices. The inverter with Bi 2 MoO 6 gate dielectric is also achieved, yielding a high gain of 86.1 at supply voltage of 5 V. This work enriches the high-κ gate dielectric family and provides considerable application potential in high-temperature electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized high-κ bismuth molybdate nanosheets for MoS₂ transistors, achieving stable operation up to 500 K. The devices maintained an on/off ratio above 10⁴ and delivered an inverter gain of 86.1, supporting high-temperature semiconductor applications.

articles.title_original: Twist-engineered arbitrary polarization detection for intelligent polarimetric sensing
articles.title_en: Twisted black phosphorus metasurfaces enable full-Stokes polarization sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Twist-photonics offers a powerful route to engineer light-matter interactions beyond conventional planar architectures. Although twist-photonic platforms, including twist-stacked metasurfaces, van der Waals (vdW) materials and photonic crystals have successfully engineered chiral optical responses, anomalous dispersion and high- Q localized modes, most platforms remain passive. Their translation into on-chip optoelectronic sensing is hindered by an intrinsic trade-off: photosensitive absorbers can quench twist-engineered resonances, whereas passive twist-photonic modes often couple inefficiently to active photocarrier-generation regions. Here, we report an emerging twist-photonic paradigm that integrates anisotropic metasurfaces with anisotropic black phosphorus (BP). Coupled to a vectorial cavity, this twisted stack produces quasi-pure circular-polarization photoresponses and enables arbitrary polarization selectivity across the full Poincaré sphere at multiple wavelengths. Then, we establish an ultra-compact on-chip full-Stokes polarimeter using only two metasurface-BP twisted stacks, achieving high-accuracy full-Stokes reconstruction with a root-mean-square error below 1.3%, and the highest responsivity among reported vdW material-based full-Stokes polarimeters. We further implement an in-sensor kernel matrix that directly maps polarization states into synaptic weights for polarization-programmable multimodal convolutional image processing, reducing electrical switching energy by 1 to 3 orders of magnitude and reconfiguration latency by 2 to 4 orders of magnitude, as the array scales from the 10k-pixel to megapixel level.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated anisotropic metasurfaces with black phosphorus to achieve arbitrary polarization selectivity across the Poincaré sphere. A compact on-chip polarimeter delivered full-Stokes reconstruction with under 1.3% RMS error and enabled energy- and latency-efficient polarization-based image processing.

articles.title_original: How Graphene Surface Structure and Flexibility Govern Gallium Droplet Impact Behaviors
articles.title_en: Graphene Surface Structure Controls Gallium Droplet Impact
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Liquid metals (LMs) have garnered increasing attention in flexible electronics for their high conductivity and excellent processability. However, inherently high surface tension makes precise control of droplet spreading and adhesion on substrates challenging. Understanding how surface structures and substrate flexibility regulate droplet impact behaviors of LMs is essential for the development of flexible electronics, printing, and microfluidic technologies. Here, molecular dynamics simulations were employed to systematically compare the impact dynamics of gallium (Ga) droplets on graphene surface structures at room temperature, along with differences in impact behaviors between rigid and flexible graphene substrates. Key dynamic parameters were quantitatively analyzed, revealing scaling relationships between the spreading factor, dimensionless time, and Weber number (We). Specifically, these findings revealed that surface structure configurations can effectively regulate droplet rebound behavior by modulating interfacial wettability and the redistribution of impact energy. In addition, flexible graphene substrates introduced the elastic deformation energy channels during impact, which markedly shortened the contact time. These results elucidate the distinct regulatory roles of surface structural engineering and substrate compliance in governing LM droplet impact behaviors, offering mechanistic insights and actionable theoretical guidance for the rational design of functional interfaces tailored to flexible electronics and advanced patterning technologies.
articles.summary_en: ACS research uses molecular dynamics simulations to show that graphene surface structure and substrate flexibility regulate gallium droplet spreading, rebound, and contact time. The findings provide design guidance for liquid-metal patterning in flexible electronics, printing, and microfluidics.

articles.title_original: Graphene Phononic Crystal Thermal Triode Based on Coherent Phonon Wave Modulation
articles.title_en: Graphene phononic crystal enables three-terminal thermal logic
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract To address the severe localized heat dissipation challenges in advanced microelectronic devices, solid-state thermal logic devices offer a potential route toward active thermal management. However, existing research has largely focused on two-terminal thermal diodes. Realizing practical thermal logic requires extending these devices into three-terminal architectures, where an additional gate modulates heat transport in the main channel. This transition requires new structural strategies for phonon transport, beyond the passive thermal rectification enabled by structural asymmetry alone. To this end, this work uses suspended monolayer graphene phononic crystals as a platform, establishing a cross-scale research framework combining the finite element method (FEM) and molecular dynamics (MD). Using MD and FEM as complementary approaches, the modulation of thermal rectification by pore asymmetry and array periodicity is first investigated at the diode level from atomistic and continuum-wave perspectives. The two methods provide complementary descriptions, laying the groundwork for triode design. Building on this, a three-terminal thermal triode model is further constructed. Varying the gate pore diameter produces a pronounced non-monotonic modulation of normalized drain energy transmission, with the strongest reduction when the gate pore diameter matches the main-channel pore diameter at $d_G = d = 6$ nm. For comparison, the two-terminal baseline has an energy flux coefficient of 0.5220, whereas the pore-free three-terminal reference is 0.7074 under the three-terminal input configuration. articles.summary_en: Researchers modeled a graphene phononic-crystal thermal triode that actively modulates heat transport through a gate pore. Molecular-dynamics and finite-element simulations found maximum static modulation of 47.6% when the gate and channel pore diameters both measured 6 nm, indicating a potential route to active thermal management in microelectronics.

articles.title_original: Boron Nitride-Enhanced Thermally Conductive, Color-Developer-Free Thermochromic Polyurethane Composite Phase Change Material
articles.title_en: Boron Nitride Enhances Thermochromic Polyurethane Phase-Change Materials
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Traditional thermochromic phase-change materials (TC-PCMs) face several limitations, including the use of potentially toxic color developers, low heat storage/release efficiency, and the compositional complexity of conventional color-developing systems. In this study, we synthesized a negative photochromic spiropyran (SPOH) that undergoes heat-driven ring-opening isomerization, thereby enabling a direct color change. SPOH was employed as the thermochromic unit, lauric acid (LA) as the phase-change energy storage component, and amino-functionalized boron nitride (BN-NH2) as a thermally conductive filler. Through the reaction of polyethylene glycol (PEG2K) with hexamethylene diisocyanate (HDI) and its trimer (THDI), a cross-linked polyurethane network (TC-CPCMs) was constructed to encapsulate SPOH, LA, and BN-NH2. The TC-CPCMs exhibited high thermal energy storage performance, with an enthalpy efficiency (φ) of 82.1%. The introduction of BN-NH2 increased the thermal conductivity to 0.9196 W/(m·K), representing a 252% enhancement compared with that of BN-free TC-CPCMs, while maintaining stable and reversible thermochromic properties, thereby enabling the functional integration of thermal energy storage and temperature indication. In applications involving wastewater waste heat recovery and the thermal management of electronic devices, TC-CPCMs demonstrated significant performance improvements while enabling visual monitoring of the energy storage process through color changes.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers developed a polyurethane composite phase-change material combining heat storage with reversible, color-based temperature indication. Amino-functionalized boron nitride increased thermal conductivity by 252% to 0.9196 W/(m·K), supporting potential electronic thermal management and wastewater waste-heat recovery applications.

articles.title_original: Crossover between superconducting and boron–carbon phases in heavily boron-doped diamond homoepitaxial layers
articles.title_en: Boron-Doped Diamond Shows Superconductivity-to-Graphitic Phase Crossover
articles.excerpt_original: Heavily boron-doped homoepitaxial diamond films grown by chemical vapor deposition on single-crystal type-IIa diamond substrates are investigated. Quantitative analysis of the nominal, structural, and active concentrations of boron atoms in the grown layers was carried out using secondary ion mass spectrometry, X-ray diffractometry, and the van der Pauw method, respectively. Nominal concentrations ranged from 8.2 × 10 20 to 2 × 10 22 cm −3 . Electrophysical measurements revealed metallic conductivity in the epitaxial layers, and a superconducting transition was observed. The dependence of the superconducting critical temperature on the boron doping level was studied. It was found that at nominal concentrations of 10 22 cm −3 and higher, diamond loses its perfection, transitioning to a graphite-containing phase that lacks the superconducting transition. Thus, this study examined the crossover from the superconducting phase to the boron–carbon phase with a gradual increase in the nominal boron concentration. The critical boron doping level was determined for diamond to exhibit superconductivity while maintaining its crystalline perfection, which is an important parameter for the formation of heavily doped diamond layers with a superconducting transition.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identified a boron-doping threshold at which homoepitaxial diamond layers retain crystalline perfection and superconductivity. At nominal boron concentrations of 10²² cm⁻³ or higher, the diamond develops a graphite-containing phase and loses its superconducting transition, informing the design of heavily doped superconducting diamond layers.

articles.title_original: Atomic layer and digital etching: Correlation between interface quality and device stability of recessed‐gate gallium nitride transistors with aluminum nitride/hafnium oxide
articles.title_en: Atomic Layer Etching Improves GaN Transistor Interface Stability
articles.excerpt_original: This work presents a comparative study of two advanced recessing processes—atomic layer etching (ALE) and digital etching (DE)—for aluminum nitride/hafnium oxide (AlN/HfO 2 ) aluminum gallium nitride/gallium nitride (AlGaN/GaN) metal‐oxide‐semiconductor high‐electron‐mobility transistors (MOS‐HEMTs). The investigation focuses on the impact of these etching methods on interface trap characteristics to evaluate device performance and reliability. The frequency‐dispersion capacitance‐voltage method was employed to extract the interface trap density ( D it ) and its distribution in the energy band. The experimental results demonstrate that while both etching methods yield high‐quality etched surfaces, atomic layer etching exhibits a lower interface trap density than digital etching. By using atomic layer etching, a high saturated output current density of 868 mA/mm has been achieved. The threshold voltage stability of fabricated devices was tested using positive‐bias stress measurement. After applying stress for 1000 seconds, the devices with atomic layer etching show less threshold voltage variation (Δ V th = 0.717 V), compared to digital etching devices (Δ V t h = 1.051 V).
articles.summary_en: A study compares atomic layer etching and digital etching for recessed-gate AlN/HfO₂ AlGaN/GaN MOS-HEMTs. Atomic layer etching produced lower interface-trap density, an 868 mA/mm saturated output current density, and improved threshold-voltage stability under 1,000-second bias stress.

articles.title_original: Electrical and optical properties of hydrothermally-reduced graphene oxide
articles.title_en: Hydrothermal Reduction Tunes Graphene Oxide’s Electrical and Optical Properties
articles.excerpt_original: Reducing graphene oxide (GO) without toxic chemicals is a goal for sustainable production of conductive carbon materials. We report a comparative study of hydrothermal reduction of GO in water and aqueous ammonia solution (GO-NH4OH). Reduction was examined at temperatures of 25–200 °C, yielding reduced GO with O/C ratios of 0.14 in water and 0.13 in aqueous ammonia. Electrical resistivities of GO reached 0.14 Ω·m in water and 0.11 Ω·m in aqueous ammonia, while optical band gaps were 1.60 eV in water and 0.64 eV in aqueous ammonia. Both water and aqueous ammonia effectively reduce GO, whereas ammonia dopes GO forming pyrrolic nitrogen at 1.20 ± 0.23 at.% at 200 °C through nucleophilic attack. Hydrothermal reduction of GO with aqueous ammonia and water is important for understanding and developing electrically conducting graphene-based materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers compared water and aqueous ammonia for reducing graphene oxide without toxic chemicals. Aqueous ammonia produced slightly lower resistivity and a substantially narrower optical band gap while introducing pyrrolic nitrogen doping, highlighting a route to conductive graphene-based materials.

articles.title_original: Wafer-scale transferable hexagonal boron nitride membranes via interfacial engineering for multilevel storage
articles.title_en: Wafer-scale transferable h-BN membranes enable high-performance multilevel memristors
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional materials hold immense potential for memristive devices, offering a pathway to overcome the von Neumann bottleneck. Specifically, hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is highly promising for low-voltage, multilevel memristors due to its robust physicochemical properties. However, synthesizing wafer-scale, transferable, and thickness-controllable h-BN (tens of nanometers thick) remains challenging, impeding its device integration. Herein, we demonstrate an interfacial modulation strategy via controlled sapphire substrate nitridation to grow high-quality, crack-free h-BN membranes. Introducing an interfacial B–O buffer layer improves the crystalline quality of epitaxial h-BN and facilitates its rapid, damage-free wet transfer onto target substrates. The fabricated memristors with these transferred membranes exhibit a low set voltage of 1.06 V, an ultrahigh ON/OFF ratio of 1.57×10 9 , an ultrafast switching speed of 30 ns, robust multilevel switching and long-term stability. Our study presents a scalable approach for advancing next-generation in-memory computing architectures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed wafer-scale, crack-free hexagonal boron nitride membranes using interfacial substrate engineering, enabling rapid damage-free transfer. The resulting memristors achieved 1.06 V set voltage, a 1.57×10^9 ON/OFF ratio, 30 ns switching, multilevel operation, and long-term stability, supporting in-memory computing applications.

articles.title_original: Axion-induced Casimir interaction between graphene plates
articles.title_en: Graphene Plates Could Enhance Axion-Induced Casimir Signals
articles.excerpt_original: Axion dark matter may induce observable electromagnetic effects in resonant cavity systems, and potentially lead to modifications of the Casimir interaction. In this context, graphene represents a particularly attractive platform owing to its distinctive and tunable electromagnetic properties, and the fact that its electromagnetic response can be modeled microscopically from first principles within quantum field theory. The electromagnetic response induced by axion dark matter is investigated in a planar cavity geometry consisting of parallel graphene interfaces in the presence of a homogeneous external magnetic field, incorporating finite temperature, chemical potential and dissipation effects through the graphene conductivity. Closed analytical expressions are obtained for the induced electric field and the resulting pressure exerted on the interfaces. The pressure exhibits resonant enhancement, at a series of plate separations satisfying d n = 2 π n − ϕ ( r ) m a , where m a is the axion mass and the phase ϕ ( r ) is determined by the reflection coefficient r , which depends on the graphene conductivity evaluated at the axion frequency ω = m a . The resonant structure is strongly influenced by the graphene chemical potential and damping parameter. In particular, increased doping, for example via a gate voltage, sharpens the resonances and amplifies the axion-induced signal. By comparing the resonantly enhanced signal with the conventional Casimir background, the parametric regimes in which the effect could become experimentally relevant are identified, with the strongest sensitivity obtained for highly doped low-dissipation graphene configurations operated near resonance. articles.summary_en: Theoretical research models how axion dark matter could modify Casimir interactions between parallel graphene interfaces in a magnetic-field cavity. Gate-tunable doping and low dissipation may sharpen resonances and improve experimental sensitivity near selected plate separations.

articles.title_original: Design, fabrication, and characterisation of graphene-based microelectromechanical systems acoustic sensors
articles.title_en: Graphene MEMS Acoustic Sensors Fabricated via Thermal Scanning Probe Lithography
articles.excerpt_original: Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) have experienced a great development in line with the technological trend of miniaturisation, pushing forward the study of sound with revolutionary MEMS acoustic sensors. Graphene is a two-dimensional (2D) material that possesses many excellent properties in mechanical, electrical and thermal aspects. The development of graphene-based MEMS acoustic sensors has become an important topic. This thesis presents the design, fabrication, and characterisation of graphene-based MEMS acoustic sensors. An advanced technology, thermal scanning probe lithography (t-SPL) has been studied for the patterning of graphene, which is a direct-write patterning method that uses a heated scanning probe tip to induce modifications in a thermal resist layer locally. As the thickness of graphene is naturally low as a 2D material, the limitation of low patterning depth that t-SPL has can be perfectly avoided when applied to the patterning of graphene. A new thermal resist, parylene C, has been introduced in this thesis, which has been used as a substrate, dielectric or passivation material in MEMS before. In addition to preserving many impressive features of t-SPL, parylene C has several unique advantages as a thermal resist under our experimental conditions. The unique deposition process makes parylene C resist layer conformal, uniform and pinhole-free. The resolution of t-SPL with parylene C can be as high as ~40 nm, and the process latitude can be as wide as 650-1050°C. Thermally patterned features in parylene C resist layer can be transferred to the silicon substrate with or without a silicon dioxide hard mask layer. articles.summary_en: A thesis investigates the design, fabrication, and characterization of graphene-based MEMS acoustic sensors. It demonstrates thermal scanning probe lithography with parylene C resist, achieving feature resolution of approximately 40 nm for capacitive microphone fabrication.

articles.title_original: Efficient and non-invasive platform for the diagnosis and subtyping of X-linked Alport syndrome leveraging interfacial synergistic engineered MXene@AuNWs
articles.title_en: MXene–gold nanowire platform enables biomarker detection for Alport syndrome
articles.excerpt_original: Introduction X-linked Alport syndrome (XLAS) is a hereditary nephropathy caused primarily by mutations in the COL4A5 gene and is characterized by progressive nephritis, hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities. Early diagnosis and the identification of specific biomarkers are critical for the effective management of XLAS. Methods We developed a laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry (LDI-MS) metabolomics approach based on a gold nanowire-modified MXene (MXene@AuNWs) nanoplatform to acquire the metabolic fingerprints of urine and serum from XLAS patients and healthy controls. The platform combines the high ionization efficiency of AuNWs with the ordered two-dimensional structure and abundant surface terminations of MXene, enabling the selective enrichment and sensitive detection of small-molecule metabolites; urinary homocysteine and serum phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) were quantified by an orthogonal enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Results The platform tolerated high concentrations of salt and protein and was applicable to both urine and serum. The metabolite at m/z 278.43, assigned to urinary homocysteine, was the finding most significantly associated with XLAS (AUC = 0.752), and the ELISA independently confirmed a significantly decreased urinary homocysteine level in patients, whereas serum PAH showed no significant difference between the groups. Discussion These results establish MXene@AuNWs-assisted LDI-MS metabolic fingerprinting, cross-validated by immunoassay, as a rapid and label-free route to biomarker discovery in XLAS, and hold substantial potential for future clinical applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an MXene@AuNW laser desorption/ionization mass-spectrometry platform for non-invasive metabolic profiling of X-linked Alport syndrome in urine and serum. articles.title_original: Built-in electric field modulation of spontaneous magnetism and thermospin transport in boron-nitrogen–doped zigzag graphene nanoribbons
articles.title_en: Boron–nitrogen doping enables switchable spin-caloritronics in graphene nanoribbons
articles.excerpt_original: Zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs) host large magnetic moments at two zigzag edges due to spontaneous magnetism, whose ground state is antiferromagnetically coupled spin-order edge state (AF state). In this paper, the spontaneous magnetism and thermoelectricity of ZGNRs with periodic substituted doping of boron and nitrogen atoms along the axial direction are investigated by first principle calculation. The doping induces an internal electric field, which modulates the magnetic moments at the two zigzag edges and the band structure with spin splitting. For varying doping configuration, the ground state could be AF state, ferromagnetically coupled spin-order edge state (FM state), or degenerated pair of AF and FM states. External transversal static electric field can further modulate the magnetic moments and the band structure. By designing the doping configuration and the external field, pure thermal spin current with the absence of thermal charge current can be generated at room temperature, which can be switched on and off by flipping the magnetic configuration between AF and FM states. Thus, the doped ZGNRs can be applied as prototype devices for spin-caloritronic.
articles.summary_en: First-principles calculations show that periodic boron–nitrogen doping creates an internal electric field that tunes magnetism and spin-split band structures in zigzag graphene nanoribbons. The structures could generate switchable pure thermal spin currents at room temperature, indicating potential for prototype spin-caloritronic devices.

articles.title_original: Molecular Regulation of Excited‐State Dynamics Enables Photochemically Stable Organic Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Molecular regulation improves organic photovoltaic stability
articles.excerpt_original: Photochemical degradation fundamentally limits the operational stability of organic photovoltaics (OPVs), yet the molecular processes linking excited‐state dynamics to irreversible chemical reactions remain poorly understood. Here, we show that excited‐state vibrational processes represent a previously underexplored molecular degree of freedom governing photochemical stability and can be regulated to suppress degradation. By incorporating melatonin into the donor layer of an OPV device, excited‐state molecular motions are effectively modulated, reducing vibrationally induced structural fluctuations, suppressing radical generation, and mitigating subsequent photochemical degradation under prolonged illumination. Comprehensive characterization reveals that molecular regulation modifies excited‐state relaxation pathways, thereby decreasing the probability of irreversible chemical transformations while preserving efficient charge generation and transport. As a result, D18/L8‐BO based binary device achieves a power conversion efficiency of 21.10% (certified as 20.6%), together with a more than threefold enhancement in T 80 lifetime under continuous illumination. The effectiveness of this strategy is further validated across multiple systems, demonstrating its general applicability. These findings establish a molecular connection between excited‐state vibrational dynamics and photochemical degradation, and identify regulation of excited‐state molecular motions as an effective strategy for simultaneously achieving high efficiency and long‐term stability in OPV devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used melatonin in the donor layer of organic photovoltaic devices to regulate excited-state molecular motion and suppress photochemical degradation. The resulting D18/L8-BO device achieved 21.10% efficiency and more than threefold longer T80 lifetime under continuous illumination, with results validated across multiple systems.

articles.title_original: Indentation-induced polar domain reconfiguration in the charge-density-wave semiconductor EuTe4
articles.title_en: Mechanical Reconfiguration of Polar Domains Demonstrated in EuTe4
articles.excerpt_original: Controlling polar domains in conducting materials by external fields could unlock polarisation-based electronic functionalities, yet remains experimentally challenging. While mechanical actuation driven by local strain, stress, or strain gradients has been proposed as an external-voltage-free route, its experimental demonstration in relatively conducting polar materials remains limited. Here we demonstrate mechanically induced polar-domain reconfiguration in the charge-density-wave (CDW) semiconductor EuTe 4 at room temperature, whose resistivity is on the order of 10 mΩcm. Polarised-light microscopy and second-harmonic-generation measurements reveal CDW-induced in-plane polarisation domains with an approximately 90° domain configuration. Local indentation with a ~ 1 µm-apex-radius needle reconfigures these domains, producing write/erase-like changes in wedge-shaped regions. These results establish local mechanical-field domain engineering in a relatively conducting CDW semiconductor, with possible contributions from both ferroelastic-like and flexoelectric mechanisms.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated room-temperature, indentation-induced reconfiguration of charge-density-wave polar domains in the relatively conducting semiconductor EuTe4. The write/erase-like behavior suggests a potential route to mechanically controlled polarization-based electronic functionality without external voltage.

articles.title_original: Tailored Mn Doping Enables Substantially Boosted Fluorescence Emission in 2D Hybrid Perovskite Ferroelectric Scintillator
articles.title_en: Mn Doping Dramatically Boosts Luminescence in 2D Perovskite X-ray Scintillator
articles.excerpt_original: Organic‐inorganic ferroelectric materials, due to their advantages such as spontaneous polarization, controllable electric domains and multi‐physical field coupling effects, are widely applied in fields including sensors, actuators and optoelectronics. However, there are few successful cases that combine ferroelectricity with dopant‐induced efficient luminescence effects in ferroelectric materials. Herein, through delicate Mn 2+ ion doping, we have successfully designed a multifunctional luminescent ferroelectric material, (GABA) 2 CdCl 4 :4%Mn 2+ (GABA = γ‐aminobutyric acid) which retains its excellent ferroelectric properties with a spontaneous polarization of 4.0 µC cm −2 . Meanwhile, its photoluminescence intensity can be systematically modulated by varying the Mn 2+ doping concentration, demonstrating excellent controllability and functional versatility. Notably, Mn 2+ doping induces a distinct bulk orange‐red luminescence at 610 nm, dramatically boosting the quantum yield from 0.11% to 67%. Leveraging such superior bulk luminescence, (GABA) 2 CdCl 4 :4%Mn 2+ delivers a high light yield of 52 170 photons MeV −1 and a low detection limit of 62.3 nGy s −1 , along with good environmental and radiation stability, marking the first Mn 2+ ‐doped organic‐inorganic hybrid perovskite ferroelectric x‐ray scintillator.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a Mn2+-doped organic–inorganic ferroelectric perovskite that increased photoluminescence quantum yield from 0.11% to 67%. The material achieved a light yield of 52,170 photons MeV−1 and a detection limit of 62.3 nGy s−1, indicating potential for sensitive X-ray detection.

articles.title_original: Moire-induced interlayer electron-phonon coupling in graphene/hBN superlattices
articles.title_en: Moiré superlattices reveal enhanced electron–phonon coupling in graphene/hBN
articles.excerpt_original: Electron-phonon coupling (EPC) plays a vital role in the electrical and optical properties of materials, ranging from superconductivity to charge dynamics. In moir'e superlattices, out-of-plane vibrations can modulate the moir'e potential and enhance interlayer EPC. Here we report the first direct observation of a resonance arising from coupling between moir'e electronic excitations and phonons in graphene-based moir'e superlattices. Using Fourier-transform infrared photocurrent spectroscopy, we detect the nominally silent hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) out-of-plane optical (ZO) phonon as a pronounced absorption peak. The phonon interferes with moir'e flat-band excitations to form a characteristic Fano resonance. Displacement field-dependent measurements confirm that the feature originates from coupling to the moir'e electronic continuum rather than simple zone folding. We further observe similar resonances in devices with different graphene layer numbers and twist configurations. This enhanced EPC provides a pathway for understanding and controlling emerging quantum phenomena, such as superconductivity, and engineering novel optoelectronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly observed resonant coupling between moiré electronic excitations and hBN phonons in graphene-based superlattices using infrared photocurrent spectroscopy. articles.title_original: MXene and TEGA Compared: Stability, Manufacturing and Scale
articles.title_en: Preprint Compares TEGA Carbon Material with MXene for Scale-Up
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes, two-dimensional transition-metal carbides first reported in 2011, are again promoted as materials for future batteries, supercapacitors, electromagnetic shielding and water treatment. Before any large-scale use, three practical questions decide their fate: how long the material keeps its properties, how it is made, and how much of it can be produced. This preprint compares MXene with TEGA (thermally expanded graphite Arbok), a graphene-like carbon material produced in-house by ARBOK. In water dispersions Ti3C2Tx MXene oxidizes to titanium dioxide, and its conductivity falls to about 7% of the original value in 27 days unless it is stored at −80°C. MXene is made by etching MAX-phase ceramics in hydrofluoric acid, in some protocols for 90-118 hours. TEGA is pure carbon, does not oxidize, withstands up to 1500°C, is made from oxidized natural graphite at 50-100 USD per tonne and is sold at about 50 USD/kg. One TEGA line produces 50-300 kg/h, or 400-2,000 t/yr, against a world graphene output of 3,500-4,000 t in 2023. ARBOK data for TEGA-based supercapacitor electrodes and electromagnetic absorbers are given: 180-250 F/g, 500,000 cycles, more than 60 dB shielding. A scenario estimate puts the saving at 1-2 bln USD a year if one third of the electromagnetic shielding and supercapacitor markets moved to TEGA. Keywords: MXene, TEGA, thermally expanded graphite, oxidation stability, supercapacitor, electromagnetic shielding, scalable production

articles.title_original: Structure-transport relationships in water confined between graphene sheets
articles.title_en: Water transport behavior in sub-nanometer graphene channels
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Water confined within sub-nanometer graphene channels exhibits discrete molecular layering and transport properties that differ markedly from those of bulk water. Here, we use equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the structure and transport of SPC/E and TIP4P/2005 water confined between parallel graphene sheets with interlayer distances of 0.7-1.3 nm at several water densities. We evaluate the self-diffusion coefficient, interfacial friction coefficient, and effective shear viscosity, alongside analyses of hydrogen bonding, layer-assignment dynamics, and layer-resolved molecular mobility. All three transport coefficients exhibit a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence on confinement width, but their extrema do not necessarily coincide. Our analysis demonstrates that the count and spatial connectivity of the hydrogen-bond network, together with structural heterogeneity and geometric frustration near water-layer transition boundaries, are essential for understanding the nonmonotonic transport behavior and the differences between the water models.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations show that water’s diffusion, interfacial friction, and effective viscosity vary nonmonotonically with confinement between graphene sheets. articles.title_original: Electron dynamics in graphene irradiated by a quantum wave packet versus a classical point charge
articles.title_en: Quantum simulations reveal energy-dependent electron backscattering in graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Electron irradiation is essential for materials characterization and modification, though the fundamental interactions between incident electrons and host materials remain under investigation. Using quantum-mechanical first-principles simulations, we study electron dynamics under external irradiation. While we set out to quantify differences in key observables, including kinetic energy loss, secondary electron emission, and backscattered electrons between classical and quantum-mechanical descriptions of the incident electron, we uncover an unexpected regime in which their backscattering predictions differ markedly: At an incident energy of around 400 eV, the quantum wave packet yields a finite backscattering yield, while the sampled classical ensemble predicts a vanishing yield. This wave-packet backscattering yield remains finite and gradually decreases at higher incident energies. Our results provide clear guidance for selecting appropriate computational descriptions of incident electrons based on their kinetic energy. More importantly, our results identify a targeted experimental energy window in which the classical and quantum–mechanical descriptions of the incident electron can be sensitively benchmarked. This enables the rational design and characterization of 2D materials with quantum electronic effects via high-resolution electron-beam nanofabrication techniques.
articles.summary_en: First-principles simulations compare quantum wave-packet and classical point-charge descriptions of electron irradiation in graphene. They identify a pronounced difference near 400 eV, offering guidance for electron-beam characterization and nanofabrication of two-dimensional materials.

articles.title_original: MXene@SiC Nanocomposite-Modified Electrode for Sensitive Electrochemical Detection of Cadmium (II) Ions
articles.title_en: MXene–SiC Electrode Enables Sensitive Cadmium-Ion Detection
articles.excerpt_original: Cadmium (II) ions are highly toxic contaminants that can pose significant risks to environmental and human health, necessitating the development of sensitive and reliable analytical methods for their determination. In this study, an MXene@SiC nanocomposite-modified glassy carbon electrode (MXene@SiC/GCE) was developed for the electrochemical detection of Cd (II) ions. Carbon-based materials have been widely investigated for electrochemical sensing due to their high electrical conductivity, large specific surface area, and properties that enhance electron transfer. The MXene@SiC nanocomposite was prepared by combining Ti3C2Tx MXene and SiC at a 1:1 mass ratio. The structural and surface characteristics of the prepared materials were investigated by SEM, EDS, and FTIR analyses, confirming the successful integration of MXene and SiC. The electrochemical properties of the modified electrode were evaluated by cyclic voltammetry using the [Fe(CN)6]3−/[Fe(CN)6]4− redox probe. The effect of key experimental parameters, including scan rate, pH, accumulation time, and deposition potential, was investigated. The optimum conditions were found to be pH 5, an accumulation time of 350 s, and a deposition potential of −1.2 V. Under optimized conditions, the MXene@SiC/GCE exhibited a well-defined Cd(II) stripping response at approximately −0.9 V. Two linear concentration ranges were obtained: 0.5–1000 μg/L with the calibration equation I = 0.2932C + 1.5916 (R2 = 0.9893) and a higher concentration range with I = 0.04911C + 33.6442 (R2 = 0.9643). The developed electrode demonstrated a concentration-dependent response and satisfactory electrochemical characteristics, indicating that the MXene@SiC nanocomposite is a promising electrode-modifying material for Cd(II) determination in aqueous

articles.title_original: Engineering Multifunctional TBC/CHS–Ti3C2Tx MXene Nanocomposites for Photothermal-Assisted Antibacterial Wound Therapy

articles.excerpt_original: Bacterial biofilms drive wound chronicity and resist conventional antimicrobial therapies. To address this clinical bottleneck, we engineered a multifunctional, photothermally active sponge-like nanocomposite comprising TEMPO-oxidized bacterial cellulose (TBC), chitosan (CHS), and Ti3C2Tx MXene via in situ modification and cryogenic freeze-drying. Among the formulations evaluated, the TBC/CHS/5%MXene composite exhibited the highest water uptake and the lowest water contact angle, together with improved tensile properties. Upon near-infrared (NIR) irradiation (808 nm, 1.0 W·cm−2), the material rapidly reached 53–55 °C, confirming a pronounced MXene-driven photothermal response. This localized hyperthermia markedly enhanced antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, achieving reductions of 96% and 95%, respectively. Notably, in an ex vivo porcine skin biofilm model, 10 min of NIR irradiation resulted in a 99% reduction in viable bacterial counts, demonstrating pronounced antibiofilm activity. Furthermore, the composite demonstrated intrinsic hemostatic properties, high cytocompatibility, and hemocompatibility. Collectively, these findings support TBC/CHS/5%MXene as an NIR-responsive platform for further investigation of its efficacy and safety in preclinical models of infected wound healing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a bacterial-cellulose/chitosan/Ti3C2Tx MXene sponge that heats under near-infrared irradiation and reduced bacterial biofilms in laboratory and ex vivo porcine-skin models.
