articles.title_original: Metal–Organic Framework-Derived Magnetic Nanoparticles Inducing Interfacial Polarization Enabling MXene-Based Composite Films with High-Efficiency Electromagnetic Interference Shielding
articles.title_en: MXene Composite Films Achieve High EMI Shielding and Thermal Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: With outstanding conductivity, tunable structure, and rich surface functional groups, two-dimensional (2D) MXene is extensively used for the electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding field. However, MXene suffers from self-stacking and secondary reflection pollution, which weakens the electromagnetic wave (EMW) attenuation performance. Herein, we introduced one-dimensional (1D) PPy nanotubes (NTs) and (FeO)0.198(MnO)0.802 (FMO) magnetic nanoparticles derived from FeMn-metal-organic frameworks into the MXene system. Furthermore, combined with K+-induced filtration and freeze-drying technology, MXene/PPy NTs/FMO (MPFMO) composite films with three-dimensional (3D) porous structures were successfully constructed, thereby achieving significantly enhanced EMI shielding performances. The introduction of conductive PPy NTs not only refines the 3D conductive architecture embedded within the composite film but also induces forming hydrogen bonding and supports adjacent MXene nanosheets to increase the mechanical properties. The abundant heterogeneous interfaces can generate interfacial polarization and promote EMW absorption, and the intrinsic magnetic loss of FMO can further attenuate EMWs. Profiting from multiple synergy mechanisms, the MPFMO porous composite film delivers a high EMI SE of 62.43 dB, an absorption loss ratio of 72.50%, and specific shielding effectiveness SSEt of 1.21 × 104 dB cm2 g-1 at a thickness of only 55 μm. Notably, the as-prepared composite membrane also demonstrates a superior thermal conductivity of 18.82 W m-1 K-1.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed porous MXene/PPy nanotube/magnetic nanoparticle films that combine electromagnetic-wave absorption with shielding, reaching 62.43 dB EMI shielding effectiveness and 72.5% absorption at 55 μm thickness. The films also exhibited thermal conductivity of 18.82 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, indicating potential for multifunctional electromagnetic protection and thermal-management applications.

articles.title_original: Modulating FCC/HCP phase boundaries in inverse Co@BOx catalysts via crystal-phase-ratio variation for propane oxidative dehydrogenation
articles.title_en: Defect engineering boosts cobalt-boride catalyst performance for propane conversion
articles.excerpt_original: The oxidative dehydrogenation of propane offers a promising route to propylene, but developing low-temperature catalysts that simultaneously achieve high activity and selectivity remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a Co@BO x inverse catalyst featuring engineered defects localized at face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed phase boundaries within the subsurface cobalt promoter. Using an oxidative atmosphere-induced exsolution strategy, we continuously tune the face-centered cubic/hexagonal close-packed phase ratio, maximizing the density of stacking faults at a 1:1 phase ratio. Catalytic activity exhibits a strong positive correlation with stacking fault density, with the optimal Co F/H-1.0 @BO x catalyst achieving 32% propane conversion and 83% olefin selectivity at 450 °C—5.1 times that of pristine cobalt boride. Density functional theory reveals that stacking faults modulate Co atomic spacing, weakening the excessively strong BO x -Co interfacial interaction. In situ spectroscopy demonstrates that maximized stacking faults strengthen O-H bonds in surface boron hydroxyl species and optimize radical initiation kinetics. This work establishes subsurface defect engineering as a potential strategy to enhance oxide overlayer reactivity in inverse catalytic systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers tuned FCC/HCP phase ratios in an inverse Co@BOx catalyst to maximize stacking faults at phase boundaries. The optimized catalyst achieved 32% propane conversion and 83% olefin selectivity at 450°C, with activity linked to modified cobalt spacing and improved radical initiation kinetics.

articles.title_original: Metrology challenges and trends for through-glass vias in advanced semiconductor packaging
articles.title_en: Review identifies metrology challenges for through-glass vias in advanced packaging
articles.excerpt_original: Through-glass vias (TGVs) are emerging as a key technology for three-dimensional heterogeneous integration and advanced semiconductor packaging because of their low electrical loss, tailorable thermal expansion, and compatibility with large-format panel-level processing. However, the optical transparency, refractive properties, and brittleness of glass create significant inspection challenges, making reliable high-throughput metrology a major barrier to TGV manufacturing. This review presents a requirements-driven framework for TGV metrology that links fabrication processes and defect mechanisms to quantitative measurement needs. Key defects associated with laser ablation, laser-induced deep etching, and metallization including microcracks, nanovoids, sidewall roughness, via taper, copper protrusion, and thermomechanical cracking are examined. Representative metrology requirements include detection of sub-1 µm microcracks and sub-2 µm voids, characterization of sidewall roughness below 50 nm, taper-angle uncertainty below 0.1°, and panel-scale inspection at thousands of vias per second. Established and emerging techniques, including shadowgraphy, optical coherence tomography, spectral reflectometry, digital holographic microscopy, and two-photon fluorescence, are compared in terms of measurement capability, uncertainty, calibration, traceability, and throughput. No single technique currently meets the combined requirements for resolution, field of view, defect sensitivity, and high-volume throughput. Multimodal inspection, AI-assisted defect classification, physics-informed reconstruction, virtual metrology, and TGV-specific reference artifacts and standards are therefore identified as key directions toward robust, traceable, and scalable TGV metrology.
articles.summary_en: A review finds that inspecting through-glass vias remains difficult because glass transparency, optical properties and brittleness complicate detection of microcracks, voids and metallization defects at production scale. It highlights multimodal inspection, AI-assisted classification and physics-informed reconstruction as routes toward higher-throughput, traceable TGV manufacturing.

articles.title_original: Spin-Valley Relaxation of Rydberg Excitons
articles.title_en: Rydberg Excitons Enable Tunable Spin–Valley Dynamics in WSe₂
articles.excerpt_original: Rydberg excitons, characterized by large spatial extension and reduced electron-hole overlap, must have a spin-valley dynamics different from that of ground state excitons. Here we report a direct measurement of spin relaxation of Rydberg excitons in high-quality WSe₂ monolayer using continuous-wave and time-resolved optical orientation experiments. Excited excitonic states exhibit exceptionally large photoluminescence circular polarization, approaching 90% for the 3s state. Time-resolved measurements reveal a strong increase of the spin relaxation time with the principal quantum number, from ~2 ps for the 1s exciton to values larger than ~75 ps for the 3s exciton. A microscopic model based on electron-hole exchange-driven spin relaxation quantitatively reproduces the observed trend, demonstrating that Rydberg excitons enable tunable spin–valley dynamics in two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers directly measured spin relaxation in Rydberg excitons in monolayer WSe₂, finding that relaxation time increases from about 2 ps for 1s excitons to over 75 ps for 3s excitons. The results demonstrate tunable spin–valley dynamics relevant to two-dimensional semiconductor technologies.

articles.title_original: A Dual‐Mode Triple‐Signal Flexible Pressure Sensor Based on Laser‐Induced Graphene
articles.title_en: Laser-Induced Graphene Enables Reliable Dual-Mode Flexible Pressure Sensor
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Mechanical reliability is crucial for the application of flexible sensors that are frequently subjected to bending. Herein, to improve the mechanical reliability of flexible pressure sensors, a strategy based on signal redundancy and the complementary integration of piezocapacitive and piezoresistive sensing modes was used to implement a dual‐mode triple‐signal flexible pressure sensor. The sensor consists of a pair of interdigital electrodes, an Ecoflex elastomer loaded with a laser‐induced graphene (LIG) layer, and a bottom electrode. Under external pressure, the resistive channel formed by the interdigital electrodes and LIG layer generates a piezoresistive signal, whereas two capacitive channels formed by the interdigital electrodes, elastomer, and bottom electrode generate two piezocapacitive signals. Therefore, the sensor has two redundant signals, which obviously improves its mechanical reliability. Moreover, the sensor can operate in both piezocapacitive and piezoresistive modes simultaneously, which is beneficial for improving its overall performance through mode complementarity. In the piezocapacitive mode, the sensor exhibits sensitivities of 0.1602 kPa −1 and 0.1548 kPa −1 with response/recovery times of 92/128 ms and 76/114 ms, respectively. In the piezoresistive mode, the sensor has a high sensitivity of 38.64 kPa −1 with a response/recovery time of 100/83 ms. Furthermore, the sensor maintained reliable signal outputs after more than 4000 loading cycles, demonstrating excellent durability. The application in human motion monitoring shows that the sensor can effectively detect physiological signals while maintaining a consistent response of the three output channels. This work provides a new strategy for improving the mechanical reliability of flex
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a flexible pressure sensor combining piezoresistive and dual piezocapacitive channels for redundant, complementary signal outputs. The device achieved sensitivities up to 38.64 kPa−1 and retained reliable performance after more than 4,000 loading cycles, with demonstrated human-motion monitoring.

articles.title_original: Boron-Nitride-Doped Graphene Oxide FETs for COVID-19 Detection: A Comparative Review Against Existing Market Solutions
articles.title_en: BN-Doped Graphene Oxide FET Biosensor Reviewed for COVID-19 Detection
articles.excerpt_original: COVID-19 point-of-care tests return results faster than centralized RT-PCR, but none combines high sensitivity, speed, low cost, and ease of use. This review compares a boron-nitride-doped graphene oxide (BN-GO) FET biosensor with commercial diagnostics and other graphene-based FET biosensors using LOD, PPA/NPA, detection time, cost, shelf life, and ease of use. Because the BN-GO platform is at technology readiness level 4 and has been tested only in buffer, the market comparison is treated as a gap analysis. The BN-GO FET biosensor showed promising early-stage analytical performance, responding rapidly to N-protein in buffer at its lowest tested concentration, below the detection limits of the other graphene FETs compared. However, the lowest-concentration response was obtained from an initial set of device tests. Future studies will assess the repeatability, reproducibility, clinical performance, and manufacturing scalability of the device. They will also focus on extending its shelf life, because the current estimate falls short of the WHO target product profile and would complicate stockpiling and distribution. The estimated cost per test is approximately the same as that of rapid antigen tests. These findings position the BN-GO FET biosensor as a promising next-generation candidate for point-of-care COVID-19 diagnostics if the remaining cost and shelf-life challenges are addressed.
articles.summary_en: An MDPI review compares a boron-nitride-doped graphene oxide FET biosensor with commercial and other graphene-based COVID-19 diagnostics. The platform showed rapid, low-concentration detection in buffer, but remains at technology readiness level 4 with unresolved repeatability, clinical validation, scalability, and shelf-life challenges.

articles.title_original: Tunnel junctions polarization engineering in III-nitride heterostructures
articles.title_en: Polarization Engineering Advances III-Nitride Tunnel Junction Design
articles.excerpt_original: A classical p+/n+ tunnel junction is difficult to achieve in group-III nitride (III-N) semiconductors because of the high activation energy of acceptors. However, polarization engineering in III-N materials can be used to reduce the depletion width and enhance interband tunneling in p–n junctions. This can be achieved by incorporating an undoped III-N layer (iP layer) into a p–n junction to form a p–iP–n junction. The polarization charges associated with the iP-layer interfaces attract positive charge on one side and negative charge on the other. In this review, we discuss different configurations of polarization-induced tunnel junctions (PTJs) depending on substrate polarity, the built-in electric field associated with the junction orientation (p–n vs n–p), and the electric fields arising from polarization discontinuities at the interfaces. We identify the configurations in which polarization favors carrier tunneling through the iP layer and calculate and analyze the corresponding band bending and current–voltage (I–V) characteristics. These analyses show that the I–V characteristics depend strongly on the composition and thickness of the iP layer and can be non-intuitive, particularly when the interlayer composition is varied. This behavior follows from the coupled bandgap and polarization engineering inherent to p–iP–n junctions. Consequently, careful optimization of the tunnel interlayer is essential in the design of semiconductor devices incorporating PTJs. The comparative analysis of III-N PTJs is complemented by a review of recent experimental realizations and by an outlook on future applications of PTJs in III-N devices.
articles.summary_en: A review shows that inserting an undoped polarization-engineered III-nitride layer can reduce depletion width and enhance interband tunneling in p–n junctions. Tunnel-junction behavior depends strongly on interlayer composition, thickness, polarity, and orientation, making optimization critical for future III-nitride semiconductor devices.

articles.title_original: Recent advances in the synthesis of boron-stereogenic compounds
articles.title_en: Review of Recent Advances in Boron-Stereogenic Compound Synthesis
articles.excerpt_original: Tetracoordinate boron species represent a vital class of compounds in organoboron chemistry. Owing to their unique structural features and outstanding optoelectronic properties, they exhibit broad application potential in chemical synthesis, biomedicine, and materials engineering. However, systematic synthetic protocols for chiral tetracoordinate boron complexes remain scarce. Herein, we review recent advances in the construction of stereogenic tetracoordinate boron centers, organizing catalytic approaches into six classes according to the catalyst type: copper, palladium, rhodium, nickel/cobalt, organocatalysis, and phase-transfer catalysis. The transformations covered include desymmetrization, kinetic resolution, direct asymmetric B(sp 2 )-to-B(sp 3 ) conversion, and chirality transfer. This overview aims to inspire further development of efficient routes to chiral tetracoordinate boron compounds.
articles.summary_en: The review surveys catalytic methods for constructing chiral tetracoordinate boron centers, covering copper, palladium, rhodium, nickel/cobalt, organocatalytic, and phase-transfer catalysis. It highlights desymmetrization, kinetic resolution, asymmetric B(sp2)-to-B(sp3) conversion, and chirality transfer for applications in synthesis, biomedicine, and materials engineering.

articles.title_original: In-situ H 2 S annealing for stoichiometric residue-free MoS 2 film formation
articles.title_en: In-situ H₂S Annealing Produces Cleaner, More Crystalline MoS₂ Films
articles.excerpt_original: In-situ H2S annealing for stoichiometric residue-free MoS2 film formation was demonstrated in comparison with conventional sulfur vapor annealing (SVA) using low-vapor-pressure octasulfur. At 600◦C, both annealing methods produced stoichiometric MoS2 films, and the Raman and X-ray diﬀraction results exhibited higher crystallinity of the H2S-annealed film than that of the SVA-treated film. X- ray photoelectron spectroscopy revealed S-S residue only on the SVA-treated film, accompanied by a Fermi-level shift toward the valence band. A top-gated field-eﬀect transistor (FET) fabricated with the H2S-annealed film exhibited n-type operation.
articles.summary_en: In-situ H₂S annealing at 600°C produced stoichiometric MoS₂ films with higher crystallinity and no sulfur residue compared with conventional sulfur-vapor annealing. A top-gated FET using the H₂S-treated film showed n-type operation, supporting its relevance to semiconductor device fabrication.

articles.title_original: Surface functionalization strategies to improve the dispersion stability of MXene - A review
articles.title_en: Review of MXene Surface Functionalization for Improved Dispersion Stability
articles.summary_en: The review examines surface-functionalization strategies designed to improve the dispersion stability of MXenes. It provides a materials-processing perspective relevant to the broader deployment of MXenes, but no specific commercial application or company is identified.

articles.title_original: Review on Mechanical Characterization of Epoxy Based Bio Composites Reinforced with Halloysite and MXene for Bio Medical Application
articles.title_en: MXene–Halloysite Epoxy Biocomposites for Bone Scaffold Applications
articles.excerpt_original: This project focuses on the fabrication and analysis of an epoxy resin-based biocomposite reinforced with MXene and Halloysite nanotubes for potential bone scaffold applications. Epoxy resin is widely used in engineering because of its excellent mechanical strength, chemical resistance, and bonding characteristics. However, its inherent brittleness, low thermal conductivity, and non-conductive nature limit its use in advanced biomedical applications. To overcome these limitations, reinforcing materials such as MXene and Halloysite were incorporated into the epoxy matrix to improve its mechanical and biological performance. MXene is a two-dimensional nanomaterial known for its high electrical conductivity, large surface area, and excellent surface activity, while Halloysite is a naturally occurring tubular nanoclay that offers improved strength, biocompatibility, and eco-friendly characteristics. The combination of these materials with epoxy resin aims to produce a lightweight, durable, and biologically compatible composite suitable for tissue engineering and bone regeneration applications. Previous studies have demonstrated that both MXene and Halloysite can significantly enhance the mechanical and functional properties of polymer-based composites. The fabrication process involved selecting epoxy resin, hardener, MXene, and Halloysite, followed by dispersion using bath sonication to ensure uniform distribution of fillers. The mixture was then combined with hardener, poured into molds using the casting method, and allowed to cure at room temperature. Different filler concentrations of 0.5%, 1.0%, 1.5%, and 2.0% were prepared to evaluate the influence of reinforcement content on composite performance. articles.summary_en: Researchers review epoxy composites reinforced with MXene and halloysite nanotubes for potential tissue engineering and bone regeneration applications. The study evaluates filler concentrations from 0.5% to 2.0% to improve mechanical and biological performance, though the excerpt does not report final results.

articles.title_original: Polypyrrole–functionalized Ti3C2 MXene nanocomposite for highly sensitive electrochemical detection of Pb2+ ions
articles.title_en: Polypyrrole-Functionalized MXene Enables Sensitive Lead-Ion Detection
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a polypyrrole-functionalized Ti3C2 MXene nanocomposite for electrochemical detection of Pb2+ ions. The study indicates potential for improved lead monitoring through sensitive electrochemical sensing.

articles.title_original: Interfacial electronic and optical modulation of h-BN/ZnO composites
articles.title_en: h-BN/ZnO composites offer tunable ultraviolet optoelectronic properties
articles.excerpt_original: High performance low-dimensional hybrid systems with tunable electronic and optical properties have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation optoelectronic and photonic technologies due to their light-matter interactions and interfacial effects. The combination of ZnO and hexagonal boron-nitride may induce synergistic interfacial effects capable of modulating the optoelectronic signature. In this work, the structural stability, electronic structure and optical response of the h-BN/ZnO nanocomposites are systematically explored using first principle density functional theory. The adsorption process induces a significant reduction of the h-BN band gap while preserving its semiconducting character, with the extent of the modification strongly dependent on the adsorption geometry. Optical calculations demonstrate a highly anisotropic response, with negligible absorption in the infrared and visible regions and strong activity in the ultraviolet range. The perpendicular configurations exhibit sharper and more intense deep-ultraviolet resonances and enhanced reflectivity compared with the parallel arrangements. These findings demonstrate that the orientation of ZnO provides an effective mechanism for tuning the electronic and optical properties of h-BN/ZnO systems, highlighting their potential for ultraviolet optoelectronic and photonic applications.
articles.summary_en: Density functional theory indicates that ZnO orientation can modulate the electronic structure, anisotropic optical response, and deep-ultraviolet resonances of h-BN/ZnO nanocomposites. The findings support potential use in ultraviolet optoelectronic and photonic devices, but remain theoretical.

articles.title_original: Asymmetric and Scalable Electronic Hysteresis Induced by Ratchet-like Charge Injections in van der Waals Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Ratchet-like charge injection drives asymmetric hysteresis in graphene heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Anomalous ferroelectric-like electronic hysteresis has recently been reported in intrinsically nonpolar graphene/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) heterostructures and widely exploited to realize electrically switchable superconductivity, correlated insulators, and neuromorphic functionalities. The origin of this anomalous hysteresis is still under debate, hindering its applications. Among the proposals are moiré-driven charge transfer, twist angles between hBN, conductive sliding ferroelectricity and dielectric defects. Here we study the detailed hysteretic transport properties in dual-gated hBN/graphene/hBN heterostructures. Two devices that share the same moiré and twist angle configurations exhibit strikingly distinct hysteretic responses, allowing us to unambiguously rule out moiré-induced and twist-angle-related mechanisms. Moreover, the ratchet-like charge injections give rise to unconventional hysteresis that is pronouncedly asymmetric and continuously scalable with the sweeping range of external electric fields, in sharp contrast to conventional ferroelectric behavior with fixed coercive fields that is symmetric with respect to zero field. These observations challenge the theoretical scenario in terms of spontaneous interlayer electrical polarizations and lead us to consider the defects within hBN flakes. Our analysis and simulations suggest that the interplay between the defects and conducting channel plays an important role in inducing the ratchet-like charge injections and anomalous hysteresis. Our work provides more insight in the origin of electronic hysteresis in graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures, and the observations of asymmetric and scalable electronic hysteresis could lead to new-generation ultrafast memory and synaptic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers identify defect-mediated charge injection in hBN/graphene/hBN devices as the likely origin of anomalous electronic hysteresis, ruling out moiré and twist-angle mechanisms. The asymmetric, scalable response could support ultrafast memory and neuromorphic synaptic devices.

articles.title_original: Multiscale ensemble Monte Carlo of transport and gas sensing in monolayer MoS 2
articles.title_en: Monte Carlo model advances MoS₂ transport and gas-sensing design
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional semiconductors, such as monolayer MoS 2 , combine a technologically useful band gap with a thickness of three atomic planes. The entire carrier density then lies within a few Å of the surface, which makes them useful as field-effect-transistor channels and as chemically sensitive devices. Device design for MoS 2 needs a transport model whose scattering rates are computed rather than calibrated, whose predictions are tested against experiment, and that spans the scales from electron-phonon coupling to terminal current and sensor response. We present a self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo (EMC) framework for monolayer MoS 2 built on the ViennaEMC solver, which couples a Boltzmann transport model to Poisson’s equation with degenerate free-carrier statistics. The transport model carries wavevector-dependent acoustic, polar-optical, homopolar and intervalley phonon scattering within and between the K valleys and the spin–orbit-split Q valleys, together with remote substrate phonons, screened charged impurities and surface roughness. Every intrinsic input of the transport model is computed from first principles for this work, namely the band structure of the K and Q valleys, the phonon energies, sound velocities and dielectric response, and the electron-phonon couplings from density-functional perturbation theory matrix elements at 34 explicit phonon wavevectors and from Wannier interpolation with the two-dimensional long-range treatment. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a self-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo framework for monolayer MoS₂ that models carrier transport and gas-sensor response across multiple physical scales. The model derives intrinsic scattering inputs from first-principles calculations without fitted transport parameters and validates rates against an independent Boltzmann solution.

articles.title_original: 2D Ferroelectric NbOCl2 Vertical Heterojunction with Asymmetric Contact Areas toward Ultra-Low-Limit Self-Powered X-ray Detection and Synaptic Functions
articles.title_en: Graphene–NbOCl2 heterojunction enables self-powered X-ray detection and synaptic functions
articles.excerpt_original: X-ray detection is advancing toward high efficiency, low power consumption, and intelligence, yet traditional detectors and materials are plagued by inherent limitations. Fueled by the demand for “detection-synapse” integration, two-dimensional (2D) wide-bandgap semiconductors have emerged as a key research focus. Among these, 2D NbOCl2 stands out as a promising candidate to overcome technical bottlenecks: it exhibits a wide bandgap of 2.75 eV, and its in-plane polarization-induced built-in electric field effectively facilitates the separation of photogenerated carriers─laying a critical material foundation for high-performance detection. Employing two graphene (Gr) layers as electrodes, this work reports a vertical Gr/NbOCl2/Gr heterojunction device, which achieves stable self-powered X-ray detection and synaptic behaviors via the intrinsic in-plane polarization of NbOCl2 and differences in electrode contact areas. It achieves a detection limit of 0.29 μGy s–1 and a sensitivity of 7.6 × 106 μC Gy–1 cm–2, demonstrating superior self-powered detection capability. Notably, the device displays distinct synaptic behaviors: positive bias induces potentiation, negative bias triggers depression, and its paired-pulse facilitation and depression reach 112% and 86% at a 1.5 s pulse interval, respectively. The integration of exceptional detection performance and synaptic functions underpins the advancement of next-generation X-ray detection toward miniaturization, integration, and intelligence.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a vertical graphene/NbOCl2/graphene heterojunction using asymmetric electrode areas, achieving self-powered X-ray detection with a 0.29 μGy s−1 detection limit and 7.6 × 10^6 μC Gy−1 cm−2 sensitivity. The device also exhibited synaptic potentiation, depression, and paired-pulse responses, supporting integrated intelligent detector applications.

articles.title_original: Rapid fabrication of customizable laser-induced graphene microelectrode arrays
articles.title_en: Dual-Laser Fabrication Enables High-Resolution Graphene Microelectrode Arrays
articles.excerpt_original: Laser-induced graphene (LIG) electrodes fabricated by CO2 laser scribing have been widely utilized in bioelectronic and sensing applications due to their compatibility with flexible substrates and scalable, cleanroom-free production. The digitally programmable nature of this process enables rapid and customizable electrode patterning. However, the relatively large spot size of the CO2 laser limits fabrication resolution and prevents device miniaturization. Here, we report a novel dual-laser approach for the direct writing of high-resolution, multiplexed, and integrated LIG microelectrode arrays with tunable structural and electrochemical properties. LIG electrodes were fabricated by CO2 laser scribing of flexible polyimide (PI) films. Optimization of the laser power and scribing speed generated LIG electrode tracks with a low sheet resistance (19.2 ± 0.30 Ω sq−1). Raman spectroscopy and scanning electron microscopy confirmed the formation of a three-dimensional, porous graphene-like structure. Device miniaturization was achieved through femtosecond laser micromachining of the PI adhesive insulation layer, producing microelectrode openings with diameters of 20–60 μm. Cyclic voltammetry, differential pulse voltammetry, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) demonstrated a size-dependent enhancement in electrochemical performance. The 30 μm LIG microelectrodes exhibited low electrode-to-electrode and device-to-device variability in 1 kHz impedance (coefficients of variation = 3.13–6.17% and 2.52%, respectively), while maintaining their mechanical integrity, electrical conductivity, and electrochemical performance even after 100 bending cycles at 150° (5.31% ± 2.64% increase in 1 kHz impedance). articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a mask-free dual-laser process for customizable laser-induced graphene microelectrode arrays on flexible polyimide films. The approach produced 20–60 μm electrode openings with stable electrical and electrochemical performance after repeated bending, supporting miniaturized flexible sensing devices.

articles.title_original: Bifunctional Catalytic Performance of Bimetallic MXene-Supported Co Single-Atom Catalysts for Overall Water Splitting: A First-Principles Study
articles.title_en: Bimetallic MXene-Supported Cobalt Catalysts Studied for Overall Water Splitting
articles.summary_en: A first-principles study evaluates bimetallic MXene-supported cobalt single-atom catalysts for bifunctional activity in overall water splitting. The work provides computational insight into catalyst design for hydrogen production, but does not report experimental validation or commercialization.

articles.title_original: All-Dielectric Near-Field Stokes Skyrmions from Spin-Redirection Berry Phase
articles.title_en: hBN Waveguide Enables Near-Field Optical Skyrmions for On-Chip Photonics
articles.excerpt_original: Optical skyrmions have been explored predominantly in free-space structured fields, whereas their realization in low-loss dielectric near-field platforms remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate spin–orbit conversion mediated by the spin-redirection Berry phase in a suspended-layer dielectric waveguide of wide-bandgap hexagonal boron nitride (hBN), producing near-field Stokes skyrmions and their symmetry-controlled lattices. Projection onto the rotating TE basis introduces a spin-dependent geometric phase, imprinting orbital angular momentum on the guided field. Under circularly polarized excitation, simulated Stokes-parameter maps reveal near-field optical skyrmions. By further exploiting boundary symmetry, we show that these textures can be reorganized into Meron and hybrid vortex–saddle lattices. The underlying mechanism is supported by photoemission electron microscopy measurements and simulation analysis. This work establishes a dielectric platform for geometric-phase engineering of near-field skyrmions, providing a route toward on-chip topological photonics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated near-field Stokes skyrmions and related meron and vortex–saddle lattices in a suspended hexagonal boron nitride dielectric waveguide. The work uses spin-redirection Berry phase engineering and could support future on-chip topological photonics.

articles.title_original: Predicting resistive-pulse signatures in nanopores by accurately modeling access regions
articles.title_en: Model improves nanopore resistive-pulse sensing accuracy
articles.excerpt_original: Resistive pulse sensing is used to characterize and count single particles in solution moving through channels under an electric bias, with nanoscale pores providing enough spatial resolution for single-molecule identification and sequencing. This technique commonly relies on measuring the ionic current change produced by the passage of a molecule and, through conductance models, translating the blockage signal into molecular dimensions. However, no generalized model exists that considers the resistive contributions of the pore exterior, i.e. the access regions, when obstructed by a molecule. This is becoming increasingly important with the advent of 2D materials and ultrathin membranes featuring low aspect ratio pores. In this work, a general method by which to model the resistance of access regions in the presence of an insulating obstruction is presented. Thin oblate spheroidal slices are used to partition access regions and infer their conductance when blocked by differently shaped objects. We show that our model accurately estimates the blocked-state conductance of 2D and finite-length pores in the presence of simple or complex structures positioned at varying distances from the pore opening. The model is shown to capture off-axis effects by predicting deeper blockages for obstructions offset from the pore’s central axis. A model-based web app was created to predict the electrical signatures of a wide range of molecule geometries translocating through differently shaped pores. The introduced model and accompanying tool will help guide future experimental designs and thus present a straightforward way to extend the quantification of the resistive pulse technique at the nanoscale.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a model that accounts for electrical resistance in nanopore access regions when molecules obstruct the pore. The method captures effects from pore geometry, obstruction shape, position and off-axis translocation, and includes a web app to support nanoscale sensing experiments.

articles.title_original: Atomically ordered few-layer molybdenum boride MBenes for enhanced electromagnetic response
articles.title_en: Atomically Ordered MoB MBenes Deliver Broad Electromagnetic Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional transition metal borides (MBenes), boride analogues of MXenes, combine layered frameworks with tunable surface chemistry, yet high-quality MBenes remain difficult to access. Existing methods for preparing MBenes often suffer from incomplete dealumination, Mo 2 AlB 2 intermediate-phase formation, multilayer restacking, or Mo vacancies. Here, we report a Lewis-acid molten-salt route that converts MoAlB into few-layer MoB MBene nanosheets with an atomically ordered Mo−B framework and a low density of Mo vacancies. Comparative thermodynamic calculations and control experiments with ZnCl 2 , ZnBr 2 , ZnF 2 , and ZnS identify molten ZnBr 2 as the preferred etchant for redox-driven Al extraction and delamination. Temperature-dependent free-energy analysis and Mo−Al−B ternary isothermal sections further define 700 °C as a processing window that suppresses Mo 2 AlB 2 formation and promotes direct conversion from MoAlB to MoB MBene. Selective Al extraction from MoAlB produces few-layer MoB MBene, retaining an ordered Mo−B framework while inducing b -axis contraction, strengthened Mo−B covalency, and enhanced electron localization. Together with O/OH and Br surface terminations, these structural and electronic features promote multiple polarizations and enable an effective absorption bandwidth of 8.7 GHz at 2.1 mm. This theory-informed molten-salt etching strategy expands redox-mediated MBene synthesis and connects atomically ordered few-layer MoB MBene with electromagnetic functionality.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed few-layer molybdenum boride (MoB) MBene nanosheets using a molten ZnBr₂ etching process that limits vacancies, restacking, and unwanted intermediate phases. The material achieved an effective electromagnetic absorption bandwidth of 8.7 GHz at 2.1 mm, indicating potential for electromagnetic-management applications.

articles.title_original: Fast-switching monolayer MoSiGeN$$_4$$ transistors: device performance at sub-5 nm high-performance nodes
articles.title_en: MoSiGeN₄ Transistor Shows Sub-5 nm Switching Potential
articles.excerpt_original: The scaling limits of silicon-based transistors have driven the search for two-dimensional field-effect transistors capable of high-speed and energy-efficient operation at sub-5-nm gate lengths. This work presents a double-gated n-type field-effect transistor built from monolayer Janus MoSiGeN\((_4)\), a two-dimensional semiconductor, evaluated using first-principles density functional theory combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function formalism. On-state current, subthreshold swing, intrinsic delay, and power-delay product are examined across gate lengths from 2 to 5 nm. Without any source or drain underlap, the device satisfies International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors high-performance targets projected for the year 2028, down to a 4-nm gate length. Introducing a modest underlap restores electrostatic control at shorter channels, extending compliant scaling to a 2-nm gate length while boosting the on-state current to the roadmap target. Most notably, the intrinsic delay and power-delay product remain far below roadmap limits across every gate length studied, falling as low as 0.006 ps and 0.004 fJ/\((\mu)\)m, respectively, well over an order of magnitude below the corresponding 2028 targets. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of such switching speed and energy-efficiency potential in this material, with performance metrics substantially exceeding roadmap requirements. These findings establish the double-gated monolayer MoSiGeN\((_4)\) field-effect transistor as a compelling device for next-generation high-speed, energy-efficient logic beyond the 5-nm node.
articles.summary_en: First-principles and non-equilibrium Green’s function simulations indicate that double-gated monolayer Janus MoSiGeN₄ transistors could meet projected high-performance targets at gate lengths down to 2 nm with underlap engineering. The modeled devices show exceptionally low intrinsic delay and power-delay product, highlighting potential for next-generation logic beyond the 5-nm node.

articles.title_original: Global Structure Search of Single Atom Platinum Adsorbed on Graphene Flake Edges
articles.title_en: Study Maps Platinum Single-Atom Structures at Graphene Edges
articles.excerpt_original: Using a global optimization algorithm, we explored structures of edge-adsorbed platinum single atom on the graphene edge. This was modeled with a small molecular fragment of flake graphene, enabling flexible modeling of the graphene edge with different coordination environments. We identified structures with different numbers of carbon and hydrogen atoms depending on the hydrogen chemical potential and discuss their catalytic reactivity towards the oxygen reduction reaction.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used global optimization to identify how hydrogen chemical potential shapes the coordination of single platinum atoms adsorbed at graphene flake edges. The work also evaluates the structures’ catalytic reactivity toward the oxygen reduction reaction, supporting catalyst design research.

articles.title_original: Hybrid Plasmon-Phonon Eigenmodes and Vortex States in a Graphene Ring on a Silica Substrate
articles.title_en: Graphene Ring Enables Hybrid Plasmon–Phonon Vortex States
articles.excerpt_original: We investigate hybrid plasmon-phonon eigenmodes and localized electromagnetic vortex states in a graphene ring supported by a dispersive silica substrate. The interaction between graphene plasmons and infrared-active optical phonons of the substrate gives rise to distinct spectral branches of surface polaritons, whose dispersion characteristics are established analytically and validated by full-wave numerical simulations. Geometric confinement of these hybrid surface excitations produces spectrally separated families of localized multipolar eigenmodes with corresponding azimuthal symmetries. Particular attention is devoted to quadrupolar eigenstates, which exhibit nearly identical normalized spatial field distributions despite their substantial spectral separation and different attenuation characteristics. We demonstrate that coherent superposition of orthogonal quadrupolar field patterns gives rise to localized vortex states with opposite azimuthal phase winding. The preservation of the spatial eigenmode structure across distinct spectral branches is consistent with a quasistatic description in which the resonator geometry governs the modal symmetry, whereas the dispersive material response determines the spectral properties. These findings reveal a route toward controlling structured electromagnetic near fields through plasmon--phonon hybridization and establish a physical basis for multiband vortex states in deeply subwavelength graphene resonators.
articles.summary_en: Researchers model and simulate hybrid plasmon–phonon eigenmodes in a graphene ring on silica, identifying localized multipolar modes with distinct spectral branches. Coherent quadrupolar-mode superposition produces oppositely winding electromagnetic vortex states, suggesting multiband near-field control in deeply subwavelength resonators.

articles.title_original: Antiferromagnetic semiconductor NdAsTe: a new member of LnAsTe (Ln = Lanthanoids) compounds
articles.title_en: NdAsTe Identified as an Antiferromagnetic Semiconductor
articles.excerpt_original: Rare-earth-based intermetallic compounds are at the forefront of materials science, providing valuable insights into the interplay among magnetism, topology, and structural correlations. The interesting properties of these materials, driven by localized 4-electrons, strong spin-orbit coupling, and crystal electric field effect, make them a focal point in solid-state physics for designing advanced functional materials. We have synthesized NdAsTe using the solid-state reaction route and explored the temperature and field-dependent magnetic properties, which demonstrate long-range antiferromagnetic (AFM) ordering belowK. The low-temperature Curie-Weiss temperatureK implies a net AFM interaction between theions. Furthermore, the isothermal magnetization data exhibit signatures of spin-reorientation of the AFM-aligned spins at, corroborated through magnetic entropy studies. The signature of AFM transition is also manifested as a peak atin the temperature-dependent specific heat which gradually shifts towards lower temperatures at higher applied fields. The derived parameters from specific heat data suggest the presence of strong electronic correlations in NdAsTe. The magnetic susceptibility and specific heat data suggest that the magnetic ground state is a Kramers' doublet with effective spinat low temperatures. The electrical transport study revealed the semiconducting nature with a band gap of 70 MeV. Furthermore, the low temperature (20 K) magnetotransport studies unfold a crossover from positive to negative magnetoresistance behavior.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized NdAsTe and found antiferromagnetic ordering, spin reorientation, strong electronic correlations, and semiconducting behavior with a reported 70 meV band gap. Low-temperature magnetotransport also showed a crossover from positive to negative magnetoresistance, highlighting potential relevance for magnetic semiconductor research.

articles.title_original: Limiting Absorption Principle for Long-Range Perturbation in a Graphene Setting
articles.title_en: Limiting Absorption Principle for Long-Range Perturbation in a Graphene Setting

articles.title_original: Competing intraflake and interflake effects of functionalization on thermal transport in graphene aerogels
articles.title_en: Functionalization Effects on Thermal Transport in Graphene Aerogels
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines how functionalization affects thermal transport through competing intraflake and interflake mechanisms in graphene aerogels. The findings may inform graphene-aerogel design for thermal-management applications.

articles.title_original: GMG Signs Service Agreement with the UK Battery Industrialisation Centre to Manufacture G(R)CELLS in the United Kingdom - TradingView

articles.title_original: Phonons in Multilayer Graphene Flakes
articles.title_en: Study models phonons and heat transport in multilayer graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract― The phonon properties of monolayer, bilayer, and trilayer graphene are theoretically investigated using the valence force field (VFF) model. Phonon dispersion relations and group velocities are calculated, and changes in the phonon spectrum with increasing number of layers are analyzed. For monolayer graphene, the group velocities of long-wavelength TA and LA phonons are approximately 14 and 21 km/s, respectively. It is shown that weak interlayer coupling leads to the splitting of phonon branches, which is most pronounced near the center of the Brillouin zone. The low-frequency flexural ZA modes are the most sensitive to interlayer coupling, with their splitting persisting over a significantly broader range of wave vectors. The obtained results are important for further analysis of phonon-mediated heat transport in multilayer graphene structures.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical research uses a valence force field model to calculate phonon dispersion and group velocities in monolayer, bilayer, and trilayer graphene. It finds weak interlayer coupling splits phonon branches, with flexural ZA modes especially sensitive, informing analysis of heat transport in multilayer graphene structures.

articles.title_original: Carbon nanotube and graphene-based nanomaterials for perovskite solar cells
articles.title_en: Review Examines Graphene and Carbon Nanotubes in Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.excerpt_original: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have surpassed 27% power conversion efficiency, yet long-term stability and scalable manufacturing remain key barriers to commercialization. Carbon nanotubes (CNTs), graphene, and their derivatives offer promising solutions owing to their excellent electrical, optical, and mechanical properties. This review highlights their applications in PSC electrodes, charge-transport layers, and interfaces, focusing on charge extraction, interface engineering, and device stability. Key challenges, including film uniformity, reproducibility, and large-area fabrication, are also discussed, along with strategies for developing efficient, durable, and scalable carbon-based PSCs.
articles.summary_en: The review assesses graphene-based materials and carbon nanotubes for perovskite solar-cell electrodes, charge-transport layers, and interfaces. It identifies charge extraction and stability benefits while highlighting unresolved challenges in film uniformity, reproducibility, and large-area manufacturing.

articles.title_original: High-sensitivity multi-band graphene terahertz absorber and its applications in multi-channel biosensing
articles.title_en: Graphene Terahertz Metasurface Enables Multichannel Biosensing
articles.excerpt_original: Terahertz (THz) metasurface biosensors integrated with twodimensional materials offer immense promise for labelfree pointofcare diagnostics by exploiting characteristic molecular fingerprinting and nonionizing radiation. However, existing THz sensors frequently suffer from single or dualband limitations that hinder multiplex analyte detection, strong angularpolarization susceptibility, and an inherent compromise between dynamic electrical tunability and high refractiveindex (RI) sensitivity. Here, a multiband grapheneassisted metaldielectricmetal (MDM) terahertz metasurface biosensor operating across 1–8 THz is proposed. By integrating four nested split decagonalring resonators, the metasurface supports three distinct, sharp resonance modes at 2.68 THz, 4.22 THz, and 6.22 THz, with the highfrequency mode exhibiting the peak RI response. Owing to its rotational symmetry, the proposed design achieves polarization insensitivity and maintains robust angular stability under oblique incidence up to 70°. Furthermore, patterned graphene patches—comprising a central circular patch and four corner rectangular elements—impart dynamic electrical reconfigurability via electrostatic gate tuning. Fullwave electromagnetic simulations demonstrate exceptional sensing performance: a maximum sensitivity of 1.34 THz/RIU, a quality factor of 14.82, and an optimal figureofmerit (FOM) of 3.17 RIU-1. Numerical investigations confirm its utility in quantifying hemoglobin concentrations, distinguishing pharmaceutical solvents, and identifying trace pathogens and pesticide residues. This threeband dynamically reconfigurable platform presents a versatile solution for multiplexed, labelfree biochemical sensing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a graphene-assisted terahertz metasurface biosensor operating across 1–8 THz with three tunable resonance modes. Simulations indicate polarization-insensitive, angularly stable detection of biomolecular and chemical targets, including hemoglobin, solvents, pathogens, and pesticide residues.

articles.title_original: Electron-phonon coupling across the TMD/hBN van der Waals interface
articles.title_en: Study reveals remote electron–phonon coupling at TMD/hBN interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Many-body interactions can couple electronic states in one layer with collective excitations in the adjacent layer, providing a route to tailor properties of heterostructures. However, detecting and quantifying interlayer many-body interactions proved a major challenge. Here, we demonstrate that quasiparticles in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are dressed by a remote cloud of phonons in the adjacent hexagonal boron nitride slab. Using angle resolved photoemission, we identify replica bands in the TMDs which are a clear fingerprint of long-range electron-phonon interaction. We develop a modified Fröhlich model that shows semi-quantitative agreement with the experimental spectral functions. Our analysis shows that remote electron-phonon coupling is a generic property of interfaces with hBN. This has implications for electron mobilities in 2D materials, for superconductivity and possibly for moire correlated phases.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used angle-resolved photoemission to identify replica bands showing that phonons in adjacent hBN couple to quasiparticles in monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides. The findings could inform engineering of electron mobility, superconductivity and moiré phases in two-dimensional heterostructures.

articles.title_original: Conundrum edge orientation of hBN islands on Ir(111) resolved
articles.title_en: Study resolves edge-orientation behavior in hBN islands on iridium
articles.excerpt_original: The longstanding debate on armchair versus zigzag edges of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN islands), grown by thermal decomposition of borazine on Ir(111), is resolved. Both types do exist and they emerge at different temperatures. We report an in-situ growth study of hBN/Ir(111) by combining LEEM (Low Energy Electron Microscopy) with μLEED (selected area Low Energy Electron Diffraction) in a broad range of experimental parameters. During growth on the pristine surface at low temperature, we observe mainly armchair-type edges along the three equivalent <11-2> directions. This holds for spatially separated local areas with either <1-10> or <11-2> as prevailing step directions. The difference with graphene, for which the zigzag-type has been established as the preferred edge orientation, is attributed to the often-discarded ionic contribution to the intra-planar bonding in hBN. Growth at high temperature yields predominantly zigzag-type edges of the hBN islands, running along the three equivalent <1-10> azimuth directions, again irrespective of the prevailing <1-10> or <11-2> edges on the underlying local surface. This is attributed to the availability of atomic boron, inherently present upon the onset of BN bond breaking at high temperatures, in line with earlier Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations. Our present data on hBN growth are rationalized with BN dimers as building blocks and several degrees of their dissociation, varying from absent to complete.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that hBN islands grown on Ir(111) develop predominantly armchair edges at low temperatures and zigzag edges at high temperatures. The findings attribute this transition to ionic bonding effects and the availability of atomic boron during high-temperature growth.

articles.title_original: Interfacial reactions and properties of tungsten–silicon nitride composites prepared by spark plasma sintering
articles.title_en: Study examines interfaces in tungsten–silicon nitride composites
articles.excerpt_original: Tungsten–silicon nitride (W/Si₃N₄) composite ceramics were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1650–1800 °C with W contents of 0–20 vol%. The effects of processing on interfacial reactions, microstructure and properties were examined by X-ray diffraction, microscopy and property measurements. W₅Si₃ was detected in the specimens sintered at 1650 and 1800 °C, while its peaks were not resolved at 1700–1750 °C. A change in local nitrogen transport during densification is proposed as a possible explanation for this temperature dependence. In the WSN20 specimen sintered at 1750 °C, atomic-resolution TEM revealed a local W/Y₂O₃ contact. The two reported lattice spacings differed by approximately 1.29% in one dimension. This interfacial structure is considered alongside the measured mechanical properties and thermal conductivity. The observations identify a temperature-dependent phase response and an oxide-derived metal/ceramic interface for further investigation; the effects of local nitrogen pressure and interfacial bonding on bulk properties remain to be established.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigated tungsten–silicon nitride composite ceramics produced by spark plasma sintering, identifying temperature-dependent formation of W₅Si₃ and a localized tungsten/yttria interface. The findings clarify interfacial and phase behavior, while the implications for bulk mechanical and thermal properties require further study.

articles.title_original: Hierarchical Multidimensional Al 2 O 3 / BNNSs Networks for Enhanced Elevated‐Temperature Tribological Performance of PEI Composite Films
articles.title_en: Hierarchical Alumina–BNNS PEI Films Improve High-Temperature Wear and Heat Dissipation
articles.excerpt_original: Polyetherimide (PEI)‐based composites for sliding components at elevated temperatures require simultaneous heat dissipation and wear resistance, whereas conventional particulate reinforcement often cannot effectively provide both functions. In this work, hierarchical Al 2 O 3 /boron nitride nanosheets (BNNSs)/PEI composite films were fabricated by electrospinning followed by hot pressing. Compared with conventional blending and casting, this route can better confine and orient the fillers and construct hybrid architectures for thermal transport and sliding interfaces while suppressing agglomeration and nanosheet restacking. The effects of filler composition on fiber morphology, thermal conductivity, and dry‐sliding tribological behavior were systematically investigated. The 5% Al 2 O 3 /5% BNNSs/PEI composite exhibited the best overall performance. At room temperature, its steady‐state coefficient of friction reached approximately 0.26 and its specific wear rate was reduced by 76.2% relative to neat PEI. At 100°C under a load of 5 N, the composite maintained a coefficient of friction of approximately 0.35 and showed a 46.9% reduction in wear rate. Its thermal conductivity reached 0.422 W m −1 K −1 at 100°C. Wear‐track and counterpart‐surface observations indicate that the hybrid fillers promote a more stable transfer film, while BNNS‐containing transport pathways facilitate frictional‐heat dissipation. These results establish a processing–structure–property strategy for developing PEI‐based composites with combined thermal‐management and wear‐resistant functions under elevated‐temperature sliding conditions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers fabricated electrospun and hot-pressed polyetherimide composite films containing alumina and boron nitride nanosheets. The optimized formulation reduced wear by up to 76.2% at room temperature and maintained improved tribological performance at 100°C, while enhancing thermal conductivity.

articles.title_original: Coupled carrier transport and fractional-order thermoelastic dynamics in porous semiconductors with spatial–temporal nonlocality
articles.title_en: Modeling Nonlocal Thermoelasticity in Porous Semiconductors
articles.excerpt_original: This study develops a unified analytical framework to investigate the coupled thermoelastic response of porous semiconductor material under the fractional-order Lord–Shulman thermoelastic model. A spatiotemporal nonlocal elasticity theory, introduced and systematically developed by Lazar and Agiasofitou 59 by taking into account one dynamical scalar nonlocal kernel, is employed. In line with this theory, the isotropic nonlocal elasticity model of Klein–Gordon type, incorporating both a characteristic internal length scale and an essential internal time scale parameter, is adopted 59 , 60 . The primary objective is to examine how nonlocal interactions, thermal memory, carrier transport, and porosity collectively influence the thermo-mechanical behavior of semiconductor media under thermal loading. A two-dimensional semi-infinite porous semiconductor subjected to mechanical loading and thermal shock is formulated. The governing equations describing displacement, temperature, carrier density, void volume fraction, equilibrated stresses, and mechanical stresses are derived using the Klein–Gordon nonlocal framework and the fractional-order Lord–Shulman heat conduction model. The resulting system is solved analytically using the normal mode technique, while numerical simulations for silicon are performed to investigate the effects of spatial and temporal nonlocality. Heat-map visualizations are also employed to illustrate the spatial evolution of the physical fields. The numerical results reveal that spatial nonlocality redistributes stresses, modifies displacement fields, enhances carrier diffusion, and attenuates thermal responses through long-range interactions, whereas temporal nonlocality governs memory-dependent thermal relaxation, delayed energy transport, and wave pro
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an analytical framework combining carrier transport, fractional heat conduction, porosity, and spatial–temporal nonlocality in semiconductor materials. Simulations for silicon indicate that nonlocal effects alter stress distribution, carrier diffusion, and thermal relaxation under loading and thermal shock.

articles.title_original: Process and interface engineering of 2D TMDs for CMOS integration
articles.title_en: Process Engineering Challenges for 2D TMD CMOS Integration
articles.excerpt_original: Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) offer excellent electrostatic control for scaled transistors, but their integration into complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology requires careful control of surface and buried-interface conditions throughout fabrication. This review focuses mainly on MoS 2 and WS 2 , while selected examples involving WSe 2 , MoSe 2 , and MoTe 2 are discussed in the context of p-channel and complementary-device requirements. Particular emphasis is placed on how growth and transfer influence subsequent processing steps, including wet cleaning, lithography, doping, contact formation, and dielectric deposition, through changes in defects, contamination, charge states, and surface morphology. Representative device demonstrations are evaluated with consideration of their measurement conditions, CMOS roadmap targets, and the important distinction between individual devices, wafer-scale integration, and manufacturing-level qualification. Key challenges discussed include stable polarity control, carrier-density-dependent contact resistance, gate-stack capacitance, and the balance between promoting dielectric nucleation and preserving the underlying TMD channel. The review also considers how the processing history of the material influences chemical and structural properties, electrical variability, downstream process compatibility, and reliability. Although significant progress has been made in low-temperature processing and wafer-scale demonstrations, further validation across complete process flows and statistically meaningful device populations is needed to establish manufacturing-qualified complementary CMOS and monolithic three-dimensional integration.
articles.summary_en: A review examines how growth, transfer, cleaning, lithography, doping, contacts, and dielectric deposition affect MoS₂, WS₂, and related TMD performance in CMOS devices. It highlights remaining challenges in polarity control, contact resistance, dielectric integration, process compatibility, variability, and manufacturing-scale validation.

articles.title_original: 2D Materials as SERS Substrates for the Detection of DNA and its Constituents
articles.title_en: 2D Materials Advance SERS Detection of DNA
articles.excerpt_original: Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) has emerged as a powerful ultrasensitive and label-free analytical technique for the detection of nucleic acids, including DNA and its constituents. Although conventional noble-metal-based substrates such as gold and silver provide strong electromagnetic enhancement, their practical implementation is often limited by chemical instability, reproducibility issues, and biocompatibility concerns. In recent years, two-dimensional (2D) materials have attracted growing interest as alternative or hybrid SERS platforms due to their atomically thin architectures, high surface-to-volume ratios, tunable electronic properties, and their ability to facilitate charge-transfer-driven chemical enhancement. This review highlights recent advances in the application of representative 2D materials, including graphene, molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), and black phosphorene (BP), for SERS-based detection of DNA and its constituents. Unlike previous reviews that primarily focus on plasmonic SERS substrates or provide a broad overview of 2D materials, this review presents a dedicated comparative analysis of graphene, MoS2, and BP for DNA-related SERS applications. Particular emphasis is placed on correlating enhancement mechanisms, sensing performance, and reported limits of detection (LODs) to identify the strengths, limitations, and future opportunities of each material platform. Their enhancement mechanisms, sensing performance, stability, and biocompatibility are comparatively analyzed. Graphene demonstrates excellent chemical stability and fluorescence quenching capability, while MoS2 offers versatile surface chemistry and efficient integration with plasmonic nanostructures. articles.summary_en: A review compares graphene, MoS2 and black phosphorene as surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy substrates for detecting DNA and its constituents. Graphene offers chemical stability and fluorescence quenching, while the materials’ enhancement mechanisms, sensitivity, stability and biocompatibility are assessed for biosensing applications.

articles.title_en: Simulations Assess Monolayer SnTe FETs for Sub-5 nm Electronics
articles.excerpt_original: First-principles quantum transport simulations reveal the potential of monolayer SnTe FETs for sub-5 nm applications, demonstrating competitive power-delay performance and energy efficiency among emerging two-dimensional semiconductor devices.
articles.summary_en: First-principles quantum-transport modeling indicates that monolayer tin telluride (SnTe) field-effect transistors could offer competitive power-delay performance and energy efficiency at sub-5 nm dimensions. The findings position SnTe as a candidate for emerging two-dimensional semiconductor devices, subject to experimental validation.

articles.title_original: Boron removal using magnetic graphene oxide: structural, surface, and adsorption properties
articles.title_en: Magnetic graphene oxide removes up to 69% of boron while enabling magnetic separation
articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, graphene oxide (GO), magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) and magnetic graphene oxide samples (Fe2:1GO and Fe4:1GO) were synthesized to investigate the effect of MNP on the removal of boron from aqueous solutions. FTIR, Vibrating Sample Magnetometry (VSM), N2 adsorption-desorption and surface zeta potential analyses were performed. FTIR spectra confirmed the presence of characteristic GO functional groups (C-O, C=C, C=O) and Fe-O stretching vibrations in the MNP samples.VSM analysis demonstrated that magnetic nanoparticle incorporation effectively imparted magnetic properties to the GO samples; however, at higher MNP loadings, the saturation magnetization decreased, which is attributed to increased structural disorder. Adsorption experiments revealed that GO exhibited the highest boron removal efficiency (94%), which is considered to the abundance of negatively charged (-OH-), and (-COOH-) functional groups on its surface. Among the magnetic samples, Fe2:1GO showed the best overall performance, achieving a high boron removal efficiency (69%) while also exhibiting favorable magnetic properties. The study confirms that controlled incorporation of magnetite into GO can achieve magnetic separability while maintaining high boron adsorption capacity.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized graphene oxide–magnetite samples and evaluated their structural, surface, magnetic, and adsorption properties for boron removal from water. Unmodified graphene oxide achieved 94% removal, while the best magnetic formulation reached 69% and retained magnetic separability, highlighting a trade-off between adsorption capacity and recovery.

articles.title_original: Entropy Quantification Through Degree-Based Indices of Nitrogen-Doped Graphene Nanoribbon
articles.title_en: Study Quantifies Structural Complexity in Nitrogen-Doped Graphene Nanoribbons
articles.excerpt_original: Chemical graph theory applies mathematical graph-theoretical descriptors to characterize and quantify the features of molecular structures. Among the carbon nanostructures, Graphene nanoribbons have attracted considerable attention from researchers due to their distinctive structural and functional properties. Inspired by recent developments, this study investigates nitrogen-doped graphene nanoribbons NGR((n,m)).A molecular graph representation of the nitrogen-doped graphene nanoribbon is constructed, and its structural characteristics are analyzed through vertex and edge partition techniques. Based on these partitions, several degree-based topological descriptors, including the Zagreb indices, Forgotten index, Randic index, atom-bond connectivity index, geometric-arithmetic index, Harmonic index, and Sombor index, are derived in closed form. Furthermore, Shannon-type entropy indices computed from the descriptors quantify the nanoribbon’s degree of structural complexity and information density. This work provides a mathematical characterization of the topological structure of graphene nanoribbons, serving as a precursor to subsequent QSPR investigations. This proposed methodology extends graph-theoretical analysis to nitrogen-doped graphene nanoribbons and enables deeper exploration of molecular complexity using topological indices and entropy-based descriptors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers use degree-based topological descriptors and Shannon-type entropy indices to mathematically characterize nitrogen-doped graphene nanoribbons. The work provides a foundation for future quantitative structure–property relationship studies but does not report a commercial application.

articles.title_original: Coherent effects in quantum transport models and their classical counterparts
articles.title_en: Quantum Transport Models Reveal Coherence-Driven Ballistic Effects
articles.excerpt_original: We analyze the transport properties of quasiparticles locally excited at an initial time moment in several exactly solvable quantum models. It is revealed that, in the investigated quantum systems, the time-dependent probability distribution function (PDF) exhibits behavior similar to that of classical continuous-time random walk (CTRW) models, such as L'evy walks or diffusing diffusivity. For initially excited quasiparticles interacting with the same two-dimensional phonon reservoir, the exact quantum PDF reveals a U-shaped profile due to the presence of a strong ballistic component. This ballistic component arises because the absolute value of the quasiparticle velocity is bounded from above, allowing quantum coherence effects—stemming from the interaction with the common reservoir—to play a significant role. The results obtained for the phonon-assisted hopping quantum model are compared with three alternative approaches: (i) a simple tight-binding model, (ii) a model of a heterogeneous ensemble of chains with Gaussian random hopping amplitude, and (iii) a tight-binding model with random time-dependent hopping amplitude. It is found that the PDF of the simple tight-binding model is similar to that of the phonon-assisted hopping model. For the heterogeneous ensemble of chains with a Gaussian distribution of hopping amplitudes, the PDF transforms from bimodal to monomodal via an intermediate trimodal shape as the parameters of the Gaussian distribution are varied. The spread of the PDF is ballistic for the first and the second models mentioned above.
