articles.summary_en: Researchers compare quasiparticle transport in solvable quantum models with classical continuous-time random-walk descriptions. Quantum coherence and bounded velocity produce a strong ballistic component and distinctive probability-distribution profiles.

articles.title_original: Synthesis and Gas-Sensing Properties of the WS2/g-C3N4 2D Nanocomposites
articles.title_en: WS2/g-C3N4 Nanocomposite Demonstrates Room-Temperature Gas Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract― The use of 2D materials in gas sensors makes it possible to create high-speed semiconductor adsorption sensors that do not require heating. The paper considers a 2D nanocomposite based on the WS2 and g-C3N4 materials synthesized by a single-stage calcination method. The surface morphology, phase composition and absorption spectra of the WS2/g-C3N4 nanocomposite were studied. Its gas-sensitive properties were studied when exposed to vapors of isopropanol, ethanol, and acetone at room temperature. It was established that the obtained nanocomposite contains phases of graphite-like carbon nitride and tungsten disulfide. The band gap of the nanocomposite was 2.1 eV. The agglomeration of particles during the application of nanocomposite powder onto a glass substrate was studied. The maximum response of the nanocomposite to 1000 ppm acetone was 5%. The developed WS2/gC3N4-based 2D nanocomposite can be used in gas sensors for operation in explosive environments, as well as in wearable flexible electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers synthesized a tungsten disulfide/graphitic carbon nitride 2D nanocomposite that detected isopropanol, ethanol, and acetone vapors at room temperature. The material reached a 5% response to 1,000 ppm acetone and may support gas sensors for explosive environments and wearable electronics.

articles.title_original: Towards Non-van der Waals 2D Topological Insulators
articles.title_en: Study Establishes Foundation for Non-van der Waals 2D Topological Insulators
articles.excerpt_original: Non-van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) materials derived from strongly bonded non-layered crystals have recently emerged as a novel and rising platform for nanoscale research. While uncovering and tuning their (opto-)electronic, catalytic, and magnetic properties has been the focus of intense research, the impact of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) onto their electronic structure has not yet been explored in detail. Studying these effects is, however, particularly relevant due to their surface cation termination and the presence of heavy elements in several representative compounds. Here, we investigate the effect of SOC onto the electronic structure of 2D AgBiO3, NaBiO3, and SbTlO3. While the first two systems show negligible band renormalization upon inclusion of relativistic effects around the band gap, SbTlO3 showcases a large SOC induced splitting (229 meV) for the lowest conduction bands associated with a band inversion. Substitution of Tl with Pb forming SbPbO3 brings the band-inverted feature to the Fermi level. Analysis of topological invariants and investigation of edge states of zig-zag and armchair ribbons within the 200 meV gap confirms the topological nature of the band splitting. Our work thus establishes a foundation for the systematic study of robust non-van der Waals 2D topological insulators.
articles.summary_en: Researchers investigate spin–orbit coupling in 2D AgBiO3, NaBiO3, and SbTlO3, identifying a large band splitting and band inversion in SbTlO3. The findings support systematic development of robust non-van der Waals 2D topological insulators for electronic applications.

articles.title_original: Multiparameter Electrical Encoding for Molecular Recognition with a Single Two-Dimensional Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor
articles.title_en: Single MoS₂ Transistor Enables Multiparameter Gas Recognition
articles.excerpt_original: Selective molecular recognition remains a fundamental challenge for gas sensors because gas adsorption is typically represented by a single electrical response, providing insufficient information to distinguish chemically similar analytes. Here, we show that a single transfer characteristic naturally encodes molecular identity through parameter-specific electrical perturbations induced by gas adsorption. This multidimensional electrical fingerprint enables reliable gas recognition using only one field-effect transistor. To validate this concept, MoS2 field-effect transistors fabricated on HfO2/Si substrates were characterized under ultraviolet illumination in different gaseous environments. Multiple electrical descriptors extracted from each transfer characteristic produced distinct molecular fingerprints for NH3, NO2, CH4, and acetone over five concentration levels. Combined with logistic regression, these fingerprints enabled 100% classification accuracy for all twenty gas classes, allowing simultaneous identification of both gas species and concentration using a single transistor. This work establishes parameter-specific electrical encoding as a general strategy for single-transistor molecular recognition, providing a scalable route toward compact electronic noses based on two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated that one MoS₂ field-effect transistor can identify NH₃, NO₂, CH₄, and acetone while distinguishing five concentration levels from multidimensional electrical fingerprints. Logistic-regression analysis achieved 100% classification accuracy across 20 gas classes, supporting compact electronic-nose applications.

articles.title_original: Flat-band-induced integer doping and phase transition in monolayer graphene
articles.title_en: Gate-Controlled Integer Doping and Phase Transition Demonstrated in Monolayer Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract van der Waals heterostructures are stabilized by a delicate balance between van der Waals, elastic and Coulomb energies 1–4 . Because the interfaces are not covalently bonded, the constituent crystals can slide, rotate and reconstruct, resulting in several possible competing structural phases 2,5,6 . However, controlled tuning of this balance, and hence dynamical control over the stacking, has yet to be achieved. Here we report a dynamical heterostructure in which monolayer graphene is doubly aligned to bulk hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and monolayer hexagonal boron nitride (mhBN) on either side. In such a system, a global structural phase transition, manifested as a change of crystalline symmetry observed by scanning tunnelling microscopy, could be induced by gating, magnetic field or temperature. This structural transition is accompanied by an exotic electronic transition: the doping of graphene switches between discrete levels, corresponding to an exact integer number of electrons or holes per moiré plaquette. We attribute this integer doping to charge trapping in localized, strain-induced pseudo-Landau levels (flat bands in reciprocal space 7–12 ), produced by moiré reconstruction (strongly enhanced by the mhBN). Electrical control of coupled structural and electronic phase transitions provides a route to engineering strain-induced flat bands and strain–Coulomb correlations in van der Waals heterostructures.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a graphene/hBN dynamical heterostructure in which gating, magnetic field, or temperature induces a structural phase transition and switches graphene doping between discrete integer levels. The findings link moiré reconstruction, strain-induced flat bands, and Coulomb correlations, offering a route to engineered electronic states in van der Waals devices.

articles.title_original: Plasmonic Photocatalysis Using MXenes as a Tandem Nanoantenna
articles.title_en: MXenes Proposed as Noble-Metal Alternatives for Plasmonic Photocatalysis
articles.excerpt_original: Plasmonic photocatalysis represents an emerging platform for solar energy harvesting and negative carbon conversion that is meaningful for broad research communities in energy and environmental sciences. By convention, noble metals, such as Au, Ag, and Cu, have been extensively used as plasmonic catalytic components owing to their distinct surface plasmon responses in the visible region. However, their scarcity and high cost substantially limit large‐scale applications, especially in practical sunlight‐driven photocatalytic scenarios. Notably, MXene materials have recently been shown to demonstrate quasistatic and anisotropic surface plasmon behaviors across the solar spectrum. In combination with their versatile intrinsic thermal, optical, and electrical properties, MXenes present a favorable non‐noble platform that can function as tandem antennas for constructing plasmonic photocatalytic systems. This perspective systematically overviews recent progress on MXene‐based plasmonic catalysis, emphasizing the fundamental mechanisms and niche applications in energy conversions, while also providing critical assessments of key limitations in synthesis feasibility and intrinsic carrier density deficiency. By proposing prospective improvement strategies, this work aims at industrial‐relevant solar‐to‐fuel conversion efficiencies via MXene‐based plasmonic photocatalysts upon future endeavors.
articles.summary_en: This perspective reviews MXenes as tandem nanoantennas for plasmonic photocatalysis and solar-to-fuel conversion. It highlights their broadband plasmonic behavior and intrinsic thermal, optical, and electrical properties, while noting synthesis feasibility and carrier-density limitations.

articles.title_original: MXene-Assisted High-Density NiCo Sulfide Nanorod Arrays via Dual Templates for Efficient Electrocatalytic Oxygen Evolution
articles.title_en: MXene-Supported NiCo Sulfide Arrays Improve Water-Splitting Catalysis
articles.excerpt_original: Although MXenes have limited intrinsic catalytic activity toward the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), their excellent electrical conductivity and ultra-high specific surface area make them ideal substrates for supporting single-atom catalysts and enhancing electrocatalytic performance. Improving the intrinsic activity of transition metal-based electrocatalysts, designing heterojunction electrocatalysts, and revealing their interfacial mechanisms remain urgent research topics. In this work, a three-dimensional NiCo2S4/MXene heterostructure was rationally designed and constructed via a multi-step self-assembly and sulfidation strategy. Using polymeric sulfur as a dynamic confinement agent and leveraging the conductive MXene scaffold, the resulting composite exhibits hierarchical porosity, well-defined heterointerfaces, and suppressed particle coarsening. The abundant surface functional groups of MXene enable the in situ nucleation and growth of metal sulfides, effectively mitigating nanoparticle aggregation while synergistically integrating the high catalytic activity of sulfides with the superior charge transport of MXene. The optimized NiCo2S4/MXene electrocatalyst delivers outstanding bifunctional performance, achieving low overpotentials of 151 mV for OER and 209 mV for HER at 10 mA cm–2, accompanied by small Tafel slopes of 73.8 and 99.3 mV dec–1, respectively. Furthermore, the sulfur-containing polymer prepared by polymerizing sulfur with carbon chains exhibits significantly enhanced structural and electrochemical stability compared to conventional sulfur-rich organic electrodes. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a porous NiCo₂S₄/MXene heterostructure using dual-template assembly and sulfidation. The catalyst achieved low overpotentials for both oxygen and hydrogen evolution, highlighting MXene’s role in improving conductivity, dispersion, and structural stability.

articles.title_original: Electrospun PLLA/Silk Fibroin/MXene Nanofiber Scaffolds with Polydopamine-Mediated GL13K Functionalization for Antibacterial, Immunomodulatory, and Osteogenic Bone Repair
articles.title_en: MXene Nanofiber Scaffold Shows Promise for Antibacterial Bone Repair
articles.excerpt_original: Bone defects caused by trauma, infection, or tumor resection remain difficult to repair, particularly when delayed union or nonunion is compounded by microbial colonization. Polymer nanofiber scaffolds offer a flexible platform for integrating structural support, local bioactivity, and immune modulation. Here, we report a surface-functionalized electrospun scaffold based on poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA), silk fibroin (SF), and Al–Ti3C2Tx MXene, in which the antimicrobial peptide GL13K is immobilized through polydopamine (PDA) coating. The resulting scaffold retained a uniform nanofibrous morphology, increased hydrophilicity, improved tensile strength, and measurable electrical conductivity while showing low short-term degradation. In vitro, the scaffold exhibited broad-spectrum antibacterial activity against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, supported MC3T3-E1 cell adhesion and proliferation, enhanced alkaline phosphatase activity and mineralized nodule formation, and upregulated osteogenic markers. Under lipopolysaccharide-stimulated macrophage culture, it reduced iNOS expression and increased CD206 expression, consistent with M2 polarization. In a rat calvarial defect model, the functionalized scaffold produced significantly higher bone volume fraction and trabecular thickness than control and component-only scaffolds at 4 and 8 weeks, with no obvious systemic toxicity in major organs. These results demonstrate that PDA-mediated GL13K functionalization of an electrospun PLLA/SF/MXene polymer scaffold provides an integrated antibacterial, immunomodulatory, and osteogenic design for bone defect repair.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a PLLA/silk fibroin scaffold incorporating Al–Ti3C2Tx MXene and GL13K antimicrobial peptide functionalization. The scaffold improved antibacterial activity, immune modulation, osteogenic responses, and bone repair outcomes in vitro and in a rat calvarial defect model.

articles.title_original: Dual-mode Meta-MXene utilizing moiré and quasi-bic resonances for terahertz biosensing applications
articles.title_en: Moiré Meta-MXene Enables Dual-Mode Terahertz Brain-Tissue Sensing

Numerical evaluations demonstrate that the primary q-BIC sensing channel achieves a peak Quality Factor (Q) of 28.62, whereas the induced Moiré mode acts as a stable reference benchmark with a peak Q of 42.66 and a baseline sensitivity of 208.6 GHz/RIU across the full refractive index span of brain tissue (1.333–1.483). articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a twisted Meta-MXene metamaterial combining quasi-bound-state-in-the-continuum and moiré resonances for terahertz refractive-index sensing. articles.title_en: Thermally Conductive Nanoparticles Improve LED Color Rendering and Irradiance

articles.title_original: Atomic-scale assembly of sulfur vacancy complexes for tailored in-gap states in monolayer WS$_{2}$
articles.title_en: Atomic-scale engineering of sulfur-vacancy complexes in monolayer WS₂
articles.excerpt_original: Atomic-scale defects in two-dimensional semiconductors are quasi-isolated quantum systems with promise for emerging technologies. Although their potential as spin qubits, quantum sensors and single-photon emitters has been demonstrated experimentally, creating them deterministically and identifying them chemically remains challenging, which limits control over their electronic states. In this work we assemble sulfur vacancies in monolayer WS$_{2}$ into complexes of different sizes and geometries using the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. We study their electronic properties by a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory, revealing the intricate influences of geometry, underlying point group symmetries and spin-orbit coupling on hybridized states. Among the realized sulfur vacancy complexes, we characterize two configurations that are candidates for bright single photon emitters. Our findings demonstrate an atomic-scale method for engineering quantum states within the band gap of two-dimensional semiconductors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used a scanning tunneling microscope to assemble sulfur-vacancy complexes with controlled sizes and geometries in monolayer WS₂. articles.title_original: A Coordination-Confined Liquid–Metal/MXene Interface for Stress-Adaptive Zinc Metal Anodes
articles.title_en: Coordination-Confined GaIn–MXene Interface Enables Durable Zinc Anodes
articles.excerpt_original: The continuous plating/stripping of Zn metal is accompanied by substantial interfacial stress accumulation, which promotes nonuniform deposition and dendrite growth. Liquid metals offer intrinsic deformability for accommodating mechanical stress, yet their high fluidity can induce migration and interfacial instability during prolonged cycling. Herein, we develop a coordination-confined GaIn@MXene layer that reconciles liquid-metal deformability with interfacial stability. Liquid GaIn microspheres are uniformly confined within zincophilic Ti3C2Tx MXene layers through coordination confinement between the native oxide shell of GaIn and MXene surface terminations, suppressing macroscopic liquid metal migration while preserving local deformability. The MXene framework promotes homogeneous Zn nucleation, whereas the GaIn dynamically accommodates the mechanical evolution during Zn deposition. Therefore, this dynamic conformal interface significantly reduces the anode stress from -219.9 to -11.5 MPa, enabling dendrite-free zinc growth. The volume change during zinc deposition is only about 3.6 μm, which enables the stable cycling performance of the symmetrical cell for 1100 h and an ultralong cycle life of up to 20,000 cycles at a current density of 20 A g-1 in full cells. This study offers insights into the design of stable liquid-metal-based interfaces for regulating Zn deposition and improving the durability of aqueous zinc-ion batteries.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a GaIn liquid-metal/MXene interface that accommodates stress while stabilizing zinc nucleation, suppressing dendrites and reducing anode stress. The design enabled 1,100-hour symmetric-cell cycling and up to 20,000 full-cell cycles at 20 A g⁻¹ in aqueous zinc-ion batteries.

articles.title_original: Energy–Dose Optimization and Substrate Effects in Ion-Induced Graphene Nanopore Creation
articles.title_en: Study Optimizes Ion Irradiation for Graphene Nanopore Creation
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Ion irradiation of graphene involves a trade-off among controlled nanopore formation, collateral defect generation, and retained mechanical integrity. Here, molecular dynamics simulations are used to establish a first-order quantitative guideline linking ion energy, ion dose, and target pore geometry for argon-ion-induced nanopore formation in free-standing graphene. By mapping this coupled dependence, we identify the threshold conditions for complete pore opening and the energetically favorable pathways toward prescribed pore sizes. Substrate thickness and substrate type are found to alter sputtering through two competing mechanisms: at low and intermediate energies, the substrate suppresses net damage by limiting atom escape and promoting rapid recombination, whereas at higher energies, recoil and backscattering enhance carbon displacement. We further show that the mechanical strength of nanoporous graphene is strongly reduced when irradiation-induced defects form near the pore edge, because of amplified local stress concentration and earlier crack initiation. These results provide a unified description of pore opening thresholds, energy optimization, substrate-mediated damage evolution, and defect-controlled mechanical weakening in ion-irradiated graphene.
articles.summary_en: Molecular dynamics simulations link argon-ion energy and dose to nanopore size, while showing that substrate properties alter damage through suppression, recombination, recoil, and backscattering. The findings also identify defect-driven weakening near pore edges, informing the design of mechanically robust nanoporous graphene membranes.

articles.title_original: Cellulose nanofiber-enabled MXene textronics for wearable therapeutic applications
articles.title_en: Cellulose Nanofiber–MXene Textiles for Wearable Therapeutics
articles.excerpt_original: Electronic textiles (e-textiles) are advancing wearable healthcare by integrating electronics into soft, breathable, and scalable fabrics. Composites of cellulose nanofibers (CNFs) and two-dimensional MXenes have gained attention due to their complementary properties. CNFs offer flexibility, mechanical strength, biodegradability, and rich surface chemistry, while MXenes provide high conductivity and tunable multifunctionality. Strong interfacial interactions enable the development of durable, flexible, and environmentally compatible textronic architectures for wearable applications. This review examines the structural role of CNFs in MXene-based textronics across hierarchical formats, from fibers to fabrics. Key fabrication strategies, coating, spinning, electrospinning, and hybrid assembly, are discussed, with emphasis on comfort and performance balance. CNF-MXene textiles enable a range of functions, including wearable energy storage (supercapacitors), physiological and strain/pressure sensing, electrical stimulation, thermotherapy, and controlled drug delivery, positioning them as multifunctional platforms for both power-supporting and therapeutic wearable technologies. Key challenges, such as durability, washability, moisture resistance, and stability, are assessed, with future directions focusing on MXene stability, scalable production, and sustainable end-of-life strategies.
articles.summary_en: A review examines cellulose nanofiber–MXene composites for flexible electronic textiles, highlighting applications in supercapacitors, physiological and pressure sensing, electrical stimulation, thermotherapy, and controlled drug delivery. Key commercialization challenges include washability, moisture resistance, MXene stability, scalable production, and sustainable disposal.

articles.title_original: Asymmetric Interlocked MXene/Tissue Paper Architecture for Highly Sensitive Piezoresistive Sensors
articles.title_en: MXene–Tissue Paper Sensor Reaches High Sensitivity Across a Wide Pressure Range
articles.excerpt_original: Flexible pressure sensors have shown tremendous potential in fields of human‐machine interaction, artificial intelligence, and physiological monitoring. Nevertheless, constrained by the inherent mechanical limitations of soft materials, most flexible pressure sensors suffer from a persistent trade‐off between high sensitivity and wide sensing range. Herein, we propose a novel asymmetric interlocked sensor based on hierarchical wrinkled MXene/tissue paper to provide sufficient deformation space. This structure enables progressive contact evolution and hierarchical stress regulation during compression, which effectively modulates interfacial conductive pathways and enhances the piezoresistive response. Benefiting from this architecture, the fabricated sensor exhibits a maximum sensitivity of as high as 606 kPa −1 , a wide sensing range of 210 kPa, and a fast response/recovery time of 50/38 ms, along with exceptional long‐term stability over 10 000 cycles. Furthermore, the sensor enables the real‐time monitoring of arterial pulses and limb movements, as well as sound recognition. Moreover, its integration into a smart glove for robotic arm control underscores its significant potential for advanced human‐machine interface applications.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an asymmetric interlocked MXene/tissue-paper piezoresistive sensor with sensitivity up to 606 kPa⁻¹, a 210 kPa sensing range, and stability over 10,000 cycles. articles.title_original: Graphene phosphoprotein hybrid synaptic interfaces: engineering disease-specific plasticity restoration in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models
articles.title_en: Graphene–Phosphoprotein Interfaces Proposed for Disease-Specific Synaptic Repair
articles.excerpt_original: Synaptic dysfunction is an important early feature of Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and Parkinson’s disease (PD), in which impaired long-term potentiation (LTP), long-term depression (LTD) and metaplasticity accompany disturbances in postsynaptic phosphosignalling. Neuroproteomic studies implicate receptor phosphorylation, kinase–phosphatase imbalance, cytoskeletal remodelling and neuromodulator-dependent pathways in these deficits. Alongside the NMDAR–CaMKII–PSD-95 axis, acetylcholine- and glutamate-regulated small-GTPase cascades provide mechanistic links between biochemical signalling and dendritic spine plasticity. Advances in graphene-based neuromorphic devices demonstrate programmable conductance states and electrical analogues of synaptic learning, suggesting a possible engineering framework informed by molecular disease signatures. This narrative review critically examines synaptic phosphoproteomic alterations in AD and PD, their implications for designing phosphoprotein-functionalised graphene interfaces, and the conceptual integration of glutamatergic and neuromodulatory inputs into device operation. Importantly, electronic emulation of LTP/LTD has not established restoration of endogenous phosphorylation networks, synaptic incorporation or therapeutic efficacy in AD or PD. We distinguish demonstrated molecular and materials findings from the proposed biochemical-to-electronic coupling mechanisms and discuss the experimental, biological and translational limitations that must be resolved before disease-specific synaptic repair can be evaluated.
articles.summary_en: A narrative review explores phosphoprotein-functionalized graphene interfaces for emulating disease-specific synaptic plasticity in Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s models. It emphasizes that current graphene neuromorphic devices have not demonstrated restoration of endogenous phosphorylation, synaptic integration, or therapeutic efficacy, making the concept experimentally and translationally unvalidated.

articles.title_original: Mechanisms of Pressure-Enhanced Thermal Boundary Conductance at van der Waals 2D-Substrate Interfaces: Roles of Bond Compression and Surface Roughness
articles.title_en: Pressure Enhances Thermal Boundary Conductance at 2D Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Two-dimensional (2D) materials offer tremendous potential for further miniaturization of electronic devices but they face thermal management challenges due to their low thermal boundary conductance, necessitating innovative solutions to improve heat transfer efficiency. In this study, we have developed a numerical model of thermal boundary conductance (TBC) that utilizes data from first-principles DFT simulations to investigate how external pressure modulates the TBC of van der Waals (vdW) interfaces between 2D materials and their substrates. Our study shows that external pressure enhances the TBC through both the compression of the interfacial vdW bonds and increased area of contact. We find that the pressure dependence of TBC is governed by substrate roughness as well as the interfacial adhesion and bending stiffness of the 2D material. On an atomically flat substrate, the enhancement is entirely due to bond compression, which strengthens phonon coupling across the interface. Adding roughness causes partial delamination, particularly when the substrate roughness is steep, so the increase in area of contact begins to contribute. Simultaneously, interfacial bonds at the peaks in the rough substrate that are surrounded by delaminated areas are compressed more strongly than in a flat substrate, which substantially enhances local TBC under external pressure. Stronger adhesion enhances the zero-pressure TBC, 0 and through it, the pressure sensitivity dG/dP, whereas stiffer 2D materials resist bending to conform to a rough substrate surface, leading to air gaps that suppress heat flow and lower G 0 . articles.summary_en: A DFT-informed numerical model shows that pressure improves heat transfer across van der Waals 2D-material/substrate interfaces by compressing interfacial bonds and increasing contact area. Substrate roughness, adhesion, and 2D-material stiffness determine the resulting thermal-boundary-conductance gains, informing thermal management design for miniaturized electronics.

articles.title_original: Graphene-Panels (AGP): Replacing Silicon and Silver in Solar Panels with a Graphene-Like TEGA Absorber
articles.title_en: Graphene-like TEGA absorber proposed for silicon- and silver-free solar panels
articles.excerpt_original: Solar panels that reach the end of their life carry silver in the front contact grid, but a tonne of silicon panels holds under 1 kg of it, 0.03-0.05% of the mass, and recycling a module costs 10-15 USD against 2-3 USD for landfill. Retired capacity is growing: about 4 million t by 2030 and 60-78 million t by 2050, and the real service life is closer to 10-12 years than 20. At the same time the silver content per watt is falling, so a recycling plant is built for a metal that next-generation cells need in smaller amounts. We describe Graphene-Panels (AGP, ARBOK TEGA Panels), a concept in which the light-absorbing layer and the conductive path are one graphene-like material, thermally expanded graphite ARBOK (TEGA). The panel needs no silver contact grid and no silicon. The calculated efficiency is 35% and above, against the 24% ceiling of silicon, which gives about 350 W per m2 instead of 240 W, 46% more, and 31% less area for the same power. For the installed fleet, the ARBOK PV-Silver module (200 m3/day) closes the recycling effluent. The estimated world effect is the removal of a silver line of about 15 bln USD a year from panel production. AGP is a concept at TRL 5 on the ARBOK scale: the 35% figure is a calculation, not a measurement.
articles.summary_en: The article describes a conceptual photovoltaic panel using thermally expanded graphite (ARBOK/TEGA) as both the light absorber and conductive path, aiming to eliminate silicon and silver contacts. Efficiency above 35% is calculated rather than experimentally measured, and the concept is stated to be TRL 5 on the author's ARBOK scale.

articles.title_original: Advancements in Multi‐Dimensional Hexagonal Boron Nitride‐Based Thermal Management Materials: A Review
articles.title_en: Review examines multidimensional boron nitride materials for thermal management
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Hexagonal boron nitride (BN), due to its high thermal conductivity (TC), excellent electrical insulation, and low dielectric constant, has become an ideal filler for designing advanced thermal management materials (TMMs), effectively addressing thermal failure and electromagnetic leakage issues in advanced chips. BN structures in different dimensions (0D, 1D, and 2D) each have their own advantages, their interface morphology directly affects the TC of composite systems. However, there is still a lack of systematic understanding of phonon transport behavior at different interfaces in composite systems and their impact on thermal conduction network construction. This review focuses on dimensional classification and compares the intrinsic TC, phonon transport mechanisms, and network formation behavior of 0D, 1D, and 2D BN fillers. In addition to the traditional filler/polymer interfaces, this analysis also focused on the phonon transport properties at the homogeneous and heterogeneous nanoadditives interfaces of BN. At the same time, the TC of mono‐, di‐, and multi‐component nanoadditives systems were systematically evaluated, revealing the synergistic effects among BN of different dimensions. This review aims to provide a reference for reducing the thermal resistance of complex interfaces and promoting the practical application of micro–nano materials in the field of thermal management.
articles.summary_en: An academic review evaluates 0D, 1D, and 2D hexagonal boron nitride fillers for thermally conductive, electrically insulating composite materials. It compares phonon transport, interface effects, and network formation to guide reduced thermal resistance and improved chip thermal management; no company or commercial activity is identified.

articles.title_original: Electrical Dipole Formation as an Alternative Photodetection Pathway in Quantum Dot/Graphene Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Dipole Modulation Offers Alternative Photodetection Path in PbS Quantum Dot/Graphene Devices
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Short‐wave infrared (SWIR) photodetectors based on colloidal PbS quantum dots (QDs) provide a cost‐effective alternative to conventional compound semiconductors, yet photocurrent generation in QD/graphene heterostructures remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigate ligand‐length‐dependent photoresponse in a graphene photodetector integrated with PbS QDs capped by oleic acid (OA), PbBr 2 , and 1,2‐ethanedithiol (EDT). Unexpectedly, PbS‐OA graphene photodetectors exhibit pronounced photoresponse despite the electrically insulating nature of the OA ligand, challenging the conventional photo‐induced charge‐transfer model. Moreover, insertion of a 10 nm Al 2 O 3 or hexagonal boron nitride insulating layer between graphene and QD does not eliminate the photoresponse, indicating an additional photocurrent‐generation pathway beyond photo‐induced charge transfer. A dipole‐induced Fermi‐level modulation mechanism is therefore proposed, suggesting a larger contribution from dipole‐induced modulation in PbS‐EDT devices, whereas photo‐induced charge transfer remains more prominent in PbS‐PbBr 2 devices. These findings support electrical dipole formation as a possible alternative photoresponse pathway in QD/graphene heterostructures and provide insights into the design of fast and stable QD/graphene SWIR photodetectors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report that PbS quantum dot/graphene short-wave infrared photodetectors can generate a photoresponse even with insulating ligands or intervening Al2O3 and hexagonal boron nitride layers. They propose electrical dipole-induced Fermi-level modulation as an alternative to photo-induced charge transfer, informing the design of faster and more stable devices.

articles.title_original: Properties of Graphene Directly Induced by Laser on Polyimides Synthesized with Different Cross-Linkers
articles.title_en: Cross-Linker-Tuned Polyimides Improve Laser-Induced Graphene Supercapacitor Electrodes
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene is a conductive material that is increasingly being considered as an electrode for energy storage applications. The properties of graphene-based electrodes depend on the type of graphene, as well as on the properties of the substrate. This study focuses on graphene induced by laser directly on chemically tailored crosslinked polyimides (PI). The PI chemical structure is tuned to optimize the properties of laser-induced graphene (LIG) for supercapacitor applications. Three new PIs containing 4,4′-methylenedianiline (MDA), 1,6-hexamethylenediamine (HMDA), and thiourea (TU) as crosslinkers were synthesized by high-temperature polymerization in solution and used as matrices for LIG. Glycerol was used as a plasticizer in HMDA-based PI synthesis to prevent structural cracking, which yielded continuous graphene on this substrate (PI-HMDAg). The prepared LIG/PI materials were characterized in terms of their structural, morphological, surface, mechanical, electrical, and electrochemical properties and compared with previously prepared LIG/PI materials and LIG on Kapton. Water contact angle measurements demonstrated that hydrophilic LIG can be obtained simply by changing the crosslinker, without additional surface treatment. Very low sheet resistance was achieved, reaching 12.8 Ω/sq for LIG/PI-HMDAg. At 10 mV/s, specific areal capacitance reached 5.89 mF/cm2 for LIG/PI-HMDAg, exceeding the values obtained for the other investigated materials. The results showed that the PI structure and synthesis conditions strongly influence the properties of LIG, while the successful use of glycerol opens a new research direction toward a more sustainable, environmentally friendly, and flexible PI substrate for next-generation energy-storage devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers showed that chemically tailored polyimide cross-linkers strongly influence laser-induced graphene’s conductivity, wettability, mechanical integrity, and electrochemical performance. A glycerol-plasticized HMDA polyimide produced continuous graphene with 12.8 Ω/sq sheet resistance and 5.89 mF/cm² areal capacitance, supporting flexible supercapacitor development.

articles.title_original: Two‐Dimensional MXenes for Ion‐Conducting Interfaces in Solid‐State Energy Storage Systems
articles.title_en: Review Examines MXene Interfaces for Solid-State Batteries
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes, a rapidly expanding family of 2D transition metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides, have emerged as promising materials for advancing solid‐state battery (SSB) technology due to their high electrical conductivity, tunable surface terminations, and structural flexibility. This review comprehensively examines the role of MXenes in solid‐state electrolyte (SSE) systems, with special focus on their use as ion‐transport regulators, interfacial modifiers, and composite hosts for multivalent‐ion transport. The exceptional combination of properties makes MXenes attractive as fillers in solid electrolytes and as buffer layers at the electrode interfaces. Recent advances in MXene‐based composites, including MXene–polymer composite electrolytes, interfacial‐engineering strategies for dendrite suppression, and MXene‐mediated transport of Li + , Na + , Zn 2+ , and Mg 2+ ions, are critically discussed. The challenges, such as chemical stability, ion selectivity, and scalability, are critically assessed. Future research directions are proposed to facilitate the deployment of MXene‐based materials in practical SSB systems. Unlike earlier MXene reviews, this work distinctively emphasizes their role in ion‐conducting interfaces for SSBs and also highlights the strategies for enhanced ion transport and dendrite suppression.
articles.summary_en: The review assesses MXenes as ion-transport regulators, interfacial modifiers, and composite hosts in solid-state energy-storage systems. It highlights applications in lithium-, sodium-, zinc-, and magnesium-ion transport while identifying chemical stability, ion selectivity, and scalability as key challenges.

articles.title_original: Structure–Property Tailoring of Long-Chain PDMS-Based Polyurethanes for Flexible MXene Strain Sensors
articles.title_en: PDMS-Based Polyurethanes Enable Flexible MXene Strain Sensors
articles.excerpt_original: Flexible and mechanically adaptable polymer substrates are critical for conformable wearable sensors capable of accurately tracking human motion and vital parameters. Here, crosslinked polyurethanes (PUs) were synthesized from a long-chain poly(ethylene oxide)-b-poly(dimethylsiloxane)-b-poly(ethylene oxide) (PEO–PDMS–PEO) macrodiol (Mn = 2400 g mol−1), 4,4′-methylenediphenyl diisocyanate, and a multifunctional hyperbranched polyester, with soft-segment contents of 15–70 wt.%. Mechanical, structural, surface, and thermal properties were evaluated by indentation methods (nanoindentation, microindentation, and microindentation creep), XRD, AFM, wettability measurements, TGA, and DSC. Increasing the soft-segment content markedly reduced stiffness; Young’s modulus decreased from 1713 MPa to 112 MPa to 80 MPa as the soft segment content was increased from 30 wt.% to 50 wt.% to 70 wt.%, respectively, while hardness decreased from 89 to 4 MPa. The predominantly amorphous networks retained good thermal stability, with degradation temperature (T(10%)) values of 249–291 °C and glass transition temperature (Tg) values of 21–25 °C. Increasing the soft-segment content also increased surface roughness (Rq: 18.3–250 nm) and water contact angle (approximately 45–90°), indicating progressive surface enrichment by the low-surface-energy PDMS-containing phase. PU-50 was selected as the finger-motion sensor substrate and coated with Ti3C2Tx MXene by spray deposition. The MXene/PU-50 sensor exhibited a gauge factor of 65.9 over 0–8% strain, response/recovery times of 138/58 ms, and a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 39.5 dB, demonstrating a reversible piezoresistive response with good short-term repeatability and the feasibility of using a long-chain PDMS-based PU substrate for rapid and sensi
articles.summary_en: Researchers tailored long-chain PDMS-based polyurethane substrates to balance flexibility, mechanical properties, and surface characteristics for wearable sensing. A Ti3C2Tx MXene-coated PU substrate achieved a gauge factor of 65.9, rapid response and recovery, and a 39.5 dB signal-to-noise ratio in finger-motion monitoring.

articles.title_original: Intrinsic linewidths of confined phonons in few-layer hBN
articles.title_en: Study measures intrinsic phonon linewidths in few-layer hBN
articles.excerpt_original: Understanding lattice vibrations in two-dimensional (2D) materials is essential for controlling thermal transport, mechanical response, and energy dissipation in nanoscale devices. However, the intrinsic lifetimes of low-energy phonon modes, particularly those that are optically silent, remain largely unexplored. Here we use helium-3 spin-echo spectroscopy to resolve low-energy phonons at the surface of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and measure their intrinsic linewidths. We report the simultaneous observation of multiple surface-confined interlayer shear modes whose energies agree closely with linear-chain model predictions. By resolving their intrinsic linewidths, we demonstrate a strong confinement-dependent reduction in phonon lifetimes, with a near order-of-magnitude increase in linewidth between the four- and two-layer modes, substantially exceeding simple inverse-layer-number scaling. The three- and four-layer linewidths show no statistically resolved temperature dependence over the measurement range, consistent with a substantial temperature-independent contribution. We also observe the flexural and Rayleigh wave modes and extract the bending rigidity of a quasi-freestanding hBN monolayer. The systematic broadening with decreasing effective layer number suggests that confinement strongly influences phonon decay. These results reveal how reduced dimensionality affects the decay of interlayer shearing modes in hBN, providing direct insight into the phonon lifetimes, confinement effects, and dissipation pathways that govern the dynamical behaviour of two-dimensional materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used helium-3 spin-echo spectroscopy to measure low-energy, surface-confined phonons in few-layer hexagonal boron nitride. They found confinement-driven broadening of interlayer shear modes and extracted the bending rigidity of monolayer hBN, providing insight into nanoscale dissipation and thermal transport.

articles.title_original: Efficient interlayer interactions in non-planar molecule/transition-metal dichalcogenide two-dimensional heterostructure
articles.title_en: Non-planar molecules enable efficient interactions in 2D heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Integration of molecules and two-dimensional (2D) atomic materials offer new opportunities for hybrid electronic devices. Most progress has focused on interfacing planar molecule. In contrast, incorporating non-planar molecules into 2D heterostructures remains challenging due to the three-dimensional orientations of ligands. Here we investigate interlayer interactions between discrete non-planar spin-crossover (SCO) molecules, [Fe(tBu2qsal)2] (FTBQS), monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), and hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) spacers through optical spectroscopies. FTBQS features bulk molecular crystal layers and can be mechanically exfoliated, enabling deterministic assembly of clean hybrid heterostructures. Robust photoluminescence (PL) quenching, even with an hBN spacer, indicates efficient Förster resonance energy transfer with a long decay distance. Gate-dependent optical spectroscopy further identifies charge transfer from the doping shifts in the TMD layers due to the TMD/FTBQS electronic band alignment. Our results establish efficient interlayer interactions between non-plana, discrete molecules and 2D crystals for hybrid electrical, optical, and spintronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated efficient optical and electronic interactions between non-planar spin-crossover molecules, transition-metal dichalcogenides and hBN spacers. The findings support development of hybrid electronic, optical and spintronic devices.

articles.title_original: Koopmans spectral functionals for excitons in materials
articles.title_en: Koopmans spectral functionals enable efficient exciton modeling
articles.excerpt_original: Accurate first-principles characterization of excitons typically relies on the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) combined with quasiparticle energies from computationally demanding GW calculations. Here, we replace the GW step with quasiparticle energies from Koopmans-compliant spectral functionals, an approach we call BSE@qKI, and implement it in an automated, reproducible AiiDA workflow. For a set of benchmark semiconductors, BSE@qKI reproduces experimental band gaps and first exciton energies with mean absolute relative errors of 13% and 4%, respectively, comparable to BSE@G0W0 for the gaps and markedly better for the excitation energies. We also apply the method to the layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3, obtaining an absorption spectrum that reproduces the main experimental features. These results establish BSE@qKI as a GW-free alternative to BSE@G0W0 for systematic studies of excitonic properties in complex materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed BSE@qKI, an automated workflow that replaces computationally intensive GW calculations with Koopmans-compliant spectral functionals for exciton simulations. The approach reproduced experimental exciton energies across benchmark semiconductors and captured key absorption features in layered magnetic semiconductor CrI3.

articles.title_original: Performance limits and benchmarking of ideal 2D topological insulator field-effect transistors
articles.title_en: Study benchmarks performance limits of topological-insulator transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Topological insulator field-effect transistors (TIFETs) have emerged as a promising alternative to overcome the scaling limits of silicon-based field-effect transistors (Si-based FETs). In this study, we establish the performance limits of ideal TIFETs and present a comprehensive benchmarking of the switching energy-delay performance of TIFETs against Si-based FETs (FinFET and LGAA) and 2-D material-based FETs ($\mathrm{MoS}_2$ and InSe) under equivalent and realistic conditions. Furthermore, we analyze the key factors influencing the switching energy-delay performance of TIFETs, including contact resistance ($R_{\mathrm{C}}$), parasitic capacitance ($C_{\mathrm{par}}$), channel length ($L$), and channel width ($W$). Notably, TIFETs achieve substantially lower switching energy and delay time, outperforming both Si-based FETs and 2-D material-based FETs, where a transition from 1-stack to 3-stack yields approximately a sixfold reduction. This benchmarking study shows that TIFETs exhibit competitive switching performance and hold strong potential for future topological electronic devices.
articles.summary_en: An academic study models ideal topological-insulator field-effect transistors and benchmarks their switching energy and delay against silicon, MoS₂, and InSe devices. It identifies contact resistance, parasitic capacitance, channel dimensions, and stacking as key performance factors, with three-stack designs showing an approximately sixfold reduction in switching metrics.

articles.title_original: Two-dimensional WSi 2 N 4 Transistors: Contact Mechanisms and Weak Fermi Level Pinning at Vertical and Horizontal Interfaces
articles.title_en: Study identifies contact-engineering strategies for WSi₂N₄ transistors
articles.excerpt_original: As conventional silicon-based field-effect transistors approach fundamental scaling limits, two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors emerge as promising channel candidates for post-Moore era. WSi 2 N 4 , a member of van der Waals MA 2 Z 4 family, possesses a suitable bandgap, high carrier mobility and environmental stability. Nevertheless, metal/semiconductor contact characteristics dominate overall device performance. Herein, density functional theory combined with nonequilibrium Green’s function quantum transport calculations is employed to systematically investigate contact behaviors between monolayer WSi 2 N 4 and six metals (Au, Pt, Ti, Ag, Sc, In) with distinct work functions. Schottky barrier heights (SBHs) and Fermi level pinning (FLP) factors are quantified for both vertical and horizontal interfaces. Vertical interfaces exhibit weak FLP with electron/hole FLP factors of 0.70 and 0.65, while a value of 0.52 is obtained via quantum transport for horizontal interfaces. Notably, Sc/WSi 2 N 4 enables n-type Ohmic contact. These findings illustrate how interfacial coupling modulates carrier injection and deliver theoretical guidelines for contact engineering of high-performance WSi 2 N 4 transistors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used density functional theory and quantum-transport calculations to assess contacts between monolayer WSi₂N₄ and six metals. The study reports weak Fermi-level pinning and identifies scandium as enabling n-type Ohmic contact, providing theoretical guidance for high-performance 2D transistor design.

articles.title_original: Reconfigurable 2D Lateral Heterostructure Platform for Unified Detection, Emission, and Logic
articles.title_en: Reconfigurable MoSe₂–WSe₂ Heterostructure Unifies Sensing, Emission and Logic
articles.excerpt_original: Heterogeneous integration of sensing, light generation, communication, and computation typically requires specialized devices, resulting in complex interconnects, fabrication overhead, parasitic losses, and energy penalties. Developing a monolithic, reconfigurable device capable of controlling carrier generation, transport, and recombination remains a longstanding challenge. Two-dimensional (2D) lateral heterostructures offer a promising approach by combining spatially distinct domains of different charge polarity with a dynamically tunable electrostatic landscape. Here, multifunctional bilayer MoSe2-WSe2 lateral heterojunctions are demonstrated, integrating photodetection, reconfigurable electroluminescence (EL), and CMOS logic operation within a unified platform. The photodetector exhibits a responsivity of 35 A W-1, a specific detectivity of 5 x 10^13 Jones, and a noise-equivalent power of 6.3 x 10^-18 W Hz^-1/2, enabled by efficient charge separation and photoconductive gain. Under electrical injection, electrostatic gating dynamically switches the radiative recombination zone among the MoSe2 domain, lateral heterointerface, and WSe2 domain, enabling spatially programmable EL, optical multiplexing, and ternary optical logic. Furthermore, the complementary transport characteristics of the two domains enable CMOS inverter operation at 0.25 kHz. These functionalities originate from a common electrostatic framework in which the gate-tunable depletion region governs carrier extraction, recombination, and transport. This work establishes 2D lateral heterostructures as multifunctional building blocks for monolithically integrated electronic and optoelectronic systems combining light sensing, generation, and information processing.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated a bilayer MoSe₂–WSe₂ lateral heterostructure integrating photodetection, electrically reconfigurable light emission and CMOS inverter operation. The platform’s gate-tunable electrostatic control could reduce interconnect complexity in integrated optoelectronic systems, although the work remains at the research stage.

articles.title_original: Resistive switching of Si2Te3 thin films with extremely low SET voltage
articles.title_en: Si₂Te₃ Thin Films Demonstrate Ultra-Low-Voltage Resistive Switching
articles.excerpt_original: Silicon telluride (Si2Te3) is a two-dimensional semiconductor material exhibiting unique properties suitable for applications in optoelectronic and electronic devices. This study investigates the resistive switching behavior of Si2Te3 thin films deposited by chemical vapor deposition (CVD). An extremely low SET voltage of 0.15 V with an on/off ratio of 3-5 orders of magnitude was demonstrated. A coupled simulation framework is employed to model the resistive switching behavior, which includes a field-driven semiconductor-to-metal phase transition and a Schottky junction-based thermionic emission theory at the interface of the metal contact. The model quantitatively reproduces the experimentally observed current-voltage characteristics, including the abrupt SET transition, nonvolatile retention of the low-resistance state, and the asymmetric RESET behavior. These findings establish Si2Te3 thin film as a promising material for non-volatile resistive memory applications, offering advantages such as reduced power consumption and increased storage density.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated resistive switching in CVD-deposited Si₂Te₃ thin films at a SET voltage of 0.15 V, with an on/off ratio of 10³–10⁵. Modeling attributes the behavior to a semiconductor-to-metal phase transition and Schottky-junction thermionic emission, supporting potential nonvolatile memory applications.

articles.title_original: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures
articles.title_en: Chemical Etching Creates Internal Heterostructures in Layered Perovskite Crystals
articles.excerpt_original: Engineering internal interfaces within single crystals remains challenging, particularly in soft ionic materials such as layered halide perovskites (LHPs), for which conventional lithographic approaches are difficult to implement. Here we report a solvent/antisolvent-driven strategy for controlled etching of LHP microcrystals, producing well-defined rectangular cavities. Etching initiates at the top surface and proceeds preferentially along the crystallographic [100] and [010] directions. Cavity dimensions are tuned through etching time, temperature and etchant composition. The reaction can be interrupted and resumed, enabling stepwise cavity evolution through successive etching cycles. The resulting cavities serve as confined templates for regrowth of compositionally distinct LHPs, yielding endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal architectures. The approach extends across diverse LHP compositions and antisolvent systems, while sequential precursor addition controls the extent of internal regrowth. This strategy establishes a route to engineering internal heterointerfaces in single-crystal perovskites through controlled chemical etching and confined growth.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a solvent/antisolvent etching method to create controllable cavities inside layered halide perovskite microcrystals. The cavities enable confined regrowth of compositionally distinct perovskites, producing endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal interfaces.

articles.title_original: Oil Removal by Graphene Oxide Aerogels Reinforced by Surfactant Free-Dispersed Carbon Nanotubes
articles.title_en: CNT-Reinforced Graphene Aerogels Improve Oil Uptake for Water Remediation
articles.excerpt_original: Reduced Graphene Oxide (rGO) aerogels were synthesized through hydrothermal reduction using ascorbic acid. The water wetting dynamics and capillary sorption kinetics of rGO aerogels were studied by hybridization with incremental fractions of carbon nanotubes (CNTs). The CNTs were intercalated within the rGO sheets by using a surfactant-free electrolyte-assisted dispersion strategy. The effect of CNT loading on the morphology, structure, and water wetting of rGO aerogels was systematically investigated. Oil uptake performance of the aerogels was studied considering engine oil, olive oil, and sunflower oil. Raman and FTIR analyses confirmed the preservation of the graphitic structure of CNTs after electrolyte-assisted dispersion and the successful reduction of graphene oxide, while SEM observations revealed that modified-CNT incorporation promoted a more homogeneous and interconnected porous architecture. Superhydrophobic aerogels were obtained for a 0.75% and 1.00% CNT loading. The aerogel containing increasing loading up to 1.0 vol.% CNT dispersion improved the gravimetric oil uptake capacity, reaching 172.24 ± 0.82, 191.51 ± 1.43, and 207.17 ± 4.12 mg mg−1 for engine, olive, and sunflower oils, respectively. Higher CNT loadings resulted in a marked decline in oil uptake performance, together with increased water infiltration. These findings provide a critical insight into the tuning of surface percolation of rGO by electrolyte-dispersed CNT for designing advanced hydrophobic graphene-based aerogels for oil-water remediation.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed reduced graphene oxide aerogels reinforced with surfactant-free-dispersed carbon nanotubes. At 1.0 vol.% CNT loading, the aerogels achieved oil uptake capacities of up to 207.17 mg mg−1 for sunflower oil, while higher loadings reduced performance and increased water infiltration.

articles.title_original: Silicon nitride subwavelength-grating microring resonators for refractive-index sensing
articles.title_en: Silicon Nitride Grating Microrings Enhance Refractive-Index Sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Subwavelength-grating microring resonators (SWGMRRs) are promising devices for enhancing light–matter interaction in evanescent-field photonic sensors. Here, we design, fabricate, and experimentally characterize silicon nitride (Si 3 N 4 ) SWGMRRs by varying waveguide widths under aqueous cladding at 1,550 nm. For the 1.2-µm-wide device under transverse-electric (TE) polarization, we demonstrate a bulk refractive index sensitivity ( S b ) of 398 nm/RIU, an intrinsic quality factor ( Q i ) of 1.3 × 10 4 , and an intrinsic limit of detection (iLOD) of 3.0 × 10 −4 RIU. In comparison, a conventional Si 3 N 4 strip microring resonator (SMRR) with the same width and thickness, fabricated on the same chip and characterized under identical conditions, exhibits an S b of 128 nm/RIU, a Q i of 5.7 × 10 4 , and an iLOD of 2.1 × 10 −4 RIU. Numerical analysis predicts a surface sensitivity ( S s ) of 5.3 × 10 −4 RIU/nm for the SWGMRR compared with 1.6 × 10 −4 RIU/nm for the SMRR under TE polarization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first experimental refractive-index sensing demonstration using a Si 3 N 4 microring in which the sensing ring is implemented entirely as a subwavelength-grating waveguide. The results establish a significant enhancement in measured bulk sensitivity and calculated surface sensitivity, while revealing a sensitivity–quality factor trade-off that yields a higher iLOD than the same-width SMRR. These findings support further investigation of Si 3 N 4 SWGMRRs for applications that prioritize enhanced bulk and surface sensing response.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated silicon nitride subwavelength-grating microring resonators with substantially higher bulk and predicted surface sensitivity than conventional strip microrings. The devices exhibited a sensitivity–quality-factor trade-off, resulting in a slightly higher intrinsic detection limit under the tested conditions.

articles.title_original: Contact-localized, strain-engineered metal contacts in 2D field-effect transistors: enabling low-barrier injection via a local stressor
articles.title_en: Contact-localized strain lowers barriers in MoS₂ transistors
articles.excerpt_original: Strain engineering has been an effective strategy for enhancing carrier transport in Si-based transistors. However, in atomically thin 2D materials, strain transfer is hindered by a weak van der Waals (vdW) interface, and global or substrate-mediated strain is difficult to apply effectively. Thus, strain engineering produces limited effects on performance improvement. To overcome these challenges, we report a contact-localized strain engineering approach using metal stressors for MoS 2 transistors. Effective strain is induced when three key mechanical conditions are satisfied: (1) metal nanoisland formation at the interface between metal and MoS 2 enabled by intermediate adhesion, moderate surface tension, and high adatom diffusivity on MoS 2 ; (2) strain generation arising from lattice and atomic registry interactions between the metal and MoS 2 at the interface; and (3) strain transfer through a finite vdW gap that suppresses hybridization while allowing shear coupling. The tensile strain in MoS 2 is exclusively confined to the footprint of the metal nanoisland and integrates to an average global strain of ~0.2%, while the interface remains non-reactive. This engineered strain lowers the effective Schottky barrier height by ~50 meV and reduces contact resistance by ~30%, thereby increasing the on-current by ~60% compared with otherwise identical unstrained devices. This work positions contact-localized strain control as a promising design knob for preparing high-performance 2D transistors.
articles.summary_en: Researchers used metal nanoisland stressors to apply localized tensile strain at MoS₂ transistor contacts, lowering the Schottky barrier by about 50 meV. The approach reduced contact resistance by approximately 30% and increased on-current by around 60% versus unstrained devices.

articles.title_original: Quantum Interband-Coherence-Driven Inverse Faraday Effect in Intrinsic Graphene
articles.title_en: Quantum theory reveals coherent optomagnetism in intrinsic graphene
articles.excerpt_original: The inverse Faraday effect converts the angular momentum of circularly polarized light into a quasistatic magnetization, providing a fundamental route to ultrafast optical control of magnetic fields. We develop an analytical quantum theory of this effect in intrinsic graphene, where massless Dirac fermions, electron-hole symmetry, and weak spin-orbit coupling suppress conventional population-based interpretations. We show that in intrinsic graphene, the helicity-dependent orbital magnetization arises from the off-diagonal zero-harmonic component of the second-order density matrix, rather than from intraband carrier circulation or diagonal population imbalance. We obtain closed expressions for the induced temporal surface magnetization, its finite-pulse dynamics, and the nonlocal stray magnetic field generated by the two-dimensional (2D) source. Optical helicity, frequency, pulse envelope, and beam profile independently control the response. Our results identify intrinsic graphene as an ideal platform for coherent orbital optomagnetism in 2D Dirac matter.
articles.summary_en: Researchers develop an analytical theory showing that graphene’s inverse Faraday effect arises from coherent orbital magnetization rather than conventional carrier-population effects. The predicted response can be controlled through optical helicity, frequency, pulse shape, and beam profile, enabling ultrafast magnetic-field control in two-dimensional materials.

articles.title_original: Interplay of valley, orbital, spin, and layer degrees of freedom in Ta 2 CS 2 MXene
articles.title_en: Ta₂CS₂ MXene Enables Tunable Valley, Spin and Orbital Physics
articles.excerpt_original: We show that the MXene Ta2CS2 provides an promising platform for hosting multiple coupled degrees of freedom, viz., valley, spin, orbital, and layer. The interplay among these degrees of freedom gives rise to a range of intriguing properties in reciprocal space, including valley–orbital and orbital–layer coupling. In the presence of spin–orbit interaction, these couplings lead to valley-dependent and layer-dependent spin splitting of the electronic bands. We further show that the intrinsic electric polarization in Ta2CS2 introduces an additional tuning parameter, enabling control over these coupled degrees of freedom and resulting in switchable valley-dependent orbital moments and Zeeman-like spin splitting. We demonstrate that these nontrivial orbital and spin textures manifest in the orbital and spin Hall effects, respectively. Our results establish noncentrosymmetric MXenes as a promising platform for exploring the interplay among multiple degrees of freedom, their tunability, and the resulting orbital and spin transport phenomena in these two-dimensional materials, thereby paving the way for next-generation spin-orbitronic devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that noncentrosymmetric Ta₂CS₂ MXene couples valley, orbital, spin and layer degrees of freedom, with intrinsic polarization enabling tunable electronic and spin textures. The predicted orbital and spin Hall effects position the material as a platform for future spin-orbitronic devices.

articles.title_original: PMMA-confined BNNT–ZnO nanoparticle hybrid networks for flexible and transparent resistive switching devices
articles.title_en: BNNT–ZnO Hybrid Enables Flexible Transparent Resistive Memory
articles.excerpt_original: In this era of data explosion, issues related to processing and storing information are increasing, making nonvolatile memory technology solutions increasingly important. Developing mechanically compliant and optically transparent nonvolatile memory technologies requires hybrid material systems capable of efficient charge management, structural robustness, and reliable switching stability under deformation. Here, we introduce a tri-component nanocomposite comprising boron nitride nanotube (BNNT) uniformly decorated with zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) and embedded within a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) matrix to realize high-performance flexible resistive switching devices. The ZnO NPs anchored on BNNT surfaces create well-defined charge-trapping centers, while the PMMA matrix provides dielectric modulation and mechanical softness, providing a dielectric environment that supports trap-mediated resistive switching within the hybrid active layer. The resulting Al/BNNT–ZnO NPs + PMMA/indium tin oxide (ITO)/polyethylene terephthalate (PET) architecture exhibits repeatable bistable switching, featuring a high ON/OFF ratio of 1.58 × 10 3 , endurance exceeding 2.5 × 10 4 cycles, and stable retention for 10 5 s. Even under a bending radius of 3 cm, the device maintains an ON/OFF ratio on the order of 10 2 , demonstrating excellent mechanical resilience. Electrical transport analysis reveals a sequential transition from ohmic conduction to space-charge-limited conduction (SCLC), followed by trap-controlled space-charge-limited conduction (TCLC) at intermediate fields and Fowler–Nordheim tunneling at higher electric fields. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a PMMA-embedded boron nitride nanotube–zinc oxide nanoparticle composite for flexible, transparent resistive switching devices. The prototype demonstrated an ON/OFF ratio up to 1.58 × 10³, endurance exceeding 25,000 cycles, and operation under bending.

articles.title_original: Heterostructured BiVO4/g-C3N4 Semiconductor Nanomaterials for Enhanced Visible-Light-Driven Degradation and Mineralization of Emerging Water Contaminants
articles.title_en: BiVO4/g-C3N4 Photocatalyst Enhances Visible-Light Water Pollutant Degradation
articles.excerpt_original: The persistence of emerging contaminants (ECs)—including pharmaceuticals, endocrine-disrupting compounds, and synthetic dyes—in aquatic ecosystems poses a critical threat to environmental and public health due to their resistance to conventional wastewater treatment processes. Semiconductor photocatalysis offers a sustainable, solar-driven pathway for complete pollutant mineralization, yet single-component photocatalysts suffer from rapid electron–hole recombination and limited visible-light utilization. In this study, we report the rational design and synthesis of a two-dimensional/three-dimensional (2D/3D) Z-scheme heterostructured bismuth vanadate/graphitic carbon nitride (BiVO4/g-C3N4) nanocomposite via a facile hydrothermal–calcination coupling strategy. Structural and morphological characterization using X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) confirms the intimate interfacial contact between monoclinic scheelite BiVO4 nanoparticles and ultrathin g-C3N4 nanosheets. Optical and photoelectrochemical analyses—including UV–Vis diffuse reflectance spectroscopy (DRS), photoluminescence (PL), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)—demonstrate extended visible-light harvesting up to 540 nm, suppressed charge-carrier recombination, and accelerated interfacial charge transfer. Under simulated visible-light irradiation (λ ≥ 420 nm), the optimized 15 wt% BiVO4/g-C3N4 heterojunction achieved 96.4% degradation of tetracycline hydrochloride within 90 min, exhibiting an apparent pseudo-first-order rate constant (k = 0.0368 min-1) that is 4.3-fold and 5.8-fold higher than pristine g-C3N4 and bare BiVO4, respectively. articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a 2D/3D BiVO4/g-C3N4 Z-scheme heterojunction for solar-driven wastewater treatment. The optimized material degraded 96.4% of tetracycline hydrochloride in 90 minutes and achieved 81.2% mineralization, outperforming the individual components.

articles.title_original: Propagation characteristics of terahertz waves in mirror-symmetric defect graphene-microplasma photonic crystals
articles.title_en: Graphene–Microplasma Photonic Crystal Enables Tunable Narrowband THz Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Practical terahertz (THz) spectroscopy, sensing, filtering, and communication systems require compact frequency-selective components whose operating frequencies can be prescribed using physically transparent design parameters. In this work, a one-dimensional photonic crystal consisting of two mirror-symmetric Bragg mirrors and a central graphene-microplasma defect cavity is proposed for frequency-selective THz absorption. A reduced Fabry-Pérot phase model is developed to estimate the key cavity thicknesses for a prescribed characteristic frequency. The absorption, reflection, transmission, and electric-field distributions are calculated using the scattering matrix method, and the numerical consistency is verified using the propagation matrix method. The results reveal a transition from irregular multimode spectra at low design frequencies to a stable frequency-tracking regime for $f_0\geq$3.5 THz, where the dominant absorption resonance remains close to the prescribed characteristic frequency. The electric-field distributions reveal pronounced localization in the central defect region, confirming the cavity-mode origin of the resonance. Increasing the Fabry-Pérot resonance order narrows the resonance linewidth while preserving the peak position, whereas oblique incidence produces a systematic frequency shift. Variations in the plasma electron density and electron collision frequency regulate the absorption response by modifying phase accumulation, dissipative loss, and impedance matching. The proposed physics-guided approach provides a basis for predictable narrowband THz absorptive filters, spectroscopic selectors, sensing structures, and plasma-assisted photonic components.
articles.summary_en: IOP Publishing researchers numerically modeled a mirror-symmetric graphene–microplasma photonic crystal for frequency-selective terahertz absorption. The design supports predictable resonance tuning for THz filters, spectroscopy, sensing, and photonic components, with resonance behavior influenced by cavity order, incidence angle, and plasma properties.

articles.title_original: Self-Assembled PTCDA Coatings on Graphene Profoundly Improve the Biocompatibility Toward Genetic Materials
articles.title_en: PTCDA Coatings Improve Graphene Biocompatibility with DNA
articles.excerpt_original: In recent years, graphene and other two-dimensional (2D) materials have garnered tremendous research attention in bio-nanomedicine. Nevertheless, their successful application has been plagued by severe nanotoxicity, particularly toward genetic materials, primarily arising from strong noncovalent van der Waals and stacking interactions between the aromatic surfaces of graphene-based materials (GBMs) and DNA nucleobases. Herein, using in silico methods based on density functional theory (DFT) and classical molecular dynamics (MD), we propose a biocompatible coating strategy for graphene using perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride (PTCDA), in which the coated heterostructures preserve the structural integrity of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA). PTCDA molecules adsorb flat on graphene through stacking interactions and form self-assembled 2D ordered monolayers and bilayers at temperatures of 500 K and above via van der Waals epitaxy. While pristine graphene leads to the gradual unwinding of the double helix through cleavage of inter-strand hydrogen bonds, monolayer PTCDA-coated graphene shows substantial improvement and near-complete preservation of dsDNA upon adsorption. Bilayer PTCDA-coated graphene, on the other hand, weakly interacts with dsDNA, and the DNA is adsorbed in a perpendicular fashion, perfectly preserving the structure. Electronic structure calculations further rule out the possibility of chemical reactions between PTCDA and nucleic acid fragments. The relative biocompatibilities of the monolayer and bilayer PTCDA-coated graphene were estimated to be ∼78% and ∼93%, respectively, compared to pristine graphene. The PTCDA bilayer-coated graphene is further shown to release the adsorbed dsDNA within a therapeutically meaningful timescale, unlike pristine grap
articles.summary_en: Density-functional and molecular-dynamics simulations indicate that self-assembled PTCDA monolayers and bilayers substantially reduce graphene-induced DNA damage. Bilayer coatings preserved DNA structure most effectively and enabled release on a therapeutically meaningful timescale, supporting potential biomedical applications.

articles.title_original: Construction of axial electron-transfer channels in a nickel phthalocyanine/MXene hybrid for efficient hydrogen evolution
articles.title_en: Nickel phthalocyanine–MXene hybrid improves hydrogen-evolution catalysis
articles.excerpt_original: A NiPc/MXene hybrid constructs axial electron-transfer channels between molecular Ni centers and conductive carbide layers. The hybrid approaches Pt/C for the HER, with accelerated kinetics, increased mass activity and reduced charge-transfer resistance. X-ray absorption measurements identify reduced Ni/Ti valence and interfacial Ni-Ti/Ti-C/N coordination. DFT reveals interfacial charge accumulation, continuous Fermi-level states, Ni-Ti bonding and optimized hydrogen adsorption. These results establish axial electronic coupling as a strategy for activating molecular catalysts in AEMWE.

articles.title_original: Constructing radiative dipolar excitons via frontier-state hybridization in 2D perovskites
articles.title_en: Frontier-State Engineering Enables Bright Dipolar Excitons in 2D Perovskites
articles.excerpt_original: Realizing dipolar excitons that simultaneously exhibit strong optical activity and long-range repulsive interactions remains a central challenge in exciton-based nonlinear optics. This challenge stems from the intrinsic trade-off between achieving spatial charge separation, which is necessary for dipole formation, and maintaining sufficient wavefunction overlap to ensure efficient radiative recombination. Here, we overcome this trade-off in the two-dimensional perovskite (AE3T)PbI 4 by leveraging organic-inorganic band-edge engineering to induce frontier-state hybridization, thereby forming bright hybridized dipolar excitons with spatially indirect character and appreciable optical transition strength. These excitons combine an out-of-plane permanent electric-dipole component, room-temperature nonlinear transport consistent with long-range dipole–dipole repulsion, and finite optical transition dipole moments. Beyond addressing a key constraint in dipolar-exciton design, this work establishes frontier-state hybridization as a molecular design principle for constructing optically active, electrically polarized excitons in low-dimensional quantum materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report hybridized dipolar excitons in a two-dimensional perovskite that combine optical activity, permanent electric dipoles and long-range repulsive interactions. The findings establish frontier-state hybridization as a design principle for optically active, electrically polarized excitons in low-dimensional quantum materials.
