articles.title_original: Bandedge-State-Limited Single-Photon Emission from Volumetric Quantum Design of 2D Colloidal Quantum Wells
articles.title_en: 2D Quantum Wells Enable Reliable Room-Temperature Single-Photon Emission
articles.excerpt_original: Present-day solution-processable single-photon sources are dominated by three-dimensionally confined colloidal quantum emitters, yet their particle-to-particle variation in single-exciton properties limits reproducibility and scalability. Here, to avoid such heterogeneity, we demonstrate reliable room-temperature single-photon emission from atomically flat two-dimensional (2D) colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) with inherently uniform one-dimensional quantum confinement, despite their long-standing limitations of efficient multiexciton emission and pronounced exciton-surface susceptibility. We resolve these challenges through volumetric quantum design (VQD) of CQWs, yielding a highly localized, single bandedge state. This design laterally confines the bandedge excitonic domain within the exciton coherent area and vertically decouples it from surface states via a thick, strain-relieved quantum-barrier shell that preserves strong confinement, overcoming the daunting thickness-confinement trade-off in 2D CQWs. Statistical single-particle spectroscopy reveals that VQD-CQWs deliver near-blinking-free (on-time: >99.5%) and fluence-insensitive antibunching (g(2)(0): ∼0.041), protected by a bandedge-state-filling bottleneck, together with linear polarization of up to 73% under cavity-free conditions, originating from synergistic transition-dipole and electric-field anisotropies. These advances establish 2D CQWs as a viable, homogeneous and scalable platform for quantum technologies.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate near-blinking-free, polarized single-photon emission from atomically flat 2D colloidal quantum wells using volumetric quantum design. The approach addresses multiexciton emission and surface-state limitations, supporting scalable quantum-photonic applications.

articles.title_original: Substrate-and defect-induced reactivity of graphene: a theoretical review
articles.title_en: Theoretical review examines how substrates and defects alter graphene reactivity
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene is often regarded as chemically inert, yet its reactivity can be substantially modified through structural defects and interactions with underlying substrates. Here, we review, from a predominantly theoretical perspective, how substrate-induced charge redistribution, interfacial hybridization, and local structural deformation influence molecular adsorption, dissociation, and covalent functionalization of graphene. Particular attention is given to the interplay between substrate interactions and defects, which can either promote molecular activation or passivate reactive sites. Static first-principles calculations are complemented by ab initio and reactive molecular dynamics studies addressing finite-temperature effects, bond rearrangements, and interfacial stability. We also discuss graphene-based single-atom catalysts (SACs), emphasizing the role of metal coordination, defective carbon environments, and electronic interactions in determining the stability of isolated metal centers and the adsorption of reaction intermediates. Across metallic, oxide, and semiconductor supports, the reviewed studies reveal reaction-dependent modifications of graphene reactivity, including reduced activation barriers for O 2 , H 2 , and H 2 O dissociation, changes in organic functionalization pathways, and stabilization of CO-derived intermediates. Importantly, enhanced chemical activation or irreversible functionalization does not necessarily establish catalytic activity, which requires consideration of complete reaction cycles. articles.summary_en: A theoretical review finds that substrate-induced charge redistribution, interfacial hybridization, and structural defects can modify graphene’s molecular adsorption, dissociation, and functionalization behavior. It highlights implications for interface design and graphene-based single-atom catalysts, while noting that chemical activation alone does not establish catalytic activity.

articles.title_original: Electrical Excitation of High‐Density Excitons Enhancing Optically‐Pumped ASE in Organic Semiconductors
articles.title_en: Electrical Excitation Enhances ASE in Organic Semiconductor Devices
articles.excerpt_original: Organic semiconductors exhibit superior optoelectronic traits and solution processability. Moreover, leveraging their high gain characteristics, low‐threshold and continuous‐wave optically pumped lasing has been achieved. However, the contradiction between high density exciton injection and high optical gain has prevented observation of contributions from electrically injected excitons to lasing. Here, electrically excited transient absorption (EETA) reveals excitonic bleaching consistent with a stimulated emission contribution. We further demonstrate electrical enhancement of optically pumped amplified spontaneous emission (ASE). Along with processes of electrically injected excitons participating in amplified spontaneous emission (ASE). The key to achieving these lies in developing devices combining high electrical injection exciton density and high gain. Through device engineering, we designed an ITO/Mo/SiO 2 electrode structure featuring low gain loss while ensuring short‐pulse electrical injection, reducing losses in ITO. We further employ 50 ns electrical pulses to suppress triplet accumulation, thereby mitigating triplet‐induced singlet quenching. Thus, we observed an electrically induced excitonic bleaching signal with an amplitude of 0.36 mOD. Co‐excitation with 40 µJ cm −2 optical pumping and 2 kA cm −2 electrical pulses amplifies ASE intensity by 21% within a 10 ns gain window. These results provide an experimental basis for developing organic electrically pumped lasers.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated that electrically injected excitons can contribute to amplified spontaneous emission in organic semiconductors. Co-excitation increased ASE intensity by 21%, supporting development of electrically pumped organic lasers.

articles.title_original: Achieving Low Loss and High Breakdown in Polyimide Films via a Rigid‐Flexible Synergistic Molecular Design

articles.excerpt_original: The development of polymer dielectrics with high energy density, low loss, and high‐temperature reliability remains challenging for advanced film capacitors. Conventional polyimide (PI) dielectrics suffer from high dielectric loss and limited breakdown strength, restricting their energy storage capability at elevated temperatures. This study proposes a “rigidity–flexibility integration” strategy by chemically incorporating flexible Poly(dimethylsiloxane) bis(3‐aminopropyl) terminated (PDMS) segments into rigid PI backbones. Systematic investigation demonstrates that PDMS effectively modulates dielectric response and breakdown characteristics. The optimized PI‐PDMS copolymer composite films exhibit a 44% reduction in dielectric loss (from 0.008 to 0.0045) and a 27% enhancement in breakdown strength (from 365 to 467.9 MV/m), while maintaining a dielectric constant of ~3.3. Consequently, the copolymer composite films achieve a discharged energy density of 4.0 J/cm 3 at room temperature and retain 2.6 J/cm 3 with over 80% efficiency at 150°C, alongside excellent cycling stability over 100,000 cycles. These improvements originate from deep‐level traps and tailored free volume introduced by PDMS segments, which suppress charge transport and polarization loss. This work provides an effective strategy for designing high‐performance polymer dielectrics with balanced properties and outstanding high‐temperature reliability for capacitive energy storage.

Finally, key challenges and areas requiring further improvement are outlined. This review aims to provide a concise framework for linking material design with biomedical performance and to guide the development of clinically relevant g-C3N4-based nanoplatforms.

articles.title_original: Correlation-driven bonding anisotropy in uniaxially strained graphene
articles.title_en: Electron Correlation Reveals Strain-Dependent Bonding Anisotropy in Graphene
articles.excerpt_original: Uniaxial strain deforms the honeycomb network of graphene into qualitatively different real-space bonding topologies depending on the loading direction. Stretching along one lattice direction isolates carbon dimers, while stretching along the other preserves extended zigzag chains. We show that the total-energy anisotropy between these two loading directions is qualitatively transformed by electron correlation. Density-functional theory and a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model both give a smooth, monotonic, essentially single-particle directional response. Variational and diffusion quantum Monte Carlo with a Jastrow-Slater wave function instead reveal a non-monotonic anisotropy that changes sign near 20% strain, a trajectory no uniform rescaling of the single-particle result could produce. Inspection of the wave function reveals two direction-dependent reorganizations accompanying this behavior: a frontier-orbital reorganization inherited from DFT, and a many-body signature in which the on-site (atomic three-body) Jastrow coefficients weaken and become spatially more uniform under y-stretch but remain large and structured under x-stretch.
articles.summary_en: Quantum Monte Carlo calculations show that electron correlation qualitatively changes graphene’s directional response to uniaxial strain, producing a non-monotonic anisotropy that reverses sign near 20% strain. The study identifies distinct frontier-orbital and many-body reorganizations for different strain directions, advancing fundamental understanding of strained graphene.

articles.title_original: Giant conductance enhancement in graphene nanoscrolls via interlayer-coupled states
articles.title_en: Graphene nanoscrolls show nearly 20-fold conductance enhancement
articles.excerpt_original: Graphene nanoscrolls form a unique radial superlattice whose geometry enables transport behaviors distinct from their flat counterparts. We theoretically demonstrate that rolling a graphene nanoribbon into a few-turn nanoscroll (1.0–1.2 turns) triggers a giant enhancement in longitudinal conductance by an order of magnitude (nearly twentyfold). We show that this effect stems from interlayer hopping between open boundaries, which not only transforms localized edge states into one-dimensional-like conducting channels and also induces a significant Fermi energy shift. Our results reveal an inverse scaling of conductance with turn number, establishing GNSs as a platform for geometry-driven quantum transport and offering a tunable approach to engineering nanoarchitectural electronic states.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical analysis finds that rolling graphene nanoribbons into few-turn nanoscrolls creates interlayer-coupled conducting channels and shifts the Fermi energy. articles.title_original: A tunable multi-gated platform for superlattice engineering in bilayer graphene
articles.title_en: Tunable multi-gate platform enables reconfigurable bilayer graphene superlattices
articles.excerpt_original: Periodic potentials with length scales much larger than crystal lattice constants can generate low-energy electronic minibands. While small-angle twisted van der Waals heterostructures have been widely used to realize such physics, correlated phases are often limited by twist-angle inhomogeneity, strain, and disorder. Here, we investigate high-quality Bernal bilayer graphene placed on a patterned graphite gate, featuring a triangular array of holes, forming a new class of "gate-engineered" superlattices tunable through three independent electrostatic gates. Near the charge neutrality point, we observe insulating states characteristic of miniband formation. Temperature-dependent transport reveals activated gaps consistent with theory, and Hall measurements indicate charge-carrier inversion. Notably, the superlattice can be reconfigured electrostatically using various gate combinations, enabling flexible band-structure design without mechanical twisting. The results highlight a new route to band engineering, potentially extendable to complex periodic structures that are untenable in natural materials.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate gate-engineered superlattices in Bernal bilayer graphene using a patterned graphite gate and three independently controlled electrostatic gates. The platform produces miniband-related insulating states and carrier inversion without mechanical twisting, offering a flexible route to band-structure engineering for advanced electronic devices.

articles.title_original: Regulating Functionalized MXene Crystal-Field Splitting toward Efficient Bifunctional Oxygen Electrocatalysis of Lithium–Oxygen Batteries
articles.title_en: Functionalized MXene improves lithium–oxygen battery electrocatalysis
articles.excerpt_original: MXenes offer fast conductive frameworks with abundant intrinsic active metal sites, making them promising cathode catalysts for lithium–oxygen batteries for addressing sluggish oxygen kinetics and severe cathode passivation. However, the predictive electronic descriptors for rationally regulating these intrinsic active sites remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate the implementation of crystal-field splitting engineering at Ti sites of Ti3C2-MXene to achieve bifunctional oxygen electrocatalysis. Through coordinated anionic and cationic modifications, we regulate the local coordination environment of Ti atoms, weakening crystal-field splitting and promoting electron delocalization within Ti3C2-MXene frameworks. X-ray absorption spectra reveal systematic shifts of Ti K-edge and contraction of the pre-edge splitting, consistent with weakened and distorted Ti ligand fields. This electronic rearrangement promotes an asymmetric Li2O2 adsorption configuration, thereby lowering the energy barriers for both ORR and OER. Consequently, the functionalized Cu–Ti3C2Br2 delivers a high discharge specific capacity of 11,662 mAh g–1 and reduces the initial charge overpotential by 50% compared with Ti3C2OF. This study indicates crystal-field splitting as a key descriptor governing oxygen electrocatalytic behavior in lithium–oxygen batteries.
articles.summary_en: Researchers engineered the crystal-field environment of Ti sites in Ti3C2 MXene to improve bifunctional oxygen reduction and evolution reactions. The functionalized Cu–Ti3C2Br2 cathode reached 11,662 mAh g⁻¹ and cut initial charge overpotential by 50% versus Ti3C2OF.

articles.title_original: Ultraviolet emission of color centers in various polytypes of 2D boron nitride—High-pressure study
articles.title_en: High-pressure study identifies carbon-dimer emission fingerprints in 2D boron nitride
articles.excerpt_original: High hydrostatic pressure studies of the low-temperature photoluminescence (PL) from the hexagonal (hBN), rhombohedral (rBN), and bernal (bBN) polytypes of sp2 boron nitride in the 3.3–4.2 eV spectral region were performed using the diamond anvil cell technique to find out the effect of the BN polytype on the PL and the PL pressure behavior of the same type of defects. The defect-associated PL energy decreased with pressure less than the bandgap, and the pressure coefficients of the PL energy depend strongly on the BN polytype. Comparison of the experimental results and theoretical calculations of the pressure dependencies of defect-related PL performed for the rBN polytype confirmed that the bright emission with a zero-phonon line at ∼302 nm (∼4.1 eV) with a few phonon replicas originates from carbon dimers, like for hBN and bBN. articles.title_original: Optical characterization of Fermi polarons in monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride
articles.title_en: Silicon Nitride Encapsulation Induces Fermi Polarons in Monolayer MoSe₂
articles.excerpt_original: Amorphous silicon nitride is the leading low-loss, CMOS-compatible platform for wafer-scale integrated photonics. Encapsulating transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) monolayers within this platform offers a promising route towards scalable TMD-photonic circuits. Yet the effect of this amorphous dielectric on the optical response of the monolayer remains poorly understood. Here, we compare monolayer MoSe$_2$ encapsulated in amorphous silicon nitride with a hexagonal boron nitride-encapsulated reference, using differential reflectivity and photoluminescence. Whereas the reference is dominated by the neutral exciton, the nitride-encapsulated monolayer shows attractive and repulsive polaron resonances separated by ${\sim}31$~meV, with emission dominated by the attractive branch. A quantitative comparison of temperature-dependent reflectance with a microscopic finite-temperature Fermi-polaron theory shows that the nitride induces substantial electron doping in the monolayer, with an electron density of $(0.8$--$0.9)\times10^{12}$~cm$^{-2}$. Using the extracted density and trion binding energy as the only input parameters, the theory reproduces the photoluminescence spectra up to ${\sim}80$ K in excellent quantitative agreement with experiments, thus corroborating the Fermi-polaron description of the observed excitonic response.
articles.summary_en: Researchers found that amorphous silicon nitride encapsulation substantially electron-dopes monolayer MoSe₂, producing attractive and repulsive Fermi-polaron resonances. The findings support scalable TMD–photonic circuit integration using CMOS-compatible, wafer-scale silicon nitride platforms.

articles.title_original: Cation migration suppression for efficient photoluminescence and photoelectrical response in two-dimensional perovskite heterostructure
articles.title_en: hBN Layer Suppresses Cation Migration in 2D Perovskite Heterostructures
articles.excerpt_original: Understanding the ion migration and charge transfer at the interface is the key issue in developing high-performance two-dimensional organic–inorganic hybrid perovskites (2D OIHPs) vdW heterostructures. In this study, a van der Waals heterostructure composed of (PEA)2(MA)Pb2I7 (n = 2) and (PEA)2PbI4 (n = 1) is fabricated with and without an inserted hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) layer. Anomalous photoluminescence (PL) intensity evolution from n = 2 on the heterojunction is revealed, in which the PL intensity first increased and then decreased with increasing inserted hBN thickness. To address the mechanism, transient and variable temperature PL spectroscopy is carried out and reveals cation redistribution in the heterostructure to form localized n = 2 defects in the n = 1 layer. Both the recombination of the defects and the charge transfer from n = 1 to n = 2 cause the fast non-radiated carrier decay in the n = 1 layer. The insertion of the hBN layer is found to effectively block cation migration, while being relatively inefficient in blocking carrier transfer across the interface. With increasing inserted hBN thickness, a transition from charge recombination dominating to charge transfer dominating appears, which is responsible for the anomalous PL evolution. This study highlights the critical role of interfacial cation migration on the interfacial properties of 2D OIHP-heterostructure and offers a generalizable structural design strategy for improving the optoelectronic performance.
articles.summary_en: Researchers show that inserting hexagonal boron nitride between layered perovskites suppresses cation migration while only partly blocking charge transfer. The findings clarify interfacial recombination and offer a design strategy for improving photoluminescence and photoelectrical performance.

articles.title_original: Comparative Study of Immobilized TiO2, h-BN and h-BN/TiO2-Modified PES Membranes for Photocatalytic Degradation of Ciprofloxacin

articles.excerpt_original: This work reports on the development of immobilized mixed-matrix PES membranes incorporating TiO2, h-BN, and h-BN/TiO2 nanocomposite for the photocatalytic degradation of ciprofloxacin (CIP) as a model pharmaceutical pollutant. The membranes were fabricated via phase inversion using different nanomaterial loadings (0.5–2 wt%) and characterised using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), and contact angle analysis. The incorporation of the nanomaterials into the polymer matrix was confirmed with variations in membrane morphology and surface hydrophilicity depending on the nanomaterial and loading. Under UV irradiation, the TiO2-modified membrane (T1-PES) achieved a maximum CIP degradation efficiency of 43.18% with a pseudo-first-order rate constant of 0.00239 min−1. In contrast, the h-BN-modified membranes exhibited the lowest overall performance, with the maximum degradation being observed for the h-BN2-PES, achieving 18.15% degradation with a rate constant of 0.000907 min−1, attributed to its limited photocatalytic activity despite successful incorporation into the membrane. The h-BN/TiO2-modified membranes showed the highest overall photocatalytic performance, with h-BNT1.5-PES demonstrating the highest overall performance, achieving 51.04% degradation, while h-BNT2-PES exhibited the fastest apparent kinetics, with a rate constant of 0.00263 min−1. These findings demonstrate that photocatalytic performance depends on both nanomaterial composition and loading, with the optimum loading for degradation efficiency differing from that for reaction kinetics. The results highlight the potential of h-BN/TiO2-modified PES membranes as immobilized photocatalytic systems for pharmaceutical contaminant removal.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed PES membranes modified with TiO2, h-BN, and h-BN/TiO2 nanocomposites for pharmaceutical-pollutant removal under UV light. The h-BN/TiO2 membrane achieved up to 51.04% ciprofloxacin degradation, outperforming the single-material membranes.

articles.title_original: Magnon band structure and topology in a periodically deformed kagome lattice with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction
articles.title_en: Research explores topological magnons in deformed kagome lattices
articles.excerpt_original: We study the band structure and topology of magnons for a Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction on a deformed kagome lattice. For simplicity, we focus on a periodically deformed lattice with hexagonal symmetry and an enlarged unit cell. This enlarged unit cell gives rise to a more complex band structure than in the undeformed case. Analyzing band topology, there is a distinction between the topologically trivial case with antiferromagnetic coupling and the topologically nontrivial case with ferromagnetic coupling. In the antiferromagnetic case, a spin-space symmetry, also present in the classical ground state, enforces these topologically trivial states. In the ferromagnetic case, this symmetry is spontaneously broken by the classical ground state. Consequently, the band structure also hosts numerous topological features. Specifically, we observe many topological transitions and bands with Chern numbers ranging from $+2$ to $\ensuremath{-}2$, which makes the system richer than in the undeformed case. This emergent topological structure demonstrates that deformed magnets can host new and exciting physics.
articles.summary_en: Researchers modeled magnon band structures in periodically deformed kagome lattices with Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction. The study identifies ferromagnetic topological phases, multiple transitions, and bands with Chern numbers from +2 to −2, but reports no direct commercial application.

articles.excerpt_original: As silicon‐based electronic devices approach their physical limits, two‐dimensional (2D) layered materials have attracted increasing attention because of their excellent electrical, optical, and thermal properties. These materials show broad application potential in electronics, optoelectronics, and energy conversion. With the continuous increase in device integration and the growing demand for thermal management, the study of thermal transport in 2D layered materials has become a major research focus. Compared with bulk materials, 2D layered materials have ultrathin thickness, strong interface effects, and clear anisotropy. As a result, their thermal transport behavior is strongly influenced by size effects, interlayer interactions, defects, and crystal structure. Therefore, accurate measurement of their thermal properties requires high‐sensitivity and high‐resolution techniques. This review summarizes recent advances in thermal transport measurements of two‐dimensional layered materials from a combined measurement and metrology perspective. Representative techniques, including optothermal Raman thermometry, time‐domain thermoreflectance, frequency‐domain thermoreflectance, and suspended micro‐bridge calorimetry, are discussed. Attention is given to key metrological issues in two‐dimensional thermal measurements. In addition, this review summarizes thermal transport results in typical two‐dimensional materials, discusses the modulation of thermal transport by factors such as thickness, defects, and strain, and further analyzes thermal management issues at the device scale. This review is expected to provide useful guidance for understanding the thermal properties of 2D layered materials, selecting appropriate measurement methods, and designing thermal management strate
articles.summary_en: A review examines metrology techniques for measuring thermal transport in two-dimensional layered materials, including optothermal Raman thermometry, thermoreflectance, and suspended micro-bridge calorimetry. It also analyzes how thickness, defects, strain, interfaces, and anisotropy affect thermal management at the device scale.

articles.excerpt_original: Energy levels of trions in a bulk semiconductor crystal are calculated by two different numerical methods. On the one hand, we construct the finite-element solution of the Schrödinger equation in the total angular momentum representation. On the other hand, we use the Gaussian expansion method (GEM), applied to each of the three Faddeev components of the wave function. The results for the total angular momenta $J=0$ and $J=1$ of the trion were obtained for a wide range of the hole-to-electron mass ratios covering most existing semiconductor compounds. The dependencies of the energies on the mass ratio for trions in a bulk crystal qualitatively agree with the results for a simplified model of a trion in a 1D quantum wire, for which the three-body energies can be calculated with arbitrary precision as well as easily approximated using Born-Oppenheimer potential-energy curves. A comparison of our results with data from other publicly available three-body codes as well as with the energies of well-known atomic counterparts, in particular, with vibrational energy levels of the molecular hydrogen ion, shows a good agreement and confirms the accuracy of the numerical data. We found that GEM significantly improves the precision of the obtained trion energies compared to previous calculations. Our calculations demonstrate that, for most semiconductor compounds, only one trion state with zero total angular momentum exists.
articles.summary_en: Researchers calculated trion energy levels across a broad range of hole-to-electron mass ratios using finite-element and Gaussian expansion methods. The Gaussian expansion method improved precision, and results indicate that most semiconductor compounds support only one zero-total-angular-momentum trion state.

articles.title_original: Shubnikov–de Haas characterization of superconductor–semiconductor heterostructures
articles.title_en: Shubnikov–de Haas Method Characterizes Superconductor–Semiconductor Interfaces
articles.excerpt_original: Hybrid superconductor–semiconductor nanostructures are a central component for research spanning condensed matter physics and quantum information processing. Continued progress relies critically on the ability to characterize, control, and optimize several intrinsic material properties, including spin–orbit coupling, band offsets, and disorder, in a device-relevant stack that necessarily couples the electronic states of a superconducting metal film and a semiconductor. Here, we report a new method to extract fundamental material parameters utilizing simple Shubnikov–de Haas oscillation measurements in heterostructures in which metallic electronic states are coupled to a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) residing in an InAs quantum well beneath an aluminum thin film. Proper analysis of the full magnetoresistance data facilitates extraction of the quantum well carrier density, spin–orbit coupling strength, and both transport and quantum scattering times. Most importantly, the extracted scattering times in the 2DEG are impacted by the metal–semiconductor coupling strength, allowing us to quickly measure an upper bound for superconductor–semiconductor coupling without any fabrication or mK measurements. The wealth of information that is accessed with these simple measurements positions this methodology as an important tool for hybrid materials optimization.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrate that Shubnikov–de Haas oscillation measurements can extract carrier density, spin–orbit coupling, and scattering times in aluminum–InAs quantum-well heterostructures. The method provides a rapid, fabrication-free approach to assess superconductor–semiconductor coupling and optimize hybrid quantum devices.

articles.title_original: Overcoming configuration bottleneck: Modular pathways to stable semiconductor spin-qubit arrays
articles.title_en: Modular Automation Pathways for Stable Semiconductor Spin-Qubit Arrays
articles.excerpt_original: Over the past decade, semiconductor spin qubits have progressed from few-qubit demonstrations toward larger-scale devices fabricated in increasingly reproducible academic and industrial processes. This progress marks an inflection point: the central challenge is no longer to demonstrate high-fidelity operation in carefully tuned devices but to discover, verify, and maintain stable operating conditions reliably across many interdependent controls, varied device geometries, and disparate material platforms. In this Perspective, we frame spin-qubit operation as a modular automation problem. We decompose the workflow into five modules: bootstrapping from minimal prior information, configuration tuning, virtualization of physical gates into effective control axes, qubit-level tuning, and an operation layer with drift-aware maintenance. Using recent demonstrations from our work and the broader community, we argue that scalability will depend on explicit interfaces between modules, standardized intermediate data products, and workflow-level metrics such as throughput, success probability, stability time, recovery time, and robustness. We close by outlining the infrastructure needed to move beyond isolated tuning demonstrations toward sustained operation: qubit-performance-aware feedback, reusable software and benchmark tasks, and tight collaboration among experimental, theoretical, and software efforts.
articles.summary_en: A perspective frames scalable semiconductor spin-qubit operation as a modular automation problem spanning configuration, control virtualization, qubit tuning, and drift-aware maintenance. It identifies standardized interfaces, reusable software, feedback, and workflow metrics as infrastructure priorities for sustained multi-qubit operation.

articles.title_original: Coupled photothermal and thermoelastic wave propagation in a nonlocal semiconductor nanobeam with carrier density effects
articles.title_en: Modeling Photothermal-Thermoelastic Waves in Semiconductor Nanobeams
articles.excerpt_original: In this paper, coupled photothermal and thermoelastic wave propagation in a nonlocal semiconductor nanobeam is carried out using an analytical method within the framework of generalized thermoelasticity. The nanobeam is subjected to harmonic photothermal excitation, and a mathematical model is developed by incorporating size-dependent nonlocal elasticity and carrier diffusion effects in semiconductors. The governing coupled field equations for temperature, carrier density, transverse deflection, and bending moment are derived based on Euler-Bernoulli beam theory. The resulting system is solved analytically using the normal mode analysis technique. Numerical results are discussed in detail to examine the influence of key physical parameters, including the carrier lifetime, nonlocal parameter, and excitation frequency, on the thermoelastic and photothermal behavior of the nanobeam. The numerical and graphical results underscore the significant influence of carrier life time, nonlocal and frequency on the temperature, transverse deflection, carrier density and bending moment distribution. The results reveal that the nonlocal parameter significantly modifies the wave propagation characteristics and enhances size-dependent effects at the nanoscale. In addition, the carrier lifetime strongly governs the evolution of carrier density and the coupled photothermal response, while the excitation frequency plays a crucial role in controlling the dynamic behavior of the system. These findings provide a comprehensive analytical framework for describing coupled photothermal-thermoelastic wave phenomena in semiconductor nanobeams and offers useful insights for the design of advanced nanoelectromechanical and photothermal semiconductor devices.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an analytical model of coupled photothermal and thermoelastic wave propagation in semiconductor nanobeams, incorporating nonlocal elasticity, carrier diffusion, carrier lifetime, and excitation frequency. The study offers theoretical insights for nanoelectromechanical and photothermal semiconductor device design, without identifying a commercial product or company.

articles.title_original: Structural performance and flexural behaviour of graphene oxide-modified recycled aggregate concrete beams
articles.title_en: Graphene oxide improves flexural performance of recycled-aggregate concrete beams
articles.excerpt_original: Recycled coarse aggregate (RCA) offers a sustainable alternative to natural coarse aggregate. However, its application in structural concrete can be affected by adhered mortar, increased porosity, and the characteristics of the interfacial transition zone. This study experimentally investigates the flexural behaviour of reinforced concrete beams incorporating 100% RCA, manufactured sand (M-sand), and graphene oxide (GO). Six reinforced concrete beams (1,400 × 150 × 150 mm) incorporating GO dosages of 0%, 0.02%, 0.03%, 0.04%, 0.05%, and 0.06% by weight of cement were cast and tested under two-point loading after 28 days of water curing. The first visible cracking load ranged from 14.3 kN for the control beam to 30.5 kN for the beam containing 0.04% GO. The measured peak load of the 0.04% GO beam was 68.6 kN, compared with 40.1 kN for the control beam. Calculated flexural capacities varied from 69.3 kN to 71.8 kN, indicating relatively small differences in theoretical flexural resistance among the mixtures. Energy absorption was evaluated up to first cracking, at a common midspan deflection of 6.5 mm, and up to the maximum recorded load using the measured load–deflection curves. Compared with the control beam, the 0.04% GO beam exhibited higher energy absorption at all three evaluation points, with first-cracking energy increasing from 17.88 J to 57.95 J, energy absorption at 6.5 mm increasing from 156 J to 290 J, and energy absorption up to the maximum recorded load increasing from 206.72 J to 617.76 J. These results indicate that the 0.04% GO beam exhibited the most favourable cracking, peak-load, and energy-absorption responses among the specimens tested. However, because only one beam was tested for each mixture, the findings should be interpreted as experimental obse
articles.summary_en: A Frontiers study tested reinforced concrete beams made with 100% recycled coarse aggregate, manufactured sand and varying graphene oxide dosages. The 0.04% graphene oxide mixture showed the strongest observed cracking resistance, peak load and energy absorption, although results are limited because only one beam was tested per mixture.

articles.title_original: Photocatalytic 1,2‐Boron Migrative Alkene Homologation to Access 1,3‐Difunctionalized Alkenes
articles.title_en: Photocatalytic Alkene Homologation Enables 1,3-Difunctionalized Alkenes
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT In contrast to well‐established methods for vicinal di‐functionalization of alkenes, remote di‐functionalization is much more challenging and has achieved limited success. Herein, we disclose a visible light photocatalytic boron‐directed alkene homologation with alkyl halides activated by a traceless tert ‐butylsulfonyl (Bus) leaving group. The reaction produces a myriad of 1,3‐difunctionalized alkenes under mild conditions with excellent functional group tolerance. β‐Elimination of the Bus group not only drives the contra‐thermodynamic 1,2‐boron migration, but also regenerates a C─C double bond, thus transforming the sulfone‐based alkyl halide into a vinylidene precursor, rather than a traditional alkyl source. The synthetic utility of this method is well demonstrated by gram‐scale synthesis, downstream transformations, and the formal total synthesis of 24‐fluoro‐25‐hydroxyvitamin D 3 analogues. This work represents a very rare example of one‐carbon homologation of ubiquitous alkenes, thus establishing a new strategic paradigm for chemical synthesis.
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a visible-light photocatalytic method for boron-directed alkene homologation, producing 1,3-difunctionalized alkenes under mild conditions. Gram-scale synthesis and downstream transformations demonstrate potential utility in complex-molecule synthesis, including vitamin D3 analogues.

articles.title_original: Combustion of Boron Nanoparticles Encapsulated within Perchlorate Matrices: A Mechanistic Study
articles.title_en: Encapsulated Boron Nanoparticles Improve High-Energy Combustion Performance
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Boron is an attractive high-energy fuel, but its practical combustion efficiency is limited by a viscous oxide layer that impedes oxygen transport and promotes agglomeration. Here, we address these limitations by assembling boron nanoparticles into spray-dried mesoparticles in which boron is encapsulated within an ammonium perchlorate (AP) matrix and a nitrocellulose binder. This architecture enhances fuel oxidizer proximity, accelerates AP decomposition onset by ∼60 °C, and enhances reaction kinetics as evidenced by a ∼50% pressurization rate and a ∼58% shorter burn time relative to the physically mixed formulation. In situ TEM, TGA/DSC, and T-jump time-of-flight mass spectrometry reveal that mesoparticles promote interfacial reactions producing both B2O3 and boron nitride (BN). BN formation is identified as a thermodynamic efficiency-loss pathway, releasing significantly less energy per mole of boron than oxidation to B2O3. Substituting AP with potassium perchlorate eliminates the nitrogen source, significantly reducing BN formation, and further improves combustion performance. These results demonstrate that mesoscale encapsulation combined with targeted oxidizer selection provides a practical strategy to enhance boron combustion efficiency.
articles.summary_en: ACS researchers assembled boron nanoparticles in ammonium perchlorate mesoparticles, increasing pressurization rates and shortening burn times versus physical mixtures. Replacing ammonium perchlorate with potassium perchlorate reduced boron nitride formation and further improved combustion efficiency, indicating potential relevance to energetic and propulsion materials.

articles.title_original: MXene-bridged Z-scheme BiOI/UiO-66(NH2) heterojunction for enhanced photocatalytic degradation of PFAS
articles.title_en: MXene-bridged heterojunction degrades PFAS in water
articles.excerpt_original: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are highly persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic chemicals that pose serious risks to human health and the environment. Their widespread presence in water and the strict global regulations highlight the urgent need for effective degradation strategies. In this study, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA), representing long- and short-chain PFAS, respectively, were degraded using a MXene-bridged Z-scheme heterojunction (BiOI/UiO-66(NH 2 )-MXene). The composite was designed by coupling visible-light-responsive BiOI with porous UiO-66(NH 2 ) to enhance adsorption, while MXene acted as a conductive bridge to improve charge separation and interfacial contact. The structural, surface, optical, and electronic properties of the developed materials were systematically evaluated to understand their role in PFAS degradation. Under optimum conditions, the heterojunction achieved 98.4% degradation of PFOA with 44.1% defluorination and 93.6% degradation of PFBA within 6 h. These findings provide mechanistic insight into PFAS degradation and highlight the potential of MXene-bridged Z-scheme systems for treating fluorinated contaminants in water.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed a BiOI/UiO-66(NH2)-MXene photocatalyst that degraded 98.4% of PFOA and 93.6% of PFBA within six hours under optimized conditions. The study reports 44.1% PFOA defluorination, indicating progress toward photocatalytic treatment of persistent fluorinated contaminants.

articles.title_original: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.title_en: Cavity control improves emission from hBN spin defects for quantum sensing
articles.excerpt_original: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.
articles.summary_en: Researchers integrated negatively charged boron-vacancy defects in hexagonal boron nitride with a tunable microcavity, enhancing photoluminescence and modifying optical decay dynamics. The findings clarify defect dipole orientation and support development of room-temperature quantum-sensing platforms.

articles.title_original: Robust Oleophobic and Sweat-Wicking Janus Fabric for Personal Passive Cooling
articles.title_en: h-BN-Coated Janus Fabric Enables Durable Passive Cooling
articles.excerpt_original: Efficient sweat transport and heat dissipation are essential for thermal comfort. However, traditional moisture-wicking textiles are susceptible to oil contamination and functional deterioration during use. Herein, an oleophobic and sweat-wicking Janus (OSJ) fabric was developed by coating spandex fibers with hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) and a crosslinked layer containing a short-chain fluorosurfactant, followed by selective deposition of polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) on the inner surface. The oleophobic/superhydrophilic outer side of the OSJ fabric facilitates water-assisted oil removal, while the wettability contrast promotes outward water transport and suppresses reverse penetration. Artificial skin experiments demonstrated improved heat and moisture management relative to commercial functional fabrics under different simulated metabolic heat loads and thermal conditions. In outdoor summer tests, the average temperature of the artificial skin covered with OSJ fabric was more than 3 °C lower than that covered with cotton and COOLMAX fabrics. The oleophobic/superhydrophilic and unidirectional liquid transport properties were retained after 1,000 stretching–release cycles, 4,000 Taber abrasion cycles, and 10 accelerated laundering cycles. The OSJ fabric and the fabrication method provide a promising strategy for developing durable passive cooling fabrics with improved heat and moisture management and resistance to oil fouling.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed an oleophobic, sweat-wicking Janus fabric using hexagonal boron nitride, fluorosurfactant, and PDMS coatings. It reduced artificial-skin temperature by more than 3 °C versus cotton and COOLMAX in outdoor tests, while retaining performance after stretching, abrasion, and laundering.

articles.title_original: First principles investigations of negative differential resistance in edge chlorinated MgO nanoribbons
articles.title_en: Chlorinated MgO nanoribbons show negative differential resistance
articles.excerpt_original: MgO nanoribbons (MgONRs) are analyzed using the first-principles approach utilizing density functional theory (DFT) for potential nanoelectronic applications. Chemically edge-modified MgONRs are investigated for their electrical characteristics. The structural investigations reveal that the nanoribbons are energetically favorable, and chlorination at the edges relatively reduces the energetic favorability of the structures. Bandstructure calculations reveal that the bare MgONRs and chlorine passivated MgONRs are all metallic structures. Further, the two-probe methodology is deployed for the voltage-current ( \(V-I\) ) characteristics. The chlorine passivation is found to significantly enhance the current magnitude, and an interesting negative differential resistance (NDR) phenomenon is noticed in all the chlorine passivated structures. MgONRs having chlorine passivation at the Mg-edge (Cl-MgO-B) have a relatively higher peak-to-valley current ratio (PVCR). The observed results show that the chlorinated MgONRs have potential relevance in future nanoelectronic applications such as switching devices, oscillators, nonlinear electronic circuits, etc.
articles.summary_en: First-principles simulations find that edge-chlorinated magnesium oxide nanoribbons exhibit enhanced current and negative differential resistance. The results indicate potential use in nanoscale switching, oscillators and nonlinear electronic circuits, although they remain theoretical.

articles.title_original: A dynamically stable 2D LiHO wide-band-gap semiconductor: Electronic, optical, and thermal properties from first-principles calculations
articles.title_en: First-principles study identifies stable 2D LiHO semiconductor
articles.summary_en: Researchers theoretically evaluate the electronic, optical, and thermal properties of dynamically stable two-dimensional LiHO, a predicted wide-band-gap semiconductor. The computational findings suggest potential relevance for future semiconductor applications, but experimental validation is not reported.

articles.title_original: Partially Reduced Graphene Oxide‐Maleimides Nanocomposites: Novel Ball‐Mill Synthesis and Characterization
articles.title_en: Ball-Milled Partially Reduced Graphene Oxide–Maleimide Nanocomposites Synthesized
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT This study included the preparation of maleimides by the reaction of anilines with maleic acid to form maleamic acids and then the preparation of maleimides. The prepared organic compounds were characterized using melting point, infrared (FT‐IR), proton nuclear magnetic resonance ( 1 H.NMR), and carbon nuclear magnetic resonance ( 13 C.NMR). Partially reduced graphene oxide sheets were also prepared by grinding coal balls moistened with drops of deionized water, and were used to prepare nanocomposites by the chemical sublimation method with the prepared maleimides in the presence of water. The prepared nanocomposites were characterized by spectroscopic methods such as infrared spectra (FT‐IR), X‐ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (FESEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and surface area (BET).
articles.summary_en: Researchers prepared partially reduced graphene oxide from coal balls through ball milling and combined it with synthesized maleimides to form nanocomposites. The materials were characterized using spectroscopic, structural, microscopy, and surface-area techniques, but no application performance was reported.

articles.title_original: Reconfigurable internal quantum Hall boundaries in graphene visualized by multimodal nanoimaging
articles.title_en: Graphene quantum Hall boundaries reconfigured and imaged in real time
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract Controlling internal boundaries in quantum Hall systems offers a route to engineering reconfigurable topological states. Here, we demonstrate the creation and tunability of incompressible quantum Hall strips separating domains with different sub-Landau level occupations in graphene on high-dielectric SrTiO 3 substrate. This strip constitutes a topological boundary, similar to a quantum Hall edge state, which we manipulate in real space by adjusting the magnetic field and the carrier density. We map the carrier density gradients of graphene using space and time resolved (space-time) terahertz nanoscopy. We also track the location of the incompressible strip with infrared nearfield photocurrent imaging. The high dielectric screening of SrTiO₃ enhances the width of the incompressible region to the micrometer scale, allowing us to directly probe the interplay of charge inhomogeneity, electrostatic screening, and quantum Hall physics across the entire device. These results establish a platform for exploring internal quantum Hall boundaries and suggest their potential utility as dynamically reconfigurable channels for topological charge transport.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated tunable incompressible quantum Hall boundaries in graphene on a high-dielectric SrTiO₃ substrate. Multimodal nanoimaging enabled micrometer-scale visualization, supporting research into dynamically reconfigurable topological charge-transport channels.

articles.title_original: Non-Hermitian tight-binding bands in graphene: optical conductivity, strain effects, and Bernal bilayer extensions
articles.title_en: Modeling Non-Hermitian Graphene Bands and Strain-Tunable Optical Conductivity
articles.excerpt_original: We introduce a geometry‐dependent tight‐binding (TB) model for graphene π ‐electrons—the Tan‐Bo model—in which nearest‐neighbor hopping integrals are parametrized by a Möbius angular factor combined with exponential decay. This construction naturally captures bond‐orientation anisotropy while preserving the gapless Dirac cone at the K point under Hermitian assembly. When the reverse‐bond hopping violates the complex‐conjugation relation, the non‐Hermitian assembly yields complex eigenenergies that diagnose non‐reciprocal band structures rather than quasiparticle lifetimes. Benchmarking against the Slater–Koster scaling demonstrates exact equivalence in the isotropic limit. Under uniaxial strain, a hybrid scheme combining Harrison/Pereira distance scaling with Möbius angular modulation generates tunable real‐band separation and non‐Hermitian imaginary components. Kubo optical conductivity reproduces the universal Dirac plateau, the TB van Hove structure, and strain‐induced σ x x / σ y y dichroism qualitatively consistent with polarized transmittance trends. This work provides a reproducible single-particle benchmark and parametrization reference for future non-Hermitian calculations including correlation effects.
articles.summary_en: Researchers introduce a geometry-dependent tight-binding model for graphene that captures bond anisotropy, non-reciprocal band structures, and strain-induced electronic effects. The model reproduces key optical-conductivity features, including the universal Dirac plateau and strain-induced dichroism, providing a reference for future theoretical studies.

articles.title_original: A Metal Edge Launches Graphene Plasmon from Silicon Waveguide
articles.title_en: Metal Edge Launches Graphene Plasmons from Silicon Waveguide
articles.excerpt_original: Processed simulation results, figure source data, evaluation criteria, and code for the article "A metal edge launches graphene plasmons from a silicon waveguide" (submitted to Plasmonics). The archive contains the processed results of every reported case (launch efficiencies from three readouts, power budgets, and check values), the source data of Figs. 2–5 and Table 1, the evaluation criteria fixed before the simulations, the Ansys Lumerical FDTD/MODE driver scripts (Python, lumapi), the post-processing code, the transfer-matrix mode solver, and the figure scripts. Raw field-monitor files are not included because of their size; they can be regenerated with the scripts or obtained from the author on request. README.md inside the archive describes the layout, software versions, and caveats. Files are under restricted access during peer review and will be made openly available when the article is published. Editors and referees can request access through this record. Data are licensed under CC BY 4.0; code is licensed under the MIT licence (see the LICENSE file in the code folder).
articles.summary_en: An academic study reports simulation data and code evaluating graphene-plasmon launch efficiencies from a silicon waveguide using a metal edge. The supporting archive includes processed results, power budgets, and reproducible electromagnetic modeling scripts, but access is restricted during peer review.

articles.title_original: Advanced design and analysis of MXene-SiC-MXene structure with quadra-cross ring metamaterial broadband solar thermal absorber machine learning-assisted prediction for solar thermal energy harvesting
articles.title_en: MXene–SiC Metamaterial Achieves Broadband Solar-Thermal Absorption
articles.excerpt_original: Broadband metamaterial absorbers are required to maximize absorption throughout the entire band for solar thermal energy harvesting. Additionally, human beings need energy to grow sustainably, and solar energy offers a major solution to this issue. In this study, we designed the broadband metamaterial absorber with the help of the Finite Element Method (FEM) and analyzed the MXene-based Quadra-Cross Ring Metamaterial Solar Absorber (MQCRMSA). A multilayer MQCRMSA consists of MXene in the resonator layer and is grounded with SiC in the substrate layer. This MQCRMSA absorption ranges from 0.2 to 2.2 μm. The quad-lobed cross surrounded by a square loop is highlighted by the MQCRMSA's uniquely shaped resonator. This novel resonator geometry supports broadband absorption and absorbs bandwidths of 460 and 620 nm with above 97% average absorption. To enhance the performance of MQCRMSA, we investigated and compared it with various substrate materials. The MQCRMSA, Transverse Electric (TE) and Magnetic (TM), indicate similar absorption, so polarization-independent features enable MQCRMSA to achieve a maximum absorption of 99.94%. For absorption prediction, Machine Learning (ML) was applied to the MQCRMSA with the help of Locally Weighted Linear Regression (LWLR). This high-performance MQCRMSA may find utilization in solar-thermal energy harvesting systems.
articles.summary_en: Researchers designed and modeled a multilayer MXene–SiC quadra-cross ring metamaterial absorber with absorption spanning 0.2–2.2 μm and up to 99.94% peak absorption. Machine-learning-assisted analysis suggests potential use in solar-thermal energy harvesting, although the study provides no evidence of commercialization.

articles.title_original: Channel-resolved origin of surface-termination-controlled lattice thermal conductivity in Ti2CT2 MXenes
articles.title_en: Surface Termination Controls Thermal Conductivity in Ti2CT2 MXenes
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines how surface termination governs lattice thermal conductivity in Ti2CT2 MXenes. The findings may inform the design of MXene-based materials for thermal management applications.

articles.title_original: High-sensitivity WSe2/Si Schottky photodetectors enabled by bio-nanomaterial assisted dual interfacial engineering
articles.title_en: Bio-Nanomaterial Engineering Enhances WSe2/Si Schottky Photodetectors
articles.summary_en: Researchers report high-sensitivity WSe2/Si Schottky photodetectors using bio-nanomaterial-assisted dual interfacial engineering. The work indicates a research advance in semiconductor photodetector performance, but no commercialization or company involvement is identified.

articles.title_original: Coherent Carrier Transport at the Interface of Water‐in‐Salt and Organic Semiconductor Single Crystals
articles.title_en: Water-in-Salt Electrolytes Enable Coherent Transport in Organic Semiconductor Crystals
articles.excerpt_original: Electric double layers at semiconductor–electrolyte interfaces enable high carrier densities and have been widely used to control electronic and electrochemical functionalities. Exploiting this effect, coherent electronic transport has been demonstrated at the surface of solution‐processed organic semiconductor (OSC) single crystals, highlighting their potential for device applications. However, the achievement of high carrier densities has so far been limited to anhydrous organic ionic liquids, restricting their applicability in abundant water‐based electrochemical systems. In this study, interfaces between aqueous electrolytes and OSC single crystals were investigated to broaden the accessible carrier density range and electronic coherence in electric double layer transistors (EDLTs). By using highly concentrated aqueous solutions containing organic salts, known as water‐in‐salt electrolytes, the sheet conductivity of the OSC single‐crystal channel reached 50 , comparable to that achieved with anhydrous ionic liquids. Furthermore, a metal–insulator transition was suggested in water‐in‐salt EDLTs, demonstrating a degenerate coherent electronic system at the interface between OSC single crystals and aqueous electrolytes. These findings open new possibilities and design strategies for EDLTs that enable advanced functionalities at aqueous electrolyte interfaces.
articles.summary_en: Researchers demonstrated coherent electronic transport at aqueous electrolyte interfaces with organic semiconductor single crystals, achieving sheet conductivity comparable to anhydrous ionic-liquid systems. The results expand electric-double-layer transistor design toward water-based electrochemical devices and suggest a metal–insulator transition.

articles.title_original: Ternary 2D/1D BP/PANi/COF heterojunction with strengthened p-n electric interface for high-performance photocatalytic H2O2 production
articles.title_en: BP/PANi/COF Heterojunction Enhances Photocatalytic H₂O₂ Production
articles.summary_en: Researchers report a ternary 2D/1D black phosphorus, polyaniline and covalent organic framework heterojunction designed to strengthen the p–n interface. The structure targets improved photocatalytic hydrogen peroxide production, but the available record provides no performance metrics or application validation.

articles.title_original: Pseudomagnetic focusing of valley-polarized beams in strained graphene
articles.title_en: Strained Graphene Proposed for Valley-Polarized Current Focusing
articles.excerpt_original: Abstract In addition to spin, the low-energy charge carriers in graphene have two inequivalent valley flavors K and K ′ related by time-reversal symmetry, which can potentially serve as carriers for additional information. One promising route of controlling the valley degree of freedom relies on strain-induced pseudomagnetic fields, which couple with opposite signs to the two valleys. In this work, we theoretically investigate quantum transport in strained graphene devices that host tailored pseudomagnetic field profiles for valley manipulation. We focus on experimentally feasible geometries and propose transverse pseudomagnetic focusing in a bent graphene ribbon as an efficient method for generating valley-polarized currents, even in presence of disorder. Our work highlights pseudomagneto-transport in graphene as a viable tool for valleytronic applications.
articles.summary_en: Theoretical work proposes using tailored strain-induced pseudomagnetic fields in bent graphene ribbons to focus valley-polarized currents. The approach could support valleytronic information processing and is designed to remain effective in the presence of disorder.

articles.title_original: Molecular Engineering of Graphene Nanoribbons for Controlled Electronic Structure and Charge Transport
articles.title_en: Molecularly Engineered Graphene Nanoribbons Enable Tunable Charge Transport
articles.excerpt_original: ABSTRACT Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs), narrow strips of graphene with remarkable electronic characteristics, have emerged as promising candidates for next‐generation nanoelectronic applications. However, their practical implementation is often limited by poor solubility. Here, we employ a highly non‐coplanar arrangement of fused aromatic building blocks to hinder efficient π–π stacking, resulting in soluble, multi‐heteroatom‐doped GNRs. The incorporation and identity of heteroatoms within the backbone allow precise tuning of the electronic and optical properties of the GNRs. In addition, we introduce a donor‐acceptor strategy into the GNR framework while preserving both their graphitic character and solution processability. Mass spectrometric analysis provided evidence for the formation of extended fused aromatic structures. The introduction of a donor‐acceptor strategy reshapes the system's low‐energy steady‐state conductivity, which is precisely captured by terahertz (THz) time‐domain spectroscopy. GNR‐1 exhibits a higher THz‐derived mobility (593.50 ± 53.95 cm 2 V −1 s −1 ) than GNR‐2 (36.69 ± 2.62 cm 2 V −1 s −1 ). This difference reflects the combined influence of their distinct chemical compositions, conjugation frameworks, and electronic band structures, with the calculated effective masses suggesting a major contribution to the contrasting transport responses. These findings highlight the complex interplay between molecular structure and charge‐transport properties in heteroatom‐containing graphene nanoribbons.
articles.summary_en: Researchers developed soluble, heteroatom-doped graphene nanoribbons with tunable electronic and optical properties. Donor–acceptor engineering produced substantially different terahertz mobilities, highlighting potential for solution-processable nanoelectronics.

articles.title_original: Advancing successive progress in the use of conducting polymer-modified 2D MXene-enhanced nanocomposite electrodes for supercapacitors
articles.title_en: Conducting Polymer–MXene Nanocomposite Electrodes for Supercapacitors
articles.summary_en: Academic research examines advances in conducting polymer-modified, MXene-enhanced nanocomposite electrodes for supercapacitors. The work focuses on electrode materials for energy-storage applications.

articles.title_original: Effect of Carbon Template Crystal Quality on the Conversion Behavior of Boron Nitride
articles.title_en: Carbon Template Crystal Quality Influences Boron Nitride Conversion
articles.summary_en: MDPI research examines how the crystal quality of carbon templates affects the conversion behavior of boron nitride. The findings may inform process optimization for boron nitride synthesis, but no specific commercial application is identified.

articles.title_original: Color centers and hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hexagonal boron nitride: A new platform for quantum optics
articles.title_en: hBN Color Centers Enable Quantum Hyperbolic Phonon Polaritons
articles.excerpt_original: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPPs) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) confine mid-infrared light to deep-subwavelength scales and may offer a powerful route to achieve strong light-matter interactions. Generation and control of HPPs are typically accessed using near-field probes driven by strong light fields, which do not allow for exploring the quantum regime. A different frontier in hBN research focuses on color centers: these bright, stable, atomically localized quantum emitters that have rapidly emerged as a promising platform for solid-state quantum optics and quantum sensing. Here we establish a link between these two directions by developing a cavity-QED framework in which a single hBN color center serves as a quantum source of HPPs. We quantify the emitter-HPP interaction and analyze both spontaneous and stimulated Raman scattering into the phonon sideband, generating a single HPP. While both methods result in generation of a quantum state of HPP, stimulation of the Raman scattering by a laser field or an optical cavity mode provides enhanced optical photon to single-frequency HPP conversion. Optical excitation thus launches ray-like propagation of HPPs with a spatial extent ultimately determined by the size of the quantum emitter. Photon antibunching in a two-emitter correlation measurement can directly test the single-polariton character of these emissions.
articles.summary_en: Researchers propose a cavity-QED framework in which a single hexagonal boron nitride color center generates quantum hyperbolic phonon polaritons. The approach could support nanoscale light–matter interactions, single-polariton emission, and quantum sensing, although the work remains academic.

Research remains broad across filtration, thermal management, electronics and metal composites, but repeatedly highlights performance trade-offs, processing sensitivity and limited deployment evidence. Overall, commercialization intent is strengthening, while technical validation and scale details remain uneven.
